[[:db/retract 17592186174160 :answer-field/choices 17592186174161] [:db/retract 17592186174160 :answer-field/choices 17592186174162] [:db/retract 17592186174160 :answer-field/choices 17592186174163] [:db/retract 17592186174160 :answer-field/choices 17592186174164] [:db/retract 17592186174160 :answer-field/choices 17592186174165] {:db/id 17592186176090 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-c75ad058-938d-576a-bc4e-215aa43fed14" "question-f6527ad8-2bed-55da-aea0-3bbb3266c020"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186175716 :question/problem "Evaluate $2^{-3}.$" :question/worked-solution "We find the reciprocal of the base $({\color{blue}{2}}),$ and then raise that reciprocal to the same power but with the *opposite* sign $({{\color{red}{+3}}}),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{2}^{-3} & ={(\frac{1}{2})}^{3} \\  & =(\frac{1}{2})\times (\frac{1}{2})\times (\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =(\frac{1\times 1\times 1}{2\times 2\times 2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186176091 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-52bff138-3308-56fb-8e00-4b3a80e44a0d"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186175717 :question/problem "Calculate the value of $\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)^{-2}.$" :question/worked-solution "We find the reciprocal of the base $\left(\dfrac 1 4\right),$ and then raise that reciprocal to the same power but with the *opposite* sign $(+{\color{blue}2}),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\frac{1}{4})}^{-2} & =(4)^{2} \\  & =4\cdot 4 \\  & =16\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186176092 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-4de46f6f-1e6b-5ab8-947e-dc550a3db276"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186175718 :question/worked-solution "First, we write $\dfrac{1}{49}$ as a base raised to a power:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{49} & =\frac{1\times 1}{7\times 7} \\  & =\frac{1}{7}\times \frac{1}{7} \\  & ={(\frac{1}{7})}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the reciprocal of the base $\left(\dfrac{1}{7}\right),$ and then raise that reciprocal to the same power but with the *opposite* sign $(-2),$ as follows:

$$
\left( \dfrac{1}{7} \right)^2 = 7^{-2}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-c75ad058-938d-576a-bc4e-215aa43fed14" :question/id #uuid "c75ad058-938d-576a-bc4e-215aa43fed14" :question/math-academy-id "q-175985" :question/problem "Expressed as a fraction in its simplest form, ${4}^{-4}=${{field-1}}." :question/worked-solution "We find the reciprocal of the base $(4),$ and then raise that reciprocal to the same power but with the *opposite* sign $(+4),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{4}^{-4} & ={(\frac{1}{4})}^{4} \\  & =(\frac{1}{4})\times (\frac{1}{4})\times (\frac{1}{4})\times (\frac{1}{4}) \\  & =(\frac{1\times 1\times 1\times 1}{4\times 4\times 4\times 4}) \\  & =\frac{1}{256}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-68579504-4350-520d-a0e5-3de9612d9cff"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-68579504-4350-520d-a0e5-3de9612d9cff" :answer-field/id #uuid "68579504-4350-520d-a0e5-3de9612d9cff" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-3006a724-b763-5eca-a3b5-b0cae30c9023" :answer-field/choices ["answer-3006a724-b763-5eca-a3b5-b0cae30c9023"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-3006a724-b763-5eca-a3b5-b0cae30c9023" :answer/id #uuid "3006a724-b763-5eca-a3b5-b0cae30c9023" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{256}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-f6527ad8-2bed-55da-aea0-3bbb3266c020" :question/id #uuid "f6527ad8-2bed-55da-aea0-3bbb3266c020" :question/math-academy-id "q-6197" :question/problem "${4}^{-3}=$" :question/worked-solution "We find the reciprocal of the base $(4),$ and then raise that reciprocal to the same power but with the *opposite* sign $(+3),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\frac{1}{9})}^{-2} & =(9)^{2} \\  & =9\cdot 9 \\  & =81\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186175066 :answer-field/correct 17592186175069 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id 17592186176317 :question/worked-solution "First, we write $\frac{9}{4}$ as a base raised to a power:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{9}{4} & =\frac{3\times 3}{2\times 2} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\times \frac{3}{2} \\  & ={(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the reciprocal of the base $(\frac{3}{2}),$ and then raise that reciprocal to the same power but with the *opposite* sign $(-2),$ as follows:

$$
{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}={(\frac{2}{3})}^{-2}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186174160 :answer-field/correct "answer-7c2fd2a0-35b0-5c42-b70a-f84a88d2104e" :answer-field/choices ["answer-fd7d8a12-8d4e-52c1-ba72-0806b3d500b1" "answer-9ddc2f7c-ba78-53a1-9db1-6d1f0654ddad" "answer-7c2fd2a0-35b0-5c42-b70a-f84a88d2104e" "answer-41f1fafd-d827-531f-8c70-6919b2012ba0" "answer-5c52ccdf-bc66-5508-a679-0e1f1417b58e"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-fd7d8a12-8d4e-52c1-ba72-0806b3d500b1" :answer/id #uuid "fd7d8a12-8d4e-52c1-ba72-0806b3d500b1" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-{(\frac{2}{3})}^{-2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-9ddc2f7c-ba78-53a1-9db1-6d1f0654ddad" :answer/id #uuid "9ddc2f7c-ba78-53a1-9db1-6d1f0654ddad" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-{(\frac{2}{3})}^{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-7c2fd2a0-35b0-5c42-b70a-f84a88d2104e" :answer/id #uuid "7c2fd2a0-35b0-5c42-b70a-f84a88d2104e" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "{(\frac{2}{3})}^{-2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-41f1fafd-d827-531f-8c70-6919b2012ba0" :answer/id #uuid "41f1fafd-d827-531f-8c70-6919b2012ba0" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "{(\frac{2}{3})}^{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-5c52ccdf-bc66-5508-a679-0e1f1417b58e" :answer/id #uuid "5c52ccdf-bc66-5508-a679-0e1f1417b58e" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "{(\frac{3}{2})}^{-2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-4de46f6f-1e6b-5ab8-947e-dc550a3db276" :question/id #uuid "4de46f6f-1e6b-5ab8-947e-dc550a3db276" :question/math-academy-id "q-128737" :question/problem "Express $\frac{36}{25}$ as a base raised to a negative exponent." :question/worked-solution "First, we write $\frac{36}{25}$ as a base raised to a power:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{36}{25} & =\frac{6\times 6}{5\times 5} \\  & =\frac{6}{5}\times \frac{6}{5} \\  & ={(\frac{6}{5})}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the reciprocal of the base $(\frac{6}{5}),$ and then raise that reciprocal to the same power but with the *opposite* sign $(-2),$ as follows:

$$
{(\frac{6}{5})}^{2}={(\frac{5}{6})}^{-2}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-f528d313-aed4-573c-9b07-3ba92a86a40f"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-f528d313-aed4-573c-9b07-3ba92a86a40f" :answer-field/id #uuid "f528d313-aed4-573c-9b07-3ba92a86a40f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-3635da9f-6e9e-5c6c-b0df-8b6493466f48" :answer-field/choices ["answer-c29dd532-663b-5c61-a8e3-572bc60ac813" "answer-2638936c-5b0f-58a4-994e-0d8105ed344e" "answer-3635da9f-6e9e-5c6c-b0df-8b6493466f48" "answer-83290b9d-c95c-5ea2-a4b2-df6ea439c113" "answer-7ce93af7-3222-5d51-a2a5-1849488558cf"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c29dd532-663b-5c61-a8e3-572bc60ac813" :answer/id #uuid "c29dd532-663b-5c61-a8e3-572bc60ac813" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-{(\frac{5}{6})}^{-2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-2638936c-5b0f-58a4-994e-0d8105ed344e" :answer/id #uuid "2638936c-5b0f-58a4-994e-0d8105ed344e" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-{(\frac{6}{5})}^{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-3635da9f-6e9e-5c6c-b0df-8b6493466f48" :answer/id #uuid "3635da9f-6e9e-5c6c-b0df-8b6493466f48" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "{(\frac{5}{6})}^{-2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-83290b9d-c95c-5ea2-a4b2-df6ea439c113" :answer/id #uuid "83290b9d-c95c-5ea2-a4b2-df6ea439c113" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "{(\frac{5}{6})}^{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-7ce93af7-3222-5d51-a2a5-1849488558cf" :answer/id #uuid "7ce93af7-3222-5d51-a2a5-1849488558cf" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "{(\frac{6}{5})}^{-2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186177087 :tutorial/content "We know how to find $2^{-1}.$ But what about $2^{-2}, 2^{-3},2^{-4},\ldots$?

To work out ${\color{blue}{2}}^{{\color{red}{-2}}},$ all we need to do is find the reciprocal of the base $({\color{blue}{2}})$ and then raise that reciprocal to the same power but with the *opposite* sign $({{\color{red}{+2}}})$.

$$
\begin{aligned}{2}^{-2} & ={(\frac{1}{2})}^{2} \\  & =(\frac{1}{2})\times (\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =(\frac{1\times 1}{2\times 2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

A similar approach can be used for other powers. Let's see another example." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186176112 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} [:db/retract 17592186316731 :answer-field/choices 17592186316512] {:db/id 17592186166960 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-ac1dfb2b-dc39-5a8f-bb78-6916e280fb3b" "question-967d4b0f-c5b8-576b-b414-bb183f8a1110"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186167292 :question/problem "$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}, & x\in [-3,0] \\ -{x}^{2}, & x\in (0,3)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the function $F(x)$ shown above. Find the value to which the Fourier series of the $6$-periodic extension $f(x)$ of $F(x)$ is converging when $x=2.$

The Fourier series converges to {{field-1}} when $x=2.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-ac1dfb2b-dc39-5a8f-bb78-6916e280fb3b" :question/id #uuid "ac1dfb2b-dc39-5a8f-bb78-6916e280fb3b" :question/math-academy-id "q-343361" :question/problem "$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}-2, & x\in [-3,0) \\ x+1, & x\in [0,3)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the function $F(x)$ shown above. Find the value to which the Fourier series of the $6$-periodic extension $f(x)$ of $F(x)$ converges when $x=-3.$

The Fourier series converges to {{field-1}} when $x=-3.$" :question/worked-solution "Suppose that $f(x)$ is a $2L$-periodic piecewise smooth function with the corresponding Fourier series

$$
S(x)=\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{L}x).
$$

Then, the series converges for all $x\in R.$

- If $f(x)$ is continuous at $x,$ then the series converges to the value of the function at this point:

$$
S(x)=f(x)
$$

- If $f(x)$ has a jump discontinuity at $x,$ then the series converges to the midpoint between the values of left- and right-sided limits of the function at this point:

$$
S(x)=\frac{{f}^{-}(x)+{f}^{+}(x)}{2}
$$

where ${f}^{-}(x)$ and ${f}^{+}(x)$ are the left- and right-sided limits of the function at this point, respectively.

Notice that the $6$-periodic extension $f(x)$ of our function $F(x)$ is not continuous at $x=-3.$ The one-sided limits at this point are the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{-}(-3) & ={lim}_{x\to -{3}^{-}}f(x)=4 \\ {f}^{+}(-3) & ={lim}_{x\to -{3}^{+}}f(x)=-2\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, the Fourier series of $f(x)$ converges to 

$$
\frac{{f}^{-}(-3)+{f}^{+}(-3)}{2}=\frac{4+(-2)}{2}=1.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-8e653195-c3d5-582e-822a-b0c443f4aade"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-8e653195-c3d5-582e-822a-b0c443f4aade" :answer-field/id #uuid "8e653195-c3d5-582e-822a-b0c443f4aade" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-857250c9-a9b1-5080-b2c5-1728296672ed" :answer-field/choices ["answer-857250c9-a9b1-5080-b2c5-1728296672ed"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-857250c9-a9b1-5080-b2c5-1728296672ed" :answer/id #uuid "857250c9-a9b1-5080-b2c5-1728296672ed" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-967d4b0f-c5b8-576b-b414-bb183f8a1110" :question/id #uuid "967d4b0f-c5b8-576b-b414-bb183f8a1110" :question/math-academy-id "q-343368" :question/problem "$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}-3, & x\in [-\frac{\pi }{2},0) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡x, & x\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the function $F(x)$ shown above. Find the value to which the Fourier series of the $\pi $-periodic extension $f(x)$ of $F(x)$ converges when $x=\frac{\pi }{2}.$

The Fourier series converges to {{field-1}} when $x=\frac{\pi }{2}.$" :question/worked-solution "Suppose that $f(x)$ is a $2L$-periodic piecewise smooth function with the corresponding Fourier series

$$
S(x)=\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{L}x).
$$

Then, the series converges for all $x\in R.$

- If $f(x)$ is continuous at $x,$ then the series converges to the value of the function at this point:

$$
S(x)=f(x)
$$

- If $f(x)$ has a jump discontinuity at $x,$ then the series converges to the midpoint between the values of left- and right-sided limits of the function at this point:

$$
S(x)=\frac{{f}^{-}(x)+{f}^{+}(x)}{2}
$$

where ${f}^{-}(x)$ and ${f}^{+}(x)$ are the left- and right-sided limits of the function at this point, respectively.

Notice that the $\pi $-periodic extension $f(x)$ of our function $F(x)$ is not continuous at $x=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ The one-sided limits at this point are the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{-}\,(\frac{\pi }{2}) & ={lim}_{x\to (\pi /2)^{-}}f(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})=0 \\ {f}^{+}\,(\frac{\pi }{2}) & ={lim}_{x\to (\pi /2)^{+}}f(x)=-3\end{aligned}

Therefore, the Fourier series of $f(x)$ converges to 

$$

$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-539ad74a-5113-59bb-99ce-f5b195bb6b58"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-539ad74a-5113-59bb-99ce-f5b195bb6b58" :answer-field/id #uuid "539ad74a-5113-59bb-99ce-f5b195bb6b58" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-752a3ed9-4c29-5165-ac74-445a7667e23c" :answer-field/choices ["answer-752a3ed9-4c29-5165-ac74-445a7667e23c"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-752a3ed9-4c29-5165-ac74-445a7667e23c" :answer/id #uuid "752a3ed9-4c29-5165-ac74-445a7667e23c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-\frac{3}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186375037 :question/problem "Consider the function $F(x)=|\operatorname{sin}⁡x|$ defined on $x\in [-\pi ,\pi ).$ The Fourier series of the $2\pi $-periodic extension $f(x)$ of $F(x)$ is given by

For example, consider two vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ shown below. Suppose we know that $|\,\mathbf{a}\,|=2$ and that the angle between the vectors is $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{4}.$

![](images/a2/a28278cf12885ab7f845407ac2fa7f4ffa00dbe30849a3f8ff41f02e134ed3a0.png)

To illustrate the projection of $\mathbf{a}$ along $\mathbf{b},$ consider the point $P$ on the line that contains $\mathbf{b}$ with $AP \perp \mathbf{b},$ as shown below.

![](images/fd/fd37bdb2a97b4125fb360990d3c4a36b48bcb50433de033a154799db00e474dd.png)

The length $OP$ is called the **scalar projection** of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}$ (or the **component** of $\mathbf{a}$ along $\mathbf{b}$). It is denoted as $\text{comp}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a},$ and we can compute it using cosine in $\triangle OPA$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{b}\,a & =OP \\  & =|\,a\,|\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =2\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

This formula is the general definition of the scalar projection:

$$
\text{comp}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a}= |\,\mathbf{a}\,| \cos\theta
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186107177 :tutorial/content "The scalar projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}$ can be negative. This happens when the vector $\mathbf{a}$ extends in the direction opposite to that of $\mathbf{b}.$

![](images/c1/c19648ea2df1935e89e10df2f7f5ab33ad537a5fdb52bb97c3555c9a0365701e.png)

For example, consider two vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b},$ where it is known that 

$$
|\,\mathbf{a}\,|=2, \qquad \theta = 135^\circ.
$$

Notice that the angle $\theta$ between the vectors is obtuse. 

Computing the scalar projection of $\mathbf a$ onto $\mathbf b$ using the formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{b}\,a & =|\,a\,|\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡({135}^{∘}) \\  & =2\cdot (-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) \\  & =-\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

In general, if $90^\circ < \theta \leq 180^\circ,$ then $\cos\theta <0$ and the scalar projection will be negative." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186107175 :tutorial/content "We have been using the following formula for the scalar projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\text{comp}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a}= |\,\mathbf{a}\,| \cos\theta
$$

However, sometimes we are not given the angle between two vectors. In such cases, we can solve for $\cos \theta$ in terms of the dot product:

$$
\begin{aligned}a\cdot b & =|\,a\,|\,|\,b\,|\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{a\cdot b}{|\,a\,|\,|\,b\,|}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into our original formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{b}\,a & =|\,a\,|\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =|\,a\,|\cdot \frac{a\cdot b}{|\,a\,|\,|\,b\,|} \\  & =\frac{a\cdot b}{|\,b\,|}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, another general formula for the scalar projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{b}\,a & =\frac{a\cdot b}{|\,b\,|}.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186105962 :activity/expected-seconds 720.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186064341 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-4f002498-444e-5f1e-b174-d456ccc0407b"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-4f002498-444e-5f1e-b174-d456ccc0407b" :question/id #uuid "4f002498-444e-5f1e-b174-d456ccc0407b" :question/math-academy-id "q-133261" :question/problem "Expressed as a polynomial in terms of $x,$ the length of Fred's plot of land is{{field-1}}
meters." :question/worked-solution "The width of the plot is $x+3$ meters, and its area is $2{x}^{2}+6x$ square meters. Since the $\text{area}=\text{length}\times \text{width},$ we factor the expression for the area to find the length.

First, we find the $\text{GCF}$ of the two terms:

$$
\text{GCF}(2{x}^{2},6x)=2x
$$

Then, we rewrite each term in the original expression as a product with the $\text{GCF}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}+6x & = \\ (2x\cdot x)+(2x\cdot 3)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we write the $\text{GCF}$ outside the parentheses and keep the remaining terms inside:

$$
\begin{aligned}(2x\cdot x)+(2x\cdot 3) & = \\ 2x(x+3)\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we conclude that the length of the plot must be $2x$ meters.

meters." :question/worked-solution "To find the required width, we need to factor the expression ${x}^{2}+3x-10.$

First, we find the factor pairs of the constant term $(-10).$ The constant term is negative, so that means one of the factors is negative, and the other is positive:

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & \times (-10) \\ (-1) & \times 10 \\ 2 & \times (-5) \\ (-2) & \times 5\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find which factor pair adds up to the coefficient of the linear term $3:$

$$
\begin{aligned}1+(-10) & =-9 & \times  \\ -1+10 & =9 & \times  \\ 2+(-5) & =-3 & \times  \\ -2+5 & =3 & ✓\end{aligned}
$$

Using the factor pair identified above, write the linear term as $3x=5x-2x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+3x-10 & ={x}^{2}+5x-2x-10\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we factor the first two terms and the last two terms separately, and then factor the expression completely:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+5x-2x-10 & = \\ ({x}^{2}+5x)+(-2x-10) & = \\ x(x+5)-2(x+5) & = \\ (x-2)(x+5)\end{aligned}

B=\{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\},\,[T]_{B|C}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 8 & 1 \\ 7 & 9\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -6\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the basis $B$ of ${R}^{2}$ (shown above) and a basis $C$ of ${R}^{3}.$
The matrix $[T]_{B|C}$ of the linear map $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{3}$ relative to these bases, and the vector $x\in {R}^{2},$ are also given. Find $[T(x)]_{C}.$" :question/worked-solution "We can find the coordinates of the image of $x$ under $T$ relative to the basis $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[T(x)]_{C} & =[T]_{B|C}\cdot [x]_{B}\end{aligned}
$$

First, we need to find $[x]_{B},$ the coordinates of $x$ relative to $B.$ So, let

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -6\end{aligned}]={x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

This gives us the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=1 \\ -3{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}=-6.\end{aligned}
$$

We now row-reduce the corresponding augmented matrix using Gaussian elimination, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 \\ -3 & 3 & -6\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 3 & -3\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $[x]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].$

Finally, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}[T(x)]_{C} & =[T]_{B|C}\cdot [x]_{B} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 8 & 1 \\ 7 & 9\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 7 \\ -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-ce679d09-ac04-52d4-b77b-07e1721ea8d2"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186125799 :tutorial/content "Let's suppose we have the linear map

$$

$$

$$

then

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t)={e}^{t}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,{T}^{′}(t)=-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "Since we are given both the derivative of the curve ${r}^{′}(t)$ and the derivative of the unit tangent ${T}^{′}(t),$ we will use the following formula for the curvature:

$$
κ(t)=\frac{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}
$$

Now, we find the magnitudes of ${T}^{′}(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{T}^{′}(t)‖ & =|-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}|\sqrt{(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\sqrt{({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)+({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)+(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\sqrt{1+1+0} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\cdot \sqrt{2} \\  & =1 \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & ={e}^{t}\sqrt{(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & ={e}^{t}\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t} \\  & ={e}^{t}\sqrt{({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)+({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)+(-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t)} \\  & ={e}^{t}\sqrt{1+1+0} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\,{e}^{t}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the curvature is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}\,{e}^{t}}=\frac{\sqrt{2}\,{e}^{-t}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-fbef7b1b-2a5f-5dce-929c-f5b8a633c936"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id To do this, we sometimes need to factor the numerator and denominator before canceling.

For example, suppose that we wish to simplify $\dfrac {4x - 12} {10x + 4}.$ To do this, we factor the numerator and denominator and cancel any factors that they have in common.

$$
\eqalign{
		\dfrac {4x - 12} {10x + 4}
		&=\dfrac {4(x - 3)} {2(5x + 2)}\[5pt]
&=\dfrac {2 \cdot 2 \cdot (x - 3)} {2(5x + 2)}\[5pt]		
		&=\dfrac {\cancel{2} \cdot 2(x - 3)} {\cancel{2}(5x + 2)}\[5pt]	
		&=\dfrac {2(x - 3)} {5x + 2}
	}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186068956 :activity/expected-seconds 540.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} [:db/retract 17592186174094 :answer-field/choices 17592186174096] [:db/retract 17592186174094 :answer-field/choices 17592186174097] [:db/retract 17592186174094 :answer-field/choices 17592186174098] [:db/retract 17592186174094 :answer-field/choices 17592186174095] [:db/retract 17592186174592 :answer-field/choices 17592186174593] [:db/retract 17592186174592 :answer-field/choices 17592186174594] [:db/retract 17592186174592 :answer-field/choices 17592186174595] [:db/retract 17592186174592 :answer-field/choices 17592186174596] [:db/retract 17592186174592 :answer-field/choices 17592186174597] {:db/id 17592186176021 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-2304365e-e658-571a-a752-03df743e6d8e" "question-548860d7-a3cd-5a87-9ba4-81882cafa76b" "question-99513b0e-90cb-593a-b1cd-0a535510b802" "question-da1f1140-0b6f-5e8e-98c1-c5bc7c260a47"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186176020 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-990eaa9e-cd8b-5349-b27e-24596fc286e8" "question-21fb3dfd-c1e0-5974-85b5-71a08b2e3884" "question-5c2c81b1-ac73-5714-9490-1d6081f1f637"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186175957 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-780f42b2-e05c-5d59-ba5e-7cf6b84ac19f" "question-a97fa6ce-6558-5992-afd2-fa81f89839cb"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-2304365e-e658-571a-a752-03df743e6d8e" :question/id #uuid "2304365e-e658-571a-a752-03df743e6d8e" :question/math-academy-id "q-118578" :question/problem "Given that $y=y(t),$ what is the carrying capacity of the following logistic growth model?

$$
P=\frac{1}{2}a=\frac{1}{2}\cdot 4\,000=2\,000.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-963b2bae-6d0b-579e-ad6a-b3bc97461b9d"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-963b2bae-6d0b-579e-ad6a-b3bc97461b9d" :answer-field/id #uuid "963b2bae-6d0b-579e-ad6a-b3bc97461b9d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-191a8fdb-4cf1-52b9-b39d-877ed2bfcf4d" :answer-field/choices ["answer-786cef4c-88dd-5537-bc9a-2d9fbba7feed" "answer-7075748d-27ae-566a-8e0a-bfe33ec489f3" "answer-191a8fdb-4cf1-52b9-b39d-877ed2bfcf4d" "answer-226ece79-c20c-52a6-9ef4-69ce428c1b6d" "answer-1fe55633-1a01-5334-8af1-1c9155c4685b"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-786cef4c-88dd-5537-bc9a-2d9fbba7feed" :answer/id #uuid "786cef4c-88dd-5537-bc9a-2d9fbba7feed" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "1\,000" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-7075748d-27ae-566a-8e0a-bfe33ec489f3" :answer/id #uuid "7075748d-27ae-566a-8e0a-bfe33ec489f3" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "1\,500" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-191a8fdb-4cf1-52b9-b39d-877ed2bfcf4d" :answer/id #uuid "191a8fdb-4cf1-52b9-b39d-877ed2bfcf4d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2\,000" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-226ece79-c20c-52a6-9ef4-69ce428c1b6d" :answer/id #uuid "226ece79-c20c-52a6-9ef4-69ce428c1b6d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "500" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1fe55633-1a01-5334-8af1-1c9155c4685b" :answer/id #uuid "1fe55633-1a01-5334-8af1-1c9155c4685b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "900" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186176389 :question/problem "The population $P(t)$ of squirrels in a certain forest follows the logistic growth model

$$
\frac{dP}{dt}=0.000\,5P(6\,000-P),\,P(0)=1\,000
$$

where $t$ is the time, measured in years. For which value of $P$ is the squirrel population growing at the fastest possible rate?" :question/worked-solution "A logistic growth equation has the form

$$
{P}^{′}=kP(a-P),
$$

where $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality, and $a>P$ is the carrying capacity.

For a logistic growth model, the fastest rate of growth occurs when $P=\frac{1}{2}a.$

![](images/9d/9d8f5340bba4d3c407e43f2bc64a4aa2ea986be89b8024baaa4e8ae65e96e5d5.png)

From our equation, we see that $a=6\,000.$ Hence, the carrying capacity is $6\,000,$ and $P$ grows at its fastest possible rate when 

$$
P=\frac{1}{2}a=\frac{1}{2}\cdot 6\,000=3\,000.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186174592 :answer-field/correct "answer-0594f223-200c-542c-be81-07e72759ac03" :answer-field/choices ["answer-0b70aa2b-729a-5da7-a35a-50ae0199754c" "answer-4341d8a3-0f2b-5ec4-84db-379db13471bb" "answer-cbb22c01-113f-5dc7-bea5-a610d7aec30d" "answer-0594f223-200c-542c-be81-07e72759ac03" "answer-f3c01786-caa1-5695-9de3-f30704bb60b6"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-0b70aa2b-729a-5da7-a35a-50ae0199754c" :answer/id #uuid "0b70aa2b-729a-5da7-a35a-50ae0199754c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "1\,000" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4341d8a3-0f2b-5ec4-84db-379db13471bb" :answer/id #uuid "4341d8a3-0f2b-5ec4-84db-379db13471bb" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "1\,500" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-cbb22c01-113f-5dc7-bea5-a610d7aec30d" :answer/id #uuid "cbb22c01-113f-5dc7-bea5-a610d7aec30d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2\,000" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-0594f223-200c-542c-be81-07e72759ac03" :answer/id #uuid "0594f223-200c-542c-be81-07e72759ac03" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "3\,000" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-f3c01786-caa1-5695-9de3-f30704bb60b6" :answer/id #uuid "f3c01786-caa1-5695-9de3-f30704bb60b6" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4\,800" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186177034 :tutorial/content "Let's go back to the following logistic growth equation:

$$
y' = 5y(10-y), \qquad y(0) = y_0.
$$

The logistic growth curve for this problem is sketched below.

![](images/0a/0a225fd04f81bd65e1bad3ff14097563d112a16e3847aac26cc86591533ea5d0.png)

The curve contains an inflection point, that is, a point where $y(t)$ is growing at its fastest possible rate. What information can we deduce about this point? 

To find the inflection point, we solve $y''(t) = 0.$ First, we differentiate the differential equation using implicit differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{″} & =(5y)^{′}\cdot (10-y)+(5y)\cdot (10-y)^{′} \\  & =5\cdot (10-y)\cdot {y}^{′}+(5y)\cdot (-1)\cdot {y}^{′} \\  & ={y}^{′}\cdot (5\cdot (10-y)+(5y)\cdot (-1)) \\  & ={y}^{′}\cdot (50-5y-5y) \\  & ={y}^{′}\cdot (50-10y)\end{aligned}
$$

We now need to solve $y''(t) = 0,$ i.e.,

$$
y'\cdot\left(50-10y\right) = 0.
$$

We know that $y'$ is increasing for all $t,$ so $y'\neq 0.$ Therefore, we must have

$$
50-10y = 0\quad \Rightarrow\quad y = 5.
$$

Let's mark this on our diagram.

![](images/75/75d0363483e1bda70decb171466fe9e506eb0da80d0e78ed893bb61551ae9d44.png)

The fact that the inflection point occurs when $y$ is precisely half the carrying capacity is *not* a coincidence. In fact, this is always the case. The general situation is shown below.

![](images/77/7754f42adbb938c1d07ab2636a4c24f1cd0bc8536c974af2497e997589efa115.png)" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186176102 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186105701 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-b6749b1c-5bbb-5e2e-a55f-6596daa98287"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186105702 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-c61c8891-41ce-5169-9fd8-85b0f9123364"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186105703 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-1d98c763-a05e-5de6-913c-903735959780"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186106111 :question/problem "Suppose that $|\,a\,|=8$, $|\,b\,|=2$ and that the angle between the vectors is $\theta ={120}^{∘}.$ Find the vector projection of $a$ onto $b$ in terms of the vector $b.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the scalar projection as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{b}\,a & =|\,a\,|\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =8\operatorname{cos}⁡({120}^{∘}) \\  & =8\cdot (-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the unit vector that is parallel to $b:$

$$
u=\frac{b}{|\,b\,|}=\frac{b}{2}=\frac{1}{2}b
$$

Finally, we compute the vector projection as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,a & ={\text{comp}}_{b}\,a\cdot u \\  & =(-4)\cdot \frac{1}{2}b \\  & =-2b\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186102542 :answer-field/correct 17592186102547 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "question-b6749b1c-5bbb-5e2e-a55f-6596daa98287" :question/id #uuid "b6749b1c-5bbb-5e2e-a55f-6596daa98287" :question/math-academy-id "q-126505" :question/problem "Suppose that $|\,p\,|=3$, $|\,q\,|=6\sqrt{2}$ and that the angle between the vectors is $\theta =\frac{3\pi }{4}.$ Find the vector projection of $q$ onto $p$ in terms of the vector $p.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the scalar projection as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{p}\,q & =|\,q\,|\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =6\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{4}) \\  & =6\sqrt{2}\cdot (-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) \\  & =-6\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the unit vector that is parallel to $p:$

$$
u=\frac{p}{|\,p\,|}=\frac{p}{3}=\frac{1}{3}p
$$

Finally, we compute the vector projection as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{p}\,q & ={\text{comp}}_{p}\,q\cdot u \\  & =-6\cdot \frac{1}{3}p \\  & =-2p\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-c9c3dd9f-ab18-5360-9b3b-eadcd53e98f0"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id Find the vector projection of $q$ onto $p.$" :question/worked-solution "Using the formula for the vector projection, we obtain

"question-1d98c763-a05e-5de6-913c-903735959780" :question/id #uuid "1d98c763-a05e-5de6-913c-903735959780" :question/math-academy-id "q-212460" :question/problem "Let $a=⟨1,2,-1⟩$ and $b=⟨1,x,2⟩.$ Given that the projection of $a$ onto $b$ is the zero vector, find the value of $x.$" :question/worked-solution "Since $a$ is a nonzero vector, its projection onto another nonzero vector $b$ equals the zero vector only when the vectors are perpendicular. 

So, we must have

$$
a⊥b\,⟹\,a\cdot b=0.
$$

Computing the dot product, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}a\cdot b & ={a}_{x}\cdot {b}_{x}+{a}_{y}\cdot {b}_{y}+{a}_{z}\cdot {b}_{z} \\  & =1\cdot 1+2\cdot x+(-1)\cdot 2 \\  & =2x-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting the dot product equal to $0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}a\cdot b & =0 \\ 2x-1 & =0 \\ 2x & =1 \\ x & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-0dfe0b7a-7e87-551d-9c63-3d3fbe0f0ee6"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-0dfe0b7a-7e87-551d-9c63-3d3fbe0f0ee6" :answer-field/id #uuid "0dfe0b7a-7e87-551d-9c63-3d3fbe0f0ee6" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-f6da670c-ad73-58eb-88ec-c72e37de6415" :answer-field/choices ["answer-b1c88e84-5bca-52a5-9ff2-25a12a68f03e" "answer-007ca704-665c-5469-bb92-8fe895a8eacd" "answer-f6da670c-ad73-58eb-88ec-c72e37de6415" "answer-09f61461-dd48-5041-ae4c-43a710a4eb72" "answer-9228ca5d-afce-5b10-b57e-7850fc591002"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b1c88e84-5bca-52a5-9ff2-25a12a68f03e" :answer/id #uuid "b1c88e84-5bca-52a5-9ff2-25a12a68f03e" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-\frac{1}{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-007ca704-665c-5469-bb92-8fe895a8eacd" :answer/id #uuid "007ca704-665c-5469-bb92-8fe895a8eacd" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-\frac{2}{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-f6da670c-ad73-58eb-88ec-c72e37de6415" :answer/id #uuid "f6da670c-ad73-58eb-88ec-c72e37de6415" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-09f61461-dd48-5041-ae4c-43a710a4eb72" :answer/id #uuid "09f61461-dd48-5041-ae4c-43a710a4eb72" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{5}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-9228ca5d-afce-5b10-b57e-7850fc591002" :answer/id #uuid "9228ca5d-afce-5b10-b57e-7850fc591002" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{3}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186059871 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-2ab44a05-012f-5af3-a42d-e6d922b9a66c" "question-353b78e0-100e-5425-97b3-923c0bd8ad1a"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186059422 :question/worked-solution "First, we write

$$
5(5^2) = 5^1 \times 5^2.
$$

So our expression can be written as

$$
5^1 \times 5^2 \times 5^4
$$

To multiply powers of the same base, we simply add the exponents:

$$
5^1 \times 5^2 \times 5^4 = 5^{1+2+4} = 5^7
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186059872 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-fa0bbd4b-06ea-5732-8998-73cc5cb59649" "question-a0176d28-d1e2-593d-8b48-e87cdf5d129a"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186059423 :question/worked-solution "To multiply powers of the same base, we add the exponents:

$$
\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^2\times \left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^2 =  \left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^{2+2} =  \left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^4
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186059873 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-0c468631-3494-5a5c-8263-59a9e6ef38aa" "question-9f94c748-cc3f-548a-899d-563289a823a1"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186059424 :question/problem "Evaluate $2^2\times 2^{-5}.$" :question/worked-solution "To multiply powers of the same base, we add the exponents:

$$
2^2\times 2^{-5} =2^{2+(-5)} = 2^{-3}
$$

To evaluate $2^{-3},$ we find the reciprocal of the base $(2)$ and then raise that reciprocal to the same power but with the opposite sign:

$$
2^{-3}  = \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^3 =\dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{1}{8}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-2ab44a05-012f-5af3-a42d-e6d922b9a66c" :question/id #uuid "2ab44a05-012f-5af3-a42d-e6d922b9a66c" :question/math-academy-id "q-68262" :question/problem "${3}^{4}\times {3}^{5}=$" :question/worked-solution "To multiply powers of the same base, we simply add the exponents:

simplest form, ${9}^{-5}\times {9}^{3}=${{field-1}}." :question/worked-solution "To multiply powers of the same base, we add the exponents:

This is called the **product rule for exponents**.
For example, in the expression 

$$
{\color{blue}3}^4 \times {\color{blue}3}^2,
$$

both powers have the same base $({\color{blue}3}).$ Therefore, we can simplify this expression by adding the exponents:

$$
{\color{blue}3}^4 \times {\color{blue}3}^2 = {\color{blue}3}^{4+2} = {\color{blue}3}^6
$$

**Note:** The product rule for exponents is really just a quicker alternative to using repeated multiplication, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{3}^{4}\times {3}^{2} & = \\ {{3\times 3\times 3\times 3}_{⏟}}_{4\text{ copies}}\times {{3\times 3}_{⏟}}_{2\text{ copies}} & = \\ {{3\times 3\times 3\times 3\times 3\times 3}_{⏟}}_{6\text{ copies}} & = \\ {3}^{6}\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186060990 :tutorial/content "We can use the product rule for exponents with negative exponents too. For instance, to simplify $3^3\times 3^{-5},$ we add the exponents:

$$
3^{3} \times 3^{-5} = 3^{3-5} = 3^{-2}
$$

Now, to evaluate $3^{-2},$ we find the reciprocal of the base $(3)$ and then raise that reciprocal to the same power but with the opposite sign:

$$
3^{-2}  = \left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^2 =\dfrac{1}{3} \times \dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{1}{9}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186059942 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186054606 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-60199b98-6c64-506f-9047-6445f428ee81"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186054396 :question/worked-solution "To evaluate this expression, we use PEMDAS. $$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186054607 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-d7d9db10-3db0-5298-a1d1-4ea150f26c84" "question-43b02df2-3069-56a3-b787-8172b48fa9f2"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186054397 :question/problem "Evaluate $(1-4)^2 \times \dfrac{1}{12}.$" :question/worked-solution "To evaluate this expression, we use PEMDAS. $$

$$

The same rules apply to numerical expressions with negative numbers. For example, let's compute the value of

$$
(-2) \times (-3)^2.
$$

To evaluate this expression, we use PEMDAS.  First, we compute the exponents:

$$
(-2)\,\times\overbrace{(-3)^2}^{\large\color{blue} 9}  = (-2) \times {\color{blue} 9}
$$

 

Then, we multiply:

$$
(-2) \times 9 = -18
$$

Therefore,

$$
(-2) \times (-3)^2 = -18.
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186054876 :activity/expected-seconds 480.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186133783 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-7284284d-f752-5dcb-a337-d7dc9bc05a72" "question-b0f53959-2e0a-59dc-bd59-359975a06abd" "question-f8dca397-728c-5f8d-9e9c-d3de23f707a0"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186133592 :question/problem "Let ![](images/25/2501c175aa25fd5d70af201c3bd0788da58b674c5782984e06a089a4447299a1.svg) and ![](images/f4/f455effab674ae3ee3a0c2b0773c011735f3d3885a1c392b0233b7c5d164ee9b.svg) Find the orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\text{Span}\{\mathbf{b}\}.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186133593 :question/problem "Let ![](images/47/479dd80d441e3da4c3f2c20a18dd124f061f47cc2ab421a1499003a70caf3465.svg) and ![](images/1f/1f190dbb10618181ed258e192d8e005947a1d38aaaf5d6e63e162ad4f399e302.svg) If $\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{y} + \mathbf{z},$ where $\mathbf{y} \in \text{Span}\{\mathbf{a}\}$ and $\mathbf{z} \perp \text{Span}\{\mathbf{a}\},$ then find $\mathbf{z}.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186133785 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-b5c59f3b-4545-527f-bcce-f690660ef3e4" "question-4cd83f2a-cc48-509b-8020-7c5ca2609e27"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186133594 :question/problem "Given the vector $\mathbf{x}$ and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of $\mathbf{x}$ onto the solution space of the system.
![](images/d0/d05e5b4f3ebf3be3a1f4d5d0b25c015adbbcd57435bcca574de9f84779694e28.svg)" :question/worked-solution "First, we need to find the basis of the solution space of the system. 

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:    

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 4 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are $2$ pivot columns ($1$st and $2$nd). Thus, $x_3$ is a free variable. Now, from the second equation, we get $x_2=4x_3.$ 
Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain  

$$
x_1+4x_3+4x_3= 0
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
x_1=-8x_3.
$$

So, the general solution is
![](images/4b/4b13b3d4dbb889a07cece9dde6f9caf69d09b4eed2dc23e77407b9b5697775a6.svg)
Consequently, ![](images/ff/ff7ca7de3065a85bdf61586cf2a021acca8b62ac7eb2f8ec5d73f0291074ebd8.svg) is a basis of the solution space of the system.

Finally, we find the projection of $\mathbf{x}$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot b}{b\cdot b}b \\  & =\frac{(-10)\cdot (-8)+20\cdot 4+2\cdot 1}{{(-8)}^{2}+{4}^{2}+{1}^{2}}b \\  & =\frac{80+80+2}{64+16+1}b \\  & =\frac{162}{81}b \\  & =2b \\  & =2[\begin{aligned}-8 \\ 4 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-16 \\ 8 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-7284284d-f752-5dcb-a337-d7dc9bc05a72" :question/id #uuid "7284284d-f752-5dcb-a337-d7dc9bc05a72" :question/math-academy-id "q-81403" :question/problem "Let $a=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ and $b=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Find the orthogonal projection of $a$ onto $\text{Span}\{b\}.$" :question/worked-solution "The orthogonal projection of $a$ onto $\text{Span}\{b\}$ is given by

$$

$$

"Given the vector $x$ and the system of  linear equations below, find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system.

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -2\end{aligned}],\,\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}=0 \\ -2{x}_{1}+6{x}_{2}=0\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we need to find a basis of the solution space of the system. 

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 0 \\ -2 & 6 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is $1$ pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}=3{x}_{2}.$ So, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}3{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]={x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Consequently, $B=\{[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\}$ is a basis of the solution space of the system.

Finally, we find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot b}{b\cdot b}b \\  & =\frac{4\cdot 3+(-2)\cdot 1}{{3}^{2}+{1}^{2}}b \\  & =\frac{10}{10}b \\  & =b \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-4cd83f2a-cc48-509b-8020-7c5ca2609e27" :question/id #uuid "4cd83f2a-cc48-509b-8020-7c5ca2609e27" :question/math-academy-id "q-86745" :question/problem "Given the vector $x$ and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system.

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ -2\end{aligned}],\,\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=0 \\ -{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=0\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we need to find a basis of the solution space of the system. 

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is $1$ pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}.$ So, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]={x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Consequently, $B=\{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\}$ is a basis of the solution space of the system.

Finally, we find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot b}{b\cdot b}b \\  & =\frac{(-4)\cdot 1+(-2)\cdot 1}{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}b \\  & =\frac{-6\,}{\,\,2\,}b \\  & =-3b \\  & =-3[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-f7164e41-9f76-56e4-a6df-6aa236623be7"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "Given the vector $x$ and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system.

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}-10 \\ -15 \\ 28\end{aligned}],\,\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}=0 \\ 2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}-3{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we need to find a basis of the solution space of the system. 

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & -3 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & -3 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are $2$ pivot columns ($1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. Now, from the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}=\frac{3}{5}{x}_{3}.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
{x}_{1}-2(\frac{3}{5}{x}_{3})=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=\frac{6}{5}{x}_{3}.
$$

So, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{6}{5}{x}_{3} \\ \frac{3}{5}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{5}{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 3 \\ 5\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Consequently, $B=\{[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 3 \\ 5\end{aligned}]\}$ is a basis of the solution space of the system.

Finally, we find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot b}{b\cdot b}b \\  & =\frac{(-10)\cdot 6+(-15)\cdot 3+28\cdot 5}{{6}^{2}+{3}^{2}+{5}^{2}}b \\  & =\frac{-60-45+140}{36+9+25}b \\  & =\frac{35}{70}b \\  & =\frac{1}{2}b \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 3 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ \frac{3}{2} \\ \frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186394133 :question/problem "Given the vector $x$ and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system.

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3 \\ 7\end{aligned}],\,\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=0 \\ 2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we need to find a basis of the solution space of the system. 

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are $2$ pivot columns ($1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. Now, from the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}={x}_{3}.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
{x}_{1}+{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=-{x}_{3}.
$$

So, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Consequently, $B=\{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\}$ is a basis of the solution space of the system.

Finally, we find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot b}{b\cdot b}b \\  & =\frac{(-2)\cdot (-1)+3\cdot 1+7\cdot 1}{(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}b \\  & =\frac{12}{3}b \\  & =4b \\  & =4[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 4 \\ 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186135046 :tutorial/content "The **orthogonal projection** of a vector $\mathbf{x}$ onto a span $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}\}$ is the vector in $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}\}$ that is "closest" to $\mathbf{x}.$ Let's work an example to clarify what we mean by "closest."

Consider the following two vectors:

![](images/a4/a4754bf048aa6c05cd7ef574af306150c30d435f90afec36f492ed4b8013e899.png)

The vector $k\mathbf a$ is called the **orthogonal projection** of $\mathbf{x}$ onto $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}\}.$

$$

Since $\mathbf{a} \perp \mathbf{z},$ we have $\mathbf{z} \cdot \mathbf{a} = 0.$ As a result,

$$

\begin{aligned}ka=\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -6 \\ 0 \\ 6\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

$$
\eqalign{
a^2\cdot a^3&=\
 (a\cdot a) \cdot (a\cdot a\cdot a)&=\
a\cdot a\cdot a\cdot a\cdot a&=\
a^5
}
$$

When written in expanded form, this formula becomes:

![](images/0c/0c782638ef4254884c9521b8c36452d241d4e95acb5f4c54ecd31b9045490143.svg)" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186129357 :activity/expected-seconds 1200.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186124484 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-750b7607-258b-55b2-8f3f-8eb360c8a574"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-750b7607-258b-55b2-8f3f-8eb360c8a574" :question/id #uuid "750b7607-258b-55b2-8f3f-8eb360c8a574" :question/math-academy-id "q-94644" :question/problem "Let $V$ be the set of polynomials of the form $a{x}^{2},$ where $a\in Q.$ Which of the following statements are true? 

I. The zero-polynomial belongs to $V.$

II. For the zero-polynomial $0$ and any $p(x)\in V,$ we have $p(x)+0=p(x).$

III. For any $p(x),q(x)\in V,$ we have $p(x)+q(x)=q(x)+p(x).$" :question/worked-solution "Let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the zero-polynomial can be represented as

$$
0=0\cdot {x}^{2}.
$$

Hence, $0\in V.$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, for the zero-polynomial $0$ and any $p(x)\in V,$ we have

$$
p(x)+0=p(x)
$$

since $0$ is the unique zero element in the set of all polynomials.

- Statement III is true. Indeed, for any $p(t),q(t)\in V,$ we obtain that 

$$
p(t)+q(t)=q(t)+p(t).

$$

$$

Thus, another equilibrium is $(2, 0.75).$

- If $x=1,$ substituting it into the first equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}2(1)(1-0.5(1))-(1)y & =0 \\ 1-y & =0 \\ y & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equilibria of the model are

$$
(0,0),\,(2,0),\,(1,1).
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-bee04d0f-21c8-5845-b5c1-0985dbd842b5" :question/id #uuid "bee04d0f-21c8-5845-b5c1-0985dbd842b5" :question/math-academy-id "q-335629" :question/problem "$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x(1-0.2x)-2xy)=1-0.4x-2y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x(1-0.2x)-2xy)=-2x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-3y+xy)=y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-3y+xy)=-3+x\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is

$$
J=[\begin{aligned}1-0.4x-2y & -2x \\ y & -3+x\end{aligned}].

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(8x(1-0.75x)-xy)=8-12x-y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(8x(1-0.75x)-xy)=-x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-4y+4xy)=4y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-4y+4xy)=-4+4x\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is

$$
J=[\begin{aligned}8-12x-y & -x \\ 4y & -4+4x\end{aligned}].
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$ to get

$$
J({x}^{∗})=[\begin{aligned}8-12(1)-(2) & -(1) \\ 4(2) & -4+4(1)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-6 & -1 \\ 8 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

To find the eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix, we write down the characteristic equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}-6-\lambda  & -1 \\ 8 & -\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-6-\lambda )(-\lambda )-8(-1) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+6\lambda +8 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the equation, we get the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=-2\text{ and }{\lambda }_{2}=-4.$ Since both eigenvalues are real and negative, our equilibrium is $\text{an asymptotically stable}$ Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(3x(1-2x)-xy)=3-12x-y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3x(1-2x)-xy)=-x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-3y+4xy)=4y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-3y+4xy)=-3+4x\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is

$$
J=[\begin{aligned}3-12x-y & -x \\ 4y & -3+4x\end{aligned}].
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}0.5 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ to get

$$
J({x}^{∗})=[\begin{aligned}3-12(0.5)-0 & -0.5 \\ 4(0) & -3+4(0.5)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-3 & -0.5 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=-3\text{ and }{\lambda }_{2}=-1.$ Since the eigenvalues are real and both negative, our equilibrium is $\text{an asymptotically stable}$ 17592186168015 :tutorial/content "The Lotka–Volterra predator-prey model with **carrying capacity** is given by 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=ax(1-hx)-bxy \\ {y}^{′}=-cy+dxy\end{aligned}
$$

where $a,b,c,d,h$ are positive real constants. Here, 

- $x=x(t)$ is the *prey population*, and

- $y=y(t)$ is the *predator population*.

The only difference from the Lotka–Volterra model is the factor $(1-hx)$ in the prey equation. Notice that if $h=0,$ we get the standard model:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=ax-bxy \\ {y}^{′}=-cy+dxy\end{aligned}
$$

In our modified version of the model, the *intrinsic growth* of prey is given by the $ax(1-hx)$ term. Now, if there are no predators ($y=0$), then 

$$
x' = ax(1-hx).
$$

Recall that general solutions to this equation are logistic functions with two horizontal asymptotes defined by the equilibrium solutions, which can be found by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}ax(1-hx)=0\,⇒\,x=0,\,\frac{1}{h}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the equilibria are $x=0$ and $x=\dfrac{1}{h}.$ The nonzero equilibrium gives the *carrying capacity* (the limit the number of prey is approaching as $t$ goes to infinity).

![](images/8b/8b7a6d12af77f6c2d2e6d3596e71a51a3d697a5c28e9f9c64c5675a01df812d5.png)" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186168028 :tutorial/content "Recall that the equilibrium (fixed) points of a system $\mathbf{x}'(t) = \mathbf{f}(x,y)$ are the points for which $f(x,y)=\mathbf{0}.$ So, for the Lotka–Volterra model 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=ax(1-hx)-bxy \\ {y}^{′}=-cy+dxy\end{aligned}
$$

the equilibria are the solutions of the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}ax(1-hx)-bxy=0 \\ -cy+dxy=0\end{aligned}
$$

Factoring the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-cy+dxy & =0 \\ y(-c+dx) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $y=0$ or $x=\dfrac{c}{d}.$ We consider both cases separately.

- If $y=0,$ substituting it into the first equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}ax(1-hx)-bx(0) & =0 \\ ax(1-hx) & =0 \\ x & =0,\,\frac{1}{h}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the first two equilibria are $(0,0)$ and $\left(\dfrac{1}{h},0\right).$

- If $x=\dfrac{c}{d},$ substituting it into the first equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}a(\frac{c}{d})(1-h(\frac{c}{d}))-b(\frac{c}{d})y & =0 \\ a(1-\frac{c}{d}h)-by & =0 \\ a(1-\frac{c}{d}h) & =by \\ y & =\frac{a}{b}(1-\frac{c}{d}h).\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, another equilibrium is $\left(\dfrac{c}{d}, \dfrac{a}{b}\left(1-\dfrac{c}{d}h\right)\right).$

Therefore, the equilibria of the model are

$$
(0,0), \qquad
\left(\dfrac{1}{h},0\right), \qquad
\left(\dfrac{c}{d}, \dfrac{a}{b}\left(1-\dfrac{c}{d}h\right)\right).
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186168029 :tutorial/content "Consider the modified Lotka–Volterra predator-prey model with carrying capacity 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=ax(1-hx)-bxy \\ {y}^{′}=-cy+dxy\end{aligned}
$$

where $a,b,c,d,h$ are positive real constants, $x=x(t)$ is the prey population, and $y=y(t)$ is the predator population.

To classify the equilibrium at the origin, we need to find the corresponding Jacobian matrix.

Let's denote $f_1(x,y)=ax(1-hx)-bxy$ and $f_2(x,y)=-cy+dxy.$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(ax(1\,-\,hx)-bxy)=a(1\,-\,2hx)-by, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(ax(1\,-\,hx)-bxy)=-bx, \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-cy+dxy)=dy, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-cy+dxy)=-c+dx.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is
![](images/1d/1db459c6fd9f3bad4e5f044d8de8a4e185aeecadddcd73fac75dff09e6fa607d.svg)

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ![](images/03/035a074e405004b43a3f5e509b46affa6e0e53dbf53e26e01149b7ae545c6f64.svg) to get

![](images/cf/cf1eb1b02f6d0dd1b690ac3a69abd1ac6777f592c713060920ef1dcee3fb5600.svg)

The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are $\lambda_1 = a > 0$ and $\lambda_2 = -c < 0.$ Since eigenvalues are real with opposite signs, our equilibrium is an *unstable saddle*.

Thus, the equilibrium at the origin for this model behaves identically to that of the standard Lotka–Volterra model." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186168016 :tutorial/content "Recall that the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=ax(1-hx)-bxy \\ {y}^{′}=-cy+dxy\end{aligned}
$$

has equilibria at

$$
(0,0), \qquad
\left(\dfrac{1}{h}, 0\right), \qquad
\left(\dfrac{c}{d}, \dfrac{a}{b}\left(1 - \dfrac{c}{d}h\right)\right).
$$

Notice that the second component of the third equilibrium point is positive only when 

$$
h < \dfrac{d}{c},
$$

which guarantees that the third fixed point will lie in the first quadrant. For now, let's consider only this case.

We now evaluate the Jacobian matrix
![](images/89/89ca57d2d308201a46a31695c27ad866604ef4f230609ad3047e186824e5dc28.svg)
at the nonzero equilibrium ![](images/f2/f2965d33d48e48fa977e876803aa3da55c1c47c3569a24cb8341b97ba43420c2.svg) to get

![](images/b2/b239f1170a7bf5a5f6ad6043492aa0772adcc2a53e7f3ebdad15ad195b1520d9.svg)

Because we are considering the case when $h < \dfrac{d}{c},$ we have that

$$
\dfrac{c}{h}\left(\dfrac{d}{c}-h\right) > 0.
$$

The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are $\lambda_1 = -a < 0$ and $\lambda_2 = \dfrac{c}{h}\left(\dfrac{d}{c}-h\right) > 0.$ Since eigenvalues are real with opposite signs, our equilibrium is an *unstable saddle*.

Analyzing the type of the third equilibrium in full generality becomes considerably more cumbersome. Therefore, we'll examine a concrete example later in the lesson. For now, we simply note that the third equilibrium is an *asymptotically stable (spiral) sink*.

A typical phase portrait of the system, in the case when $h < \dfrac{d}{c},$ looks as shown below.

![](images/8c/8c82332ed5277586a2b97e900383619a5d61cdb73ff4b60a92de3d5460165165.png)

The global picture is the following:

- There are two straight-line types of solutions:

- Along the $x$-axis, trajectories approach the equilibrium at $\left(\dfrac{1}{h},0\right).$ Indeed, in the absence of the predators, the prey approaches the carrying capacity.

- Along the $y$-axis, trajectories approach the origin. Indeed, in the absence of the prey, the predators decrease exponentially.

- The curved trajectories converge to the equilibrium point $\left(\dfrac{c}{d}, \dfrac{a}{b}\left(1 - \dfrac{c}{d}h\right)\right).$

The corresponding population dynamics graphs look as depicted below.

![](images/a7/a7673170825344e1831f2ba01ce4c20f10091380ff4e116f3b6bd9e7666e51aa.png)" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186168030 :tutorial/content "Consider the Lotka-Volterra model with carrying capacity below, where $x=x(t)$ represents the prey and $y=y(t)$ represents the predators.

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=4x(1-0.25x)-xy \\ {y}^{′}=-2y+3xy\end{aligned}
$$

We'll evaluate its Jacobian at the equilibrium point $\mathbf{x^\ast}=[4, \, 0]^T$ that lies on the $x$-axis.

Let's denote $f_1(x,y)=4x(1-0.25x)-xy$ and $f_2(x,y)=-2y+3xy.$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4x(1-0.25x)-xy)=4-2x-y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4x(1-0.25x)-xy)=-x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-2y+3xy)=3y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-2y+3xy)=-2+3x\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is
![](images/0b/0bd1edc4527b82bebf84d38f8d4a79b65062d6b38c5fa4c84b7509acaa547f42.svg)

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ![](images/30/30463f939876ccbee7cf77f8fdc80fb4e8a27fe0ad5af22cd51e1be3433a3af5.svg) to get

![](images/fc/fc40e7e568705e08b70e0dedae710b2e8514837491730ae12a90bed764261f97.svg)

The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are $\lambda_1 = 10$ and $\lambda_2=-4$. Since the eigenvalues are real with opposite signs, our equilibrium is an *unstable saddle*.

Let's now see an example with the equilibrium that lies in the first quadrant (the third equilibrium)." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186168017 :tutorial/content "Again, recall that the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=ax(1-hx)-bxy \\ {y}^{′}=-cy+dxy\end{aligned}
$$

has equilibria at

$$
(0,0), \qquad
\left(\dfrac{1}{h}, 0\right), \qquad
\left(\dfrac{c}{d}, \dfrac{a}{b}\left(1 - \dfrac{c}{d}h\right)\right).
$$

We have already considered the case when $h < \dfrac{d}{c},$ which guarantees that the third equilibrium will lie in the first quadrant. Let's now consider the remaining cases.

- When $h = \dfrac{d}{c},$ the third equilibrium coincides with the second one. So, we have only two equilibria:

$$
(0,0), \qquad
\left(\dfrac{1}{h}, 0\right) = \left(\dfrac{c}{d}, 0\right)
$$

- When $h > \dfrac{d}{c},$ the third equilibrium is in the fourth quadrant (its $y$-coordinate is negative). So, we have only two equilibria that make sense in the context of the model:

$$
(0,0), \qquad
\left(\dfrac{1}{h}, 0\right)
$$

Hence, we get only two equilibria. 

The trajectories near the origin remain similar. However, the equilibrium at

$$
\left(\dfrac{1}{h}, 0\right)
$$

will be an *asymptotically stable sink*.

A typical phase portrait of the system, in the case when $h \geq \dfrac{d}{c},$ looks as shown below.

![](images/b9/b94beebb63bc1312d56f655e48b3bc7cdb1b9badc5cdacd6b88b073c5055adc9.png)

The global picture is the following:

- There are two straight-line types of solutions:

- Along the $x$-axis, trajectories approach the equilibrium at $\left(\dfrac{1}{h},0\right).$ Indeed, in the absence of the predators, the prey approaches the carrying capacity.

- Along the $y$-axis, trajectories approach the origin. Indeed, in the absence of the prey, the predators decrease exponentially.

- The curved trajectories converge to the equilibrium point $\left(\dfrac{1}{h}, 0\right).$

The corresponding population dynamics graphs look as depicted below.

![](images/cd/cd60f32a5daff3c805b097d121814d19e04781ed1bcfead989cde82db674e5d9.png)

Eventually, the *predators go extinct* while the prey approaches the carrying capacity of the system.

Let's see a concrete example." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186167005 :activity/expected-seconds 1380.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}]

\left( \dfrac{1}{7} \right)^2 = 7^{-2}

To work out ${\color{blue}{2}}^{{\color{red}{-2}}},$ all we need to do is find the reciprocal of the base $({\color{blue}{2}})$ and then raise that reciprocal to the same power but with the *opposite* sign $({{\color{red}{+2}}})$.

The Fourier series converges to {{field-1}} when $x=-3.$" :question/worked-solution "Suppose that $f(x)$ is a $2L$-periodic piecewise smooth function with the corresponding Fourier series

$$
S(x)=\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{L}x).
$$

Then, the series converges for all $x\in R.$

- If $f(x)$ is continuous at $x,$ then the series converges to the value of the function at this point:

$$
S(x)=f(x)
$$

- If $f(x)$ has a jump discontinuity at $x,$ then the series converges to the midpoint between the values of left- and right-sided limits of the function at this point:

$$
S(x)=\frac{{f}^{-}(x)+{f}^{+}(x)}{2}
$$

where ${f}^{-}(x)$ and ${f}^{+}(x)$ are the left- and right-sided limits of the function at this point, respectively.

Notice that the $6$-periodic extension $f(x)$ of our function $F(x)$ is not continuous at $x=-3.$ The one-sided limits at this point are the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{-}(-3) & ={lim}_{x\to -{3}^{-}}f(x)=4 \\ {f}^{+}(-3) & ={lim}_{x\to -{3}^{+}}f(x)=-2\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, the Fourier series of $f(x)$ converges to 

$$
\frac{{f}^{-}(-3)+{f}^{+}(-3)}{2}=\frac{4+(-2)}{2}=1.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-8e653195-c3d5-582e-822a-b0c443f4aade"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-8e653195-c3d5-582e-822a-b0c443f4aade" :answer-field/id #uuid "8e653195-c3d5-582e-822a-b0c443f4aade" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-857250c9-a9b1-5080-b2c5-1728296672ed" :answer-field/choices ["answer-857250c9-a9b1-5080-b2c5-1728296672ed"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-857250c9-a9b1-5080-b2c5-1728296672ed" :answer/id #uuid "857250c9-a9b1-5080-b2c5-1728296672ed" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-967d4b0f-c5b8-576b-b414-bb183f8a1110" :question/id #uuid "967d4b0f-c5b8-576b-b414-bb183f8a1110" :question/math-academy-id "q-343368" :question/problem "$$

For example, consider two vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ shown below. Suppose we know that $|\,\mathbf{a}\,|=2$ and that the angle between the vectors is $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{4}.$

![](images/a2/a28278cf12885ab7f845407ac2fa7f4ffa00dbe30849a3f8ff41f02e134ed3a0.png)

To illustrate the projection of $\mathbf{a}$ along $\mathbf{b},$ consider the point $P$ on the line that contains $\mathbf{b}$ with $AP \perp \mathbf{b},$ as shown below.

![](images/fd/fd37bdb2a97b4125fb360990d3c4a36b48bcb50433de033a154799db00e474dd.png)

The length $OP$ is called the **scalar projection** of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}$ (or the **component** of $\mathbf{a}$ along $\mathbf{b}$). It is denoted as $\text{comp}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a},$ and we can compute it using cosine in $\triangle OPA$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{b}\,a & =OP \\  & =|\,a\,|\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =2\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

This formula is the general definition of the scalar projection:

$$
\text{comp}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a}= |\,\mathbf{a}\,| \cos\theta
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186107177 :tutorial/content "The scalar projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}$ can be negative. This happens when the vector $\mathbf{a}$ extends in the direction opposite to that of $\mathbf{b}.$

![](images/c1/c19648ea2df1935e89e10df2f7f5ab33ad537a5fdb52bb97c3555c9a0365701e.png)

For example, consider two vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b},$ where it is known that 

$$
|\,\mathbf{a}\,|=2, \qquad \theta = 135^\circ.
$$

Notice that the angle $\theta$ between the vectors is obtuse.

$$

$$

However, sometimes we are not given the angle between two vectors. In such cases, we can solve for $\cos \theta$ in terms of the dot product:

$$
\begin{aligned}a\cdot b & =|\,a\,|\,|\,b\,|\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{a\cdot b}{|\,a\,|\,|\,b\,|}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into our original formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{b}\,a & =|\,a\,|\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =|\,a\,|\cdot \frac{a\cdot b}{|\,a\,|\,|\,b\,|} \\  & =\frac{a\cdot b}{|\,b\,|}.\end{aligned}
$$

meters." :question/worked-solution "The width of the plot is $x+3$ meters, and its area is $2{x}^{2}+6x$ square meters. Since the $\text{area}=\text{length}\times \text{width},$ we factor the expression for the area to find the length.

First, we find the $\text{GCF}$ of the two terms:

$$
\text{GCF}(2{x}^{2},6x)=2x
$$

Then, we rewrite each term in the original expression as a product with the $\text{GCF}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}+6x & = \\ (2x\cdot x)+(2x\cdot 3)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we write the $\text{GCF}$ outside the parentheses and keep the remaining terms inside:

$$
\begin{aligned}(2x\cdot x)+(2x\cdot 3) & = \\ 2x(x+3)\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we conclude that the length of the plot must be $2x$ meters.

meters." :question/worked-solution "To find the required width, we need to factor the expression ${x}^{2}+3x-10.$

First, we find the factor pairs of the constant term $(-10).$ The constant term is negative, so that means one of the factors is negative, and the other is positive:

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & \times (-10) \\ (-1) & \times 10 \\ 2 & \times (-5) \\ (-2) & \times 5\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find which factor pair adds up to the coefficient of the linear term $3:$

$$
\begin{aligned}1+(-10) & =-9 & \times  \\ -1+10 & =9 & \times  \\ 2+(-5) & =-3 & \times  \\ -2+5 & =3 & ✓\end{aligned}
$$

Using the factor pair identified above, write the linear term as $3x=5x-2x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+3x-10 & ={x}^{2}+5x-2x-10\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we factor the first two terms and the last two terms separately, and then factor the expression completely:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+5x-2x-10 & = \\ ({x}^{2}+5x)+(-2x-10) & = \\ x(x+5)-2(x+5) & = \\ (x-2)(x+5)\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we conclude that the width must be $x-2$ meters.

$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186124752 :activity/expected-seconds 780.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186119749 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-1fed5aa4-7f90-50cb-8379-da324cfd5754"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-1fed5aa4-7f90-50cb-8379-da324cfd5754" :question/id #uuid "1fed5aa4-7f90-50cb-8379-da324cfd5754" :question/math-academy-id "q-80612" :question/problem "Find the curvature at an arbitrary point on the curve $r(t)$ given that its derivative ${r}^{′}(t)$ and the derivative of the corresponding unit tangent ${T}^{′}(t)$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t)={e}^{t}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,{T}^{′}(t)=-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "Since we are given both the derivative of the curve ${r}^{′}(t)$ and the derivative of the unit tangent ${T}^{′}(t),$ we will use the following formula for the curvature:

$$
κ(t)=\frac{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}
$$

Now, we find the magnitudes of ${T}^{′}(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{T}^{′}(t)‖ & =|-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}|\sqrt{(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\sqrt{({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)+({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)+(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\sqrt{1+1+0} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\cdot \sqrt{2} \\  & =1 \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & ={e}^{t}\sqrt{(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & ={e}^{t}\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t} \\  & ={e}^{t}\sqrt{({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)+({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)+(-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t)} \\  & ={e}^{t}\sqrt{1+1+0} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\,{e}^{t}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the curvature is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}\,{e}^{t}}=\frac{\sqrt{2}\,{e}^{-t}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-fbef7b1b-2a5f-5dce-929c-f5b8a633c936"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id &=\dfrac {2 \cdot 2 \cdot (x - 3)} {2(5x + 2)}\[5pt]

$$
{y}^{′}=9y(1-\frac{y}{1\,200}),\,y(0)=200
$$

What is ${lim}_{t\to \infty }y(t)?$" :question/worked-solution "A logistic growth equation has the form

$$
{y}^{′}=ky(a-y),
$$

where $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality, and $a>y$ is the carrying capacity.

A diagram showing a typical logistic growth curve is shown below.

![](images/57/57f4b604c546daed4f1cb3895191fae0ccac33b5c17aac705f203f0a837c7e69.png)

First, let's rewrite the right-hand side of the given equation so that it matches the form above:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =9y(1-\frac{y}{1\,200}) \\  & =9y(\frac{1\,200-y}{1\,200}) \\  & =\frac{9y}{1\,200}(1\,200-y) \\  & =\frac{3y}{400}(1\,200-y)\end{aligned}
$$

From here, we see that $a=1\,200.$ Hence, the carrying capacity is $1\,200.$

For a given logistic growth model, $y\to a$ as $t\to \infty .$ Therefore,

$$
y' = 5y(10-y), \qquad y(0) = y_0.
$$

The logistic growth curve for this problem is sketched below.

![](images/0a/0a225fd04f81bd65e1bad3ff14097563d112a16e3847aac26cc86591533ea5d0.png)

The curve contains an inflection point, that is, a point where $y(t)$ is growing at its fastest possible rate. What information can we deduce about this point? 

To find the inflection point, we solve $y''(t) = 0.$ First, we differentiate the differential equation using implicit differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{″} & =(5y)^{′}\cdot (10-y)+(5y)\cdot (10-y)^{′} \\  & =5\cdot (10-y)\cdot {y}^{′}+(5y)\cdot (-1)\cdot {y}^{′} \\  & ={y}^{′}\cdot (5\cdot (10-y)+(5y)\cdot (-1)) \\  & ={y}^{′}\cdot (50-5y-5y) \\  & ={y}^{′}\cdot (50-10y)\end{aligned}
$$

We now need to solve $y''(t) = 0,$ i.e.,

$$
y'\cdot\left(50-10y\right) = 0.
$$

We know that $y'$ is increasing for all $t,$ so $y'\neq 0.$ Therefore, we must have

$$
50-10y = 0\quad \Rightarrow\quad y = 5.
$$

Let's mark this on our diagram.

![](images/75/75d0363483e1bda70decb171466fe9e506eb0da80d0e78ed893bb61551ae9d44.png)

The fact that the inflection point occurs when $y$ is precisely half the carrying capacity is *not* a coincidence. In fact, this is always the case. The general situation is shown below.

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{b}\,a & =|\,a\,|\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =8\operatorname{cos}⁡({120}^{∘}) \\  & =8\cdot (-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the unit vector that is parallel to $b:$

$$
u=\frac{b}{|\,b\,|}=\frac{b}{2}=\frac{1}{2}b
$$

Finally, we compute the vector projection as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,a & ={\text{comp}}_{b}\,a\cdot u \\  & =(-4)\cdot \frac{1}{2}b \\  & =-2b\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186102542 :answer-field/correct 17592186102547 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "question-b6749b1c-5bbb-5e2e-a55f-6596daa98287" :question/id #uuid "b6749b1c-5bbb-5e2e-a55f-6596daa98287" :question/math-academy-id "q-126505" :question/problem "Suppose that $|\,p\,|=3$, $|\,q\,|=6\sqrt{2}$ and that the angle between the vectors is $\theta =\frac{3\pi }{4}.$ Find the vector projection of $q$ onto $p$ in terms of the vector $p.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the scalar projection as follows:

$$
