"question-1d98c763-a05e-5de6-913c-903735959780" :question/id #uuid "1d98c763-a05e-5de6-913c-903735959780" :question/math-academy-id "q-212460" :question/problem "Let $a=⟨1,2,-1⟩$ and $b=⟨1,x,2⟩.$ Given that the projection of $a$ onto $b$ is the zero vector, find the value of $x.$" :question/worked-solution "Since $a$ is a nonzero vector, its projection onto another nonzero vector $b$ equals the zero vector only when the vectors are perpendicular. 

So, we must have

$$
a⊥b\,⟹\,a\cdot b=0.
$$

Computing the dot product, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}a\cdot b & ={a}_{x}\cdot {b}_{x}+{a}_{y}\cdot {b}_{y}+{a}_{z}\cdot {b}_{z} \\  & =1\cdot 1+2\cdot x+(-1)\cdot 2 \\  & =2x-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting the dot product equal to $0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}a\cdot b & =0 \\ 2x-1 & =0 \\ 2x & =1 \\ x & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-0dfe0b7a-7e87-551d-9c63-3d3fbe0f0ee6"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-0dfe0b7a-7e87-551d-9c63-3d3fbe0f0ee6" :answer-field/id #uuid "0dfe0b7a-7e87-551d-9c63-3d3fbe0f0ee6" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-f6da670c-ad73-58eb-88ec-c72e37de6415" :answer-field/choices ["answer-b1c88e84-5bca-52a5-9ff2-25a12a68f03e" "answer-007ca704-665c-5469-bb92-8fe895a8eacd" "answer-f6da670c-ad73-58eb-88ec-c72e37de6415" "answer-09f61461-dd48-5041-ae4c-43a710a4eb72" "answer-9228ca5d-afce-5b10-b57e-7850fc591002"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b1c88e84-5bca-52a5-9ff2-25a12a68f03e" :answer/id #uuid "b1c88e84-5bca-52a5-9ff2-25a12a68f03e" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-\frac{1}{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-007ca704-665c-5469-bb92-8fe895a8eacd" :answer/id #uuid "007ca704-665c-5469-bb92-8fe895a8eacd" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-\frac{2}{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-f6da670c-ad73-58eb-88ec-c72e37de6415" :answer/id #uuid "f6da670c-ad73-58eb-88ec-c72e37de6415" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-09f61461-dd48-5041-ae4c-43a710a4eb72" :answer/id #uuid "09f61461-dd48-5041-ae4c-43a710a4eb72" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{5}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-9228ca5d-afce-5b10-b57e-7850fc591002" :answer/id #uuid "9228ca5d-afce-5b10-b57e-7850fc591002" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{3}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186059871 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-2ab44a05-012f-5af3-a42d-e6d922b9a66c" "question-353b78e0-100e-5425-97b3-923c0bd8ad1a"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186059422 :question/worked-solution "First, we write

$$

$$

$$
5^1 \times 5^2 \times 5^4
$$

$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186059872 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-fa0bbd4b-06ea-5732-8998-73cc5cb59649" "question-a0176d28-d1e2-593d-8b48-e87cdf5d129a"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186059423 :question/worked-solution "To multiply powers of the same base, we add the exponents:

$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-2ab44a05-012f-5af3-a42d-e6d922b9a66c" :question/id #uuid "2ab44a05-012f-5af3-a42d-e6d922b9a66c" :question/math-academy-id "q-68262" :question/problem "${3}^{4}\times {3}^{5}=$" :question/worked-solution "To multiply powers of the same base, we simply add the exponents:

simplest form, ${9}^{-5}\times {9}^{3}=${{field-1}}." :question/worked-solution "To multiply powers of the same base, we add the exponents:

This is called the **product rule for exponents**.
For example, in the expression 

$$
{\color{blue}3}^4 \times {\color{blue}3}^2,
$$

both powers have the same base $({\color{blue}3}).$ Therefore, we can simplify this expression by adding the exponents:

$$
{\color{blue}3}^4 \times {\color{blue}3}^2 = {\color{blue}3}^{4+2} = {\color{blue}3}^6
$$

**Note:** The product rule for exponents is really just a quicker alternative to using repeated multiplication, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{3}^{4}\times {3}^{2} & = \\ {{3\times 3\times 3\times 3}_{⏟}}_{4\text{ copies}}\times {{3\times 3}_{⏟}}_{2\text{ copies}} & = \\ {{3\times 3\times 3\times 3\times 3\times 3}_{⏟}}_{6\text{ copies}} & = \\ {3}^{6}\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186060990 :tutorial/content "We can use the product rule for exponents with negative exponents too. For instance, to simplify $3^3\times 3^{-5},$ we add the exponents:

$$
3^{3} \times 3^{-5} = 3^{3-5} = 3^{-2}
$$

Now, to evaluate $3^{-2},$ we find the reciprocal of the base $(3)$ and then raise that reciprocal to the same power but with the opposite sign:

$$
3^{-2}  = \left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^2 =\dfrac{1}{3} \times \dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{1}{9}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186059942 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186054606 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-60199b98-6c64-506f-9047-6445f428ee81"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186054396 :question/worked-solution "To evaluate this expression, we use PEMDAS. $$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186054607 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-d7d9db10-3db0-5298-a1d1-4ea150f26c84" "question-43b02df2-3069-56a3-b787-8172b48fa9f2"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186054397 :question/problem "Evaluate $(1-4)^2 \times \dfrac{1}{12}.$" :question/worked-solution "To evaluate this expression, we use PEMDAS. First, consider the expression inside the parentheses:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-3)^{4}÷9\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}(-3)^{4}÷9 & = \\ 81÷9 & = \\ \frac{81}{9} & = \\ 9\end{aligned}

First, consider the expression inside the parentheses:

$$
\begin{aligned}3\times (-5)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Applying PEMDAS to this expression, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}3\times (-5)^{2} & = \\ 3\times 25 & = \\ 75\end{aligned}

$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-10176a3c-6389-5f3b-b3b8-ccc8df0a7ec2"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-10176a3c-6389-5f3b-b3b8-ccc8df0a7ec2" :answer-field/id #uuid "10176a3c-6389-5f3b-b3b8-ccc8df0a7ec2" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-6acc2ab7-51cb-51f1-a07f-1a3b4d54d305" :answer-field/choices ["answer-9306faf8-4093-5e6f-9781-92a5fd1a0a66" "answer-1a185603-b4f1-56c6-ba48-0f42bd7d26a3" "answer-55a85215-f199-5cc4-8988-d8d0f0927e6b" "answer-6acc2ab7-51cb-51f1-a07f-1a3b4d54d305" "answer-4a2f878c-fec5-5755-96bb-1161995eeedf"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-9306faf8-4093-5e6f-9781-92a5fd1a0a66" :answer/id #uuid "9306faf8-4093-5e6f-9781-92a5fd1a0a66" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-187.5" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1a185603-b4f1-56c6-ba48-0f42bd7d26a3" :answer/id #uuid "1a185603-b4f1-56c6-ba48-0f42bd7d26a3" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-30" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-55a85215-f199-5cc4-8988-d8d0f0927e6b" :answer/id #uuid "55a85215-f199-5cc4-8988-d8d0f0927e6b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "187.5" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-6acc2ab7-51cb-51f1-a07f-1a3b4d54d305" :answer/id #uuid "6acc2ab7-51cb-51f1-a07f-1a3b4d54d305" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "30" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4a2f878c-fec5-5755-96bb-1161995eeedf" :answer/id #uuid "4a2f878c-fec5-5755-96bb-1161995eeedf" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "50" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186056019 :tutorial/content "As we already know, to evaluate numerical expressions with a mix of different operations, we must follow the order of operations (PEMDAS).

The same rules apply to numerical expressions with negative numbers. For example, let's compute the value of

$$
(-2) \times (-3)^2.
$$

To evaluate this expression, we use PEMDAS.  First, we compute the exponents:

$$
(-2)\,\times\overbrace{(-3)^2}^{\large\color{blue} 9}  = (-2) \times {\color{blue} 9}
$$

 

Then, we multiply:

$$
(-2) \times 9 = -18
$$

Therefore,

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:    

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 4 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are $2$ pivot columns ($1$st and $2$nd). Thus, $x_3$ is a free variable. Now, from the second equation, we get $x_2=4x_3.$ 
Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain  

$$
x_1+4x_3+4x_3= 0
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
x_1=-8x_3.
$$

So, the general solution is
![](images/4b/4b13b3d4dbb889a07cece9dde6f9caf69d09b4eed2dc23e77407b9b5697775a6.svg)

Finally, we find the projection of $\mathbf{x}$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot b}{b\cdot b}b \\  & =\frac{(-10)\cdot (-8)+20\cdot 4+2\cdot 1}{{(-8)}^{2}+{4}^{2}+{1}^{2}}b \\  & =\frac{80+80+2}{64+16+1}b \\  & =\frac{162}{81}b \\  & =2b \\  & =2[\begin{aligned}-8 \\ 4 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-16 \\ 8 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-7284284d-f752-5dcb-a337-d7dc9bc05a72" :question/id #uuid "7284284d-f752-5dcb-a337-d7dc9bc05a72" :question/math-academy-id "q-81403" :question/problem "Let $a=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ and $b=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Find the orthogonal projection of $a$ onto $\text{Span}\{b\}.$" :question/worked-solution "The orthogonal projection of $a$ onto $\text{Span}\{b\}$ is given by

$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we need to find a basis of the solution space of the system. 

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

$$

$$
[\begin{aligned}3{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]={x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Consequently, $B=\{[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\}$ is a basis of the solution space of the system.

Finally, we find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot b}{b\cdot b}b \\  & =\frac{4\cdot 3+(-2)\cdot 1}{{3}^{2}+{1}^{2}}b \\  & =\frac{10}{10}b \\  & =b \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

"Given the vector $x$ and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system.

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}-10 \\ -15 \\ 28\end{aligned}],\,\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}=0 \\ 2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}-3{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we need to find a basis of the solution space of the system. 

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & -3 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & -3 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are $2$ pivot columns ($1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. Now, from the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}=\frac{3}{5}{x}_{3}.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
{x}_{1}-2(\frac{3}{5}{x}_{3})=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=\frac{6}{5}{x}_{3}.
$$

So, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{6}{5}{x}_{3} \\ \frac{3}{5}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{5}{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 3 \\ 5\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Consequently, $B=\{[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 3 \\ 5\end{aligned}]\}$ is a basis of the solution space of the system.

Finally, we find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot b}{b\cdot b}b \\  & =\frac{(-10)\cdot 6+(-15)\cdot 3+28\cdot 5}{{6}^{2}+{3}^{2}+{5}^{2}}b \\  & =\frac{-60-45+140}{36+9+25}b \\  & =\frac{35}{70}b \\  & =\frac{1}{2}b \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 3 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ \frac{3}{2} \\ \frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186394133 :question/problem "Given the vector $x$ and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system.

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3 \\ 7\end{aligned}],\,\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=0 \\ 2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we need to find a basis of the solution space of the system. 

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are $2$ pivot columns ($1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. Now, from the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}={x}_{3}.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
{x}_{1}+{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=-{x}_{3}.
$$

So, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Consequently, $B=\{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\}$ is a basis of the solution space of the system.

Finally, we find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot b}{b\cdot b}b \\  & =\frac{(-2)\cdot (-1)+3\cdot 1+7\cdot 1}{(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}b \\  & =\frac{12}{3}b \\  & =4b \\  & =4[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 4 \\ 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186135046 :tutorial/content "The **orthogonal projection** of a vector $\mathbf{x}$ onto a span $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}\}$ is the vector in $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}\}$ that is "closest" to $\mathbf{x}.$ Let's work an example to clarify what we mean by "closest."

Consider the following two vectors:

![](images/00/0079b00022e2f536fc3cc60db20657be10024ed81bcca3f802d2b25d8072c0ce.svg) 

Geometrically, $\mathbf{x}$ can be written as the sum of a vector $k{\mathbf{a}}$ that lies in $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}\}$ and 
another vector $\mathbf{z}$ that belongs to the orthogonal complement of $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}\}$, as illustrated in the picture below.

![](images/a4/a4754bf048aa6c05cd7ef574af306150c30d435f90afec36f492ed4b8013e899.png)

The vector $k\mathbf a$ is called the **orthogonal projection** of $\mathbf{x}$ onto $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}\}.$

Symbolically, we can write the vector $\mathbf{x}$ as the sum

$$
\mathbf{x} = k \mathbf{a} + \mathbf{z},
$$

for some $k \in \mathbb{R}$ and ${\mathbf{z}} \perp \mathbf{a}.$ 

To compute the orthogonal projection $k \mathbf{a},$ we can first find the dot product of both sides of the equation above with $\mathbf{a}$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}x\cdot a & =(ka+z)\cdot a \\ x\cdot a & =k(a\cdot a)+z\cdot a.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\mathbf{a} \perp \mathbf{z},$ we have $\mathbf{z} \cdot \mathbf{a} = 0.$ As a result,

$$
\begin{aligned}x\cdot a & =k(a\cdot a) \\ k & =\frac{x\cdot a}{a\cdot a} \\ k & =\frac{5\cdot 3+(-1)\cdot (-6)+0\cdot 0+1\cdot 6}{{3}^{2}+(-6)^{2}+{6}^{2}} \\ k & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the orthogonal projection is

$$
\begin{aligned}ka=\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -6 \\ 0 \\ 6\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** There is a shortcut! Instead of going through this process each time, we can compute the orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{x}$ onto $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}\}$ using the following formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{a}\,x & =\frac{a\cdot x}{a\cdot a}\,a\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186134001 :activity/expected-seconds 840.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} [:db/retract 17592186052076 :answer-field/choices 17592186052080] [:db/retract 17592186052076 :answer-field/choices 17592186052081] [:db/retract 17592186052076 :answer-field/choices 17592186052077] [:db/retract 17592186052076 :answer-field/choices 17592186052078] [:db/retract 17592186052076 :answer-field/choices 17592186052079] {:db/id 17592186054704 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-2158d6ec-2be1-5446-9223-07b6831e7100" "question-24348bb2-c07f-5da2-b2dd-e3e224260e04"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186054351 :question/problem "Simplify $a^{9}\cdot a^{7}.$" :question/worked-solution "We add the exponents, as follows:

$$

$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186054705 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-7907920d-205f-5377-afe5-d6463114236a"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186054352 :question/worked-solution "We add the exponents, as follows:

$$

Therefore $x^{n}=x^9$, so $n=9.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186054706 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-1e6c10cd-7db6-5a24-8c7d-80ae10691af2"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186054353 :question/problem "Simplify $x\left(x^3 y^5\right) \left(x^2 y^9\right).$" :question/worked-solution "Here we have two variables, $x$ and $y.$ We will start by grouping the two variables separately: 

$$
\begin{aligned}x({x}^{3}{y}^{5})({x}^{2}{y}^{9}) & = \\ {x}^{1}\cdot {x}^{3}\cdot {y}^{5}\cdot {x}^{2}\cdot {y}^{9} & = \\ ({x}^{1}\cdot {x}^{3}\cdot {x}^{2})({y}^{5}\cdot {y}^{9})\end{aligned}
$$

This way, we can apply the product rule to the two variables independently:

$$
\begin{aligned}({x}^{1}\cdot {x}^{3}\cdot {x}^{2})({y}^{5}\cdot {y}^{9}) & = \\ {x}^{(1+3+2)}\cdot {y}^{(5+9)} & = \\ {x}^{6}{y}^{14}\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-2158d6ec-2be1-5446-9223-07b6831e7100" :question/id #uuid "2158d6ec-2be1-5446-9223-07b6831e7100" :question/math-academy-id "q-388" :question/problem "Simplify the expression $x\cdot {x}^{2}.$" :question/worked-solution "We add the exponents, as follows:

$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-a8328799-896e-5212-8c80-2907af8b6d2a"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-a8328799-896e-5212-8c80-2907af8b6d2a" :answer-field/id #uuid "a8328799-896e-5212-8c80-2907af8b6d2a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-c638a612-ac6b-5641-b143-681bed9091a3" :answer-field/choices ["answer-c5e9a546-66e7-5266-9000-f8a352e3b453" "answer-52df8e4e-e473-5190-9aeb-f0096927f5fb" "answer-c638a612-ac6b-5641-b143-681bed9091a3" "answer-97487b45-8238-58f3-9c27-00ee8e3855c1" "answer-d0395dd1-17ba-540c-87b8-c76d002accac"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c5e9a546-66e7-5266-9000-f8a352e3b453" :answer/id #uuid "c5e9a546-66e7-5266-9000-f8a352e3b453" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "x" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-52df8e4e-e473-5190-9aeb-f0096927f5fb" :answer/id #uuid "52df8e4e-e473-5190-9aeb-f0096927f5fb" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "{x}^{-3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c638a612-ac6b-5641-b143-681bed9091a3" :answer/id #uuid "c638a612-ac6b-5641-b143-681bed9091a3" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "{x}^{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-97487b45-8238-58f3-9c27-00ee8e3855c1" :answer/id #uuid "97487b45-8238-58f3-9c27-00ee8e3855c1" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "{x}^{4}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d0395dd1-17ba-540c-87b8-c76d002accac" :answer/id #uuid "d0395dd1-17ba-540c-87b8-c76d002accac" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "{x}^{5}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-24348bb2-c07f-5da2-b2dd-e3e224260e04" :question/id #uuid "24348bb2-c07f-5da2-b2dd-e3e224260e04" :question/math-academy-id "q-2863" :question/problem "${x}^{3}\cdot {x}^{2}=$" :question/worked-solution "We add the exponents, as follows:

$$
a^n\cdot a^m=a^{n+m}
$$

For example,

$$
a^2\cdot a^3 = a^{2+3} = a^5.
$$

To see why the product rule is true, let's take the above example and work it out again, the long way.

For the two factors $a^2$ and $a^3$ we have $a^2=a\cdot a$ and $a^3= a\cdot a\cdot a.$ If we now substitute these two expressions into $a^2\cdot a^3$, we get the same result:

$$
\eqalign{
a^2\cdot a^3&=\
 (a\cdot a) \cdot (a\cdot a\cdot a)&=\
a\cdot a\cdot a\cdot a\cdot a&=\
a^5
}
$$

The product rule is just a shortcut for the process above." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186054921 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} [:db/retract 17592186127687 :answer-field/choices 17592186127688] [:db/retract 17592186127687 :answer-field/choices 17592186127689] [:db/retract 17592186127687 :answer-field/choices 17592186127690] [:db/retract 17592186127687 :answer-field/choices 17592186127691] [:db/retract 17592186127687 :answer-field/choices 17592186127692] {:db/id 17592186129213 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-18c92889-12f7-533b-bf2f-74218efc0204"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186129032 :question/problem "Let $[\mathbf{T}]_{\mathcal{B}}$ and $[\mathbf{T}]_{\mathcal{C}}$ be the matrices of a linear transformation $\mathbf{T}$ relative to the bases $\mathcal{B}$ and $\mathcal{C},$ respectively. ![](images/db/dbd020362f950fe8bfb4c592652b9e78a73610fa01a247b0b7ead6f201bf9ea5.png)

 

Here, moving along an arrow means pre-multiplying by the corresponding matrix. Algebraically, we can write this as

$$
[\mathbf{T}]_{\mathcal{S}} = P_{\small{\mathcal{B}}\to{\mathcal{S}}} \cdot [\mathbf{T}]_{\mathcal{B}} \cdot P_{\small{\mathcal{B}}\to{\mathcal{S}}}^{-1},

and the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{S}$ is

![](images/01/01d05455345f8ec71e58f613d3bcf54c41f4ff196766c728871e54050f590fba.svg)

First, we compute the inverse of $P_{\small{\mathcal{B}}\to{\mathcal{S}}} \mathbin{:}$

$$

$$

Now, we can compute the matrix of $\mathbf{T}$ relative to the standard basis $\mathcal{S} \mathbin{:}$

$$

Here, moving along an arrow means pre-multiplying by the corresponding matrix. Algebraically, we can write this as

$$
[\mathbf{T}]_{\mathcal{C}} = P_{\small{\mathcal{B}}\to{\mathcal{C}}} \cdot [\mathbf{T}]_{\mathcal{B}} \cdot P_{\small{\mathcal{B}}\to{\mathcal{C}}}^{-1},
$$

where $P_{\small{\mathcal{B}}\to{\mathcal{C}}}$ is the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{C}.$

First, let's denote the vectors of $\mathcal{B}$ and $\mathcal{C}$ as $\{ \mathbf{b}_1,\mathbf{b}_2 \}$ and $\{ \mathbf{c}_1,\mathbf{c}_2 \}$, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{C}$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of vectors from $\mathcal{B}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C}.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of $\mathbf{b}_1$ and $\mathbf{b}_2$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C}.$ To do this, we consider the matrix

![](images/26/26210267b80b50c4296225ac67237767cb326f2863fbfeba4cbdeb3f256ef62e.svg)

We reduce $M$ using Gaussian elimination until we get the identity matrix on the left. By doing this, we obtain the required change-of-coordinates matrix on the right.

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

![](images/97/97450c835af63c4489b848a69986d5b496af1bf983355c65021aca3384826ca7.svg)

Now, we compute the inverse of $P_{\small{\mathcal{B}}\to{\mathcal{C}}} \mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to C}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{1\cdot 1-0\cdot (-1)}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can compute the matrix of $\mathbf{T}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C} \mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}[T]_{C} & ={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & -3 \\ 2 & 6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -9 \\ 2 & 6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -7 \\ 2 & 8\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-18c92889-12f7-533b-bf2f-74218efc0204" :question/id #uuid "18c92889-12f7-533b-bf2f-74218efc0204" :question/math-academy-id "q-38361" :question/problem "Let $[T]_{B}$ and $[T]_{C}$ be the matrices of a linear transformation $T$ relative to the bases $B$ and $C,$ respectively. If ${P}_{C\to B}$ is the change-of-coordinates matrix from basis $C$ to basis $B,$ which of the following statements are true?

III. $[T]_{C}={P}_{C\to B}^{-1}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{C\to B}$" :question/worked-solution "The connection between the matrices of our linear transformation $T$ relative to the bases $B$ and $C$ is given by the following diagram:

$$
[T]_{C}={P}_{C\to B}^{-1}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{C\to B},

where ${P}_{C\to B}$ is the change-of-coordinates matrix from $C$ to $B.$

Solving this equation for $[T]_{B},$ we obtain the alternative formulation

$$

Find the matrix of $T$ relative to the basis $C.$" :question/worked-solution "The connection between the matrices of our linear transformation $T$ relative to the bases $B$ and $C$ is given by the following diagram:

![](images/1b/1b81504d6fdcabee0e1f586fef3dd2af5a57a8411ba4d22429e00e09b171a4d1.png)

 

Here, moving along an arrow means pre-multiplying by the corresponding matrix. Algebraically, we can write this as

$$
[T]_{C}={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1},
$$

where ${P}_{B\to C}$ is the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C.$

First, let's denote the vectors of $B$ and $C$ as $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2}\}$ and $\{{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\}$, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of vectors from $B$ relative to the basis $C.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ relative to the basis $C.$ To do this, we consider the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} & {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

We reduce $M$ using Gaussian elimination until we get the identity matrix on the left. By doing this, we obtain the required change-of-coordinates matrix on the right.

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 8 & -5 \\ -2 & -3 & -7 & 4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 8 & -5 \\ 0 & 3 & 9 & -6\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 8 & -5 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 & -2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-3){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 & -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 3 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to C}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to C}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 3 & -2\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{(-2)\cdot (-1)-3\cdot 1}[\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 \\ -3 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can compute the matrix of $T$ relative to the basis $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[T]_{C} & ={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 3 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 3 & 5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 \\ 6 & -4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}7 & 2 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186130348 :tutorial/content "Recall that the matrices $[\mathbf{T}]_{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}$ and $[\mathbf{T}]_{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}$ of a linear transformation $\mathbf{T} : V \to V$ relative to two bases $\color{blue}\mathcal{B}$ and $\color{red}\mathcal{C}$ of a vector space $V$ are different.

If we are given the matrix $[\mathbf{T}]_{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}},$ how do we find the matrix $[\mathbf{T}]_{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}?$
To find $[\mathbf{T}]_{\color{red}\mathcal{C}},$ we use the change-of-coordinates matrix $P_{\small {\color{blue}\mathcal{B}} \to {\color{red}\mathcal{C}}}$ from $\color{blue}\mathcal{B}$ to ${\color{red}\mathcal{C}}.$

The diagram below is a commutative diagram that shows how a change of basis works at each step.

![](images/df/dff02d9f46eb7ded23f418765a50dd1971145cd0e585a82beeef1a45812df8a7.png)

Here, moving along an arrow means pre-multiplying by the corresponding matrix. So algebraically, we can write this as

$$
[\mathbf{T}]_{\color{red}\mathcal{C}} = P_{\small{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}\to{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}} \cdot [\mathbf{T}]_{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}} \cdot P_{\small{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}\to{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}}^{-1}.
$$

For instance, if ![](images/89/89530292f17bb402acb489d90a17e7628a33bab37165b02580479b116e6a2b23.svg) and ![](images/f7/f75100cf6de9ccdb537d685f4e2858278214bbe351c9828e8a94a58628c1151b.svg), we use this formula to obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}[T]_{C} & ={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -3 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}-1 & -3 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -3 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 7 \\ -2 & -3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the formula for $[\mathbf{T}]_{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}},$ we obtain the alternative formulation

$$
[\mathbf{T}]_{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}} = P_{\small{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}\to{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}}^{-1} \cdot [\mathbf{T}]_{\color{red}\mathcal{C}} \cdot P_{\small{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}\to{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}}.

From this, we can derive the equation

[\mathbf{T}]_{\color{red}\mathcal{C}} = P_{\small{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}\to{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}}^{-1} \cdot [\mathbf{T}]_{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}} \cdot P_{\small{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}\to{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}}.
$$

Solving this equation for $[\mathbf{T}]_{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}},$ we obtain the alternative formulation

$$
[\mathbf{T}]_{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}} =
	P_{\small{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}\to{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}} \cdot [\mathbf{T}]_{\color{red}\mathcal{C}} \cdot P_{\small{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}\to{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}}^{-1}.
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186130349 :tutorial/content "Consider the bases $\color{blue}\mathcal{B}=\{ \mathbf{b}_1, \, \ldots, \, \mathbf{b}_n \}$ and $\color{red}\mathcal{C}=\{ \mathbf{c}_1, \, \ldots, \, \mathbf{c}_n \}$ of a vector space $V,$ and the matrix $[\mathbf{T}]_{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}$ of a linear transformation $\mathbf{T}$ with respect to the basis $\color{blue}\mathcal{B}.$
Then the matrix of $\mathbf{T}$ relative to the basis ${\color{red}\mathcal{C}}$ is given by

where $P_{\small {\color{blue}\mathcal{B}} \to {\color{red}\mathcal{C}}}$ is the change of basis matrix from ${\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}$ to ${\color{red}\mathcal{C}}.$

When written in expanded form, this formula becomes:

![](images/0c/0c782638ef4254884c9521b8c36452d241d4e95acb5f4c54ecd31b9045490143.svg)" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186129357 :activity/expected-seconds 1200.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186124484 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-750b7607-258b-55b2-8f3f-8eb360c8a574"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-750b7607-258b-55b2-8f3f-8eb360c8a574" :question/id #uuid "750b7607-258b-55b2-8f3f-8eb360c8a574" :question/math-academy-id "q-94644" :question/problem "Let $V$ be the set of polynomials of the form $a{x}^{2},$ where $a\in Q.$ Which of the following statements are true? 

I. The zero-polynomial belongs to $V.$

II. For the zero-polynomial $0$ and any $p(x)\in V,$ we have $p(x)+0=p(x).$

III. For any $p(x),q(x)\in V,$ we have $p(x)+q(x)=q(x)+p(x).$" :question/worked-solution "Let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the zero-polynomial can be represented as

$$
0=0\cdot {x}^{2}.
$$

Hence, $0\in V.$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, for the zero-polynomial $0$ and any $p(x)\in V,$ we have

$$
p(x)+0=p(x)
$$

since $0$ is the unique zero element in the set of all polynomials.

- Statement III is true. Indeed, for any $p(t),q(t)\in V,$ we obtain that 

$$
p(t)+q(t)=q(t)+p(t).
$$

Hence, the addition of polynomials in $V$ is commutative.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-1ca2ea90-b950-5f61-9fa7-e9762d8343dd"] :db/ensure Consider the modified Lotka-Volterra model, where $x=x(t)$ represents the prey and $y=y(t)$ represents the predators. Find the maximum carrying capacity for the prey in the case of the complete absence of predators." :question/worked-solution "The Lotka-Volterra predator-prey model with carrying capacity is given by

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=ax(1-hx)-bxy \\ {y}^{′}=-cy+dxy\end{aligned}
$$

where $a,b,c,d,h$ are positive real constants. Here, $x=x(t)$ represents the prey and $y=y(t)$ represents the predators.

In our case, the equation describing the dynamics of the prey is given by

$$
x' = 6x(1-0.1x) - 3xy
$$

where 

- the $6x(1-0.1x)$ term defines the growth, and

- the $-3xy$ term defines the decay due to interaction with predators.

In the case of the complete absence of predators, we have $y = 0,$ and this equation becomes

$$
x' = 6x(1-0.1x).
$$

General solutions to this equation are logistic functions with two horizontal asymptotes defined by the equilibrium solutions, which can be found by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}6x(1-0.1x)=0\,⇒\,x=0,\,10\end{aligned}
$$

So, the equilibria are $x=0$ and $x=10.$ The nonzero equilibrium gives the maximum capacity.

Therefore, the maximum carrying capacity for the prey in the case of the complete absence of predators is $10.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186166927 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-6f820e7d-e65e-5149-80bc-fca1cd9160a9" "question-f57e9bc6-8d1b-532c-906d-19c1ec051963"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186166558 :question/problem "$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=5x(1-0.2x)-4xy \\ {y}^{′}=-6y+3xy\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the Lotka-Volterra model with carrying capacity above, where $x=x(t)$ represents the prey and $y=y(t)$ represents the predators. Find the equilibria of the model." :question/worked-solution "The equilibrium (fixed) points of a system $\mathbf{x}'(t) = \mathbf{f}(x,y)$ are the points for which $f(x,y)=\mathbf{0}.$ So, we get the following system of linear equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}5x(1-0.2x)-4xy=0 \\ -6y+3xy=0\end{aligned}
$$

Factoring the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-6y+3xy & =0 \\ y(-6+3x) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $y=0$ or $x=2.$ We consider both cases separately.

- If $y=0,$ substituting it into the first equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}5x(1-0.2x)-4x(0) & =0 \\ 5x(0.2x-1) & =0 \\ x & =0,\,5.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the first two equilibria are $(0,0)$ and $(5,0).$

- If $x=2,$ substituting it into the first equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}5(2)(1-0.2(2))-(4)(2)y & =0 \\ 10(1-0.4)-8y & =0 \\ 10(0.6)-8y & =0 \\ 6-8y & =0 \\ y & =0.75.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, another equilibrium is $(2, 0.75).$

Therefore, the equilibria of the model are

$$
(0,0), \qquad
(5, 0), \qquad
(2, 0.75).
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186166928 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-bee04d0f-21c8-5845-b5c1-0985dbd842b5"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186166559 :question/problem "Consider the Lotka-Volterra model with carrying capacity below, where $x=x(t)$ represents the prey and $y=y(t)$ represents the predators.

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=5x(1-x)-xy \\ {y}^{′}=-y+2xy\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate the Jacobian of the system at the equilibrium point $\mathbf{x^\ast}=[0.5, \, 2.5]^T,$ and classify this equilibrium point." :question/worked-solution "Let's denote $f_1(x,y)=5x(1-x)-xy$ and $f_2(x,y)=-y+2xy.$

$$
(0,0),\,(4,0),\,(2,1.5).

\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=2x(1-0.2x)-xy \\ {y}^{′}=-4y+2xy\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the Lotka-Volterra model with carrying capacity above, where $x=x(t)$ represents the prey and $y=y(t)$ represents the predators. The equilibria of the model are the following:

$(0,0),\,(${{field-1}}$,0),\,(${{field-2}}$,${{field-3}}$)$" :question/worked-solution "The equilibrium (fixed) points of a system ${x}^{′}(t)=f(x,y)$ are the points for which $f(x,y)=0.$ So, we get the following system of linear equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2x(1-0.2x)-xy=0 \\ -4y+2xy=0\end{aligned}
$$

Factoring the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-4y+2xy & =0 \\ y(-4+2x) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $y=0$ or $x=2.$ We consider both cases separately.

- If $y=0,$ substituting it into the first equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}2x(1-0.2x)-x(0) & =0 \\ 2x(0.2x-1) & =0 \\ x & =0,\,5.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the first two equilibria are $(0,0)$ and $(5,0).$

- If $x=2,$ substituting it into the first equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}2(2)(1-0.2(2))-(2)y & =0 \\ 2.4-2y & =0 \\ y & =1.2.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, another equilibrium is $(2,1.2).$

Therefore, the equilibria of the model are

$$
(0,0),\,(5,0),\,(2,1.2).
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186164714 :answer-field/correct "answer-4a6dcee2-42ae-52fe-a1fc-f22dd3a0b63c" :answer-field/choices ["answer-4a6dcee2-42ae-52fe-a1fc-f22dd3a0b63c"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4a6dcee2-42ae-52fe-a1fc-f22dd3a0b63c" :answer/id #uuid "4a6dcee2-42ae-52fe-a1fc-f22dd3a0b63c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "5" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186164715 :answer-field/correct "answer-52c89af4-34a4-51e6-a756-47e839363e25" :answer-field/choices ["answer-52c89af4-34a4-51e6-a756-47e839363e25"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-52c89af4-34a4-51e6-a756-47e839363e25" :answer/id #uuid "52c89af4-34a4-51e6-a756-47e839363e25" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186164716 :answer-field/correct "answer-16b6342b-7e5d-58b5-81a4-338225e24b5e" :answer-field/choices ["answer-16b6342b-7e5d-58b5-81a4-338225e24b5e"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-16b6342b-7e5d-58b5-81a4-338225e24b5e" :answer/id #uuid "16b6342b-7e5d-58b5-81a4-338225e24b5e" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "1.2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186370395 :question/problem "$$

\{\begin{aligned}2x(1-0.5x)-xy=0 \\ -y+xy=0\end{aligned}

Factoring the second equation, we get

$$

So, $y=0$ or $x=1.$ We consider both cases separately.

- If $y=0,$ substituting it into the first equation, we have

$$

Thus, the first two equilibria are $(0,0)$ and $(2,0).$

- If $x=1,$ substituting it into the first equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}2(1)(1-0.5(1))-(1)y & =0 \\ 1-y & =0 \\ y & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, another equilibrium is $(1,1).$

Therefore, the equilibria of the model are

$$
(0,0),\,(2,0),\,(1,1).

$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is

$$
J=[\begin{aligned}1-0.4x-2y & -2x \\ y & -3+x\end{aligned}].

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(8x(1-0.75x)-xy)=8-12x-y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(8x(1-0.75x)-xy)=-x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-4y+4xy)=4y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-4y+4xy)=-4+4x\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is

$$
J=[\begin{aligned}8-12x-y & -x \\ 4y & -4+4x\end{aligned}].
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$ to get

$$
J({x}^{∗})=[\begin{aligned}8-12(1)-(2) & -(1) \\ 4(2) & -4+4(1)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-6 & -1 \\ 8 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

To find the eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix, we write down the characteristic equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}-6-\lambda  & -1 \\ 8 & -\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-6-\lambda )(-\lambda )-8(-1) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+6\lambda +8 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the equation, we get the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=-2\text{ and }{\lambda }_{2}=-4.$ Since both eigenvalues are real and negative, our equilibrium is $\text{an asymptotically stable}$ {{field-6}}{{field-7}}." :question/worked-solution "Let's denote ${f}_{1}(x,y)=3x(1-2x)-xy$ and ${f}_{2}(x,y)=-3y+4xy.$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(3x(1-2x)-xy)=3-12x-y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3x(1-2x)-xy)=-x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-3y+4xy)=4y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-3y+4xy)=-3+4x\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is

$$
J=[\begin{aligned}3-12x-y & -x \\ 4y & -3+4x\end{aligned}].
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}0.5 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ to get

$$
J({x}^{∗})=[\begin{aligned}3-12(0.5)-0 & -0.5 \\ 4(0) & -3+4(0.5)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-3 & -0.5 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=-3\text{ and }{\lambda }_{2}=-1.$ Since the eigenvalues are real and both negative, our equilibrium is $\text{an asymptotically stable}$ 17592186168015 :tutorial/content "The Lotka–Volterra predator-prey model with **carrying capacity** is given by 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=ax(1-hx)-bxy \\ {y}^{′}=-cy+dxy\end{aligned}
$$

where $a,b,c,d,h$ are positive real constants. Here, 

- $x=x(t)$ is the *prey population*, and

- $y=y(t)$ is the *predator population*.

The only difference from the Lotka–Volterra model is the factor $(1-hx)$ in the prey equation. Notice that if $h=0,$ we get the standard model:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=ax-bxy \\ {y}^{′}=-cy+dxy\end{aligned}
$$

In our modified version of the model, the *intrinsic growth* of prey is given by the $ax(1-hx)$ term. Now, if there are no predators ($y=0$), then 

$$
x' = ax(1-hx).
$$

Recall that general solutions to this equation are logistic functions with two horizontal asymptotes defined by the equilibrium solutions, which can be found by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}ax(1-hx)=0\,⇒\,x=0,\,\frac{1}{h}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the equilibria are $x=0$ and $x=\dfrac{1}{h}.$ The nonzero equilibrium gives the *carrying capacity* (the limit the number of prey is approaching as $t$ goes to infinity).

![](images/8b/8b7a6d12af77f6c2d2e6d3596e71a51a3d697a5c28e9f9c64c5675a01df812d5.png)" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186168028 :tutorial/content "Recall that the equilibrium (fixed) points of a system $\mathbf{x}'(t) = \mathbf{f}(x,y)$ are the points for which $f(x,y)=\mathbf{0}.$ So, for the Lotka–Volterra model 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=ax(1-hx)-bxy \\ {y}^{′}=-cy+dxy\end{aligned}
$$

the equilibria are the solutions of the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}ax(1-hx)-bxy=0 \\ -cy+dxy=0\end{aligned}
$$

Factoring the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-cy+dxy & =0 \\ y(-c+dx) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $y=0$ or $x=\dfrac{c}{d}.$ We consider both cases separately.

- If $y=0,$ substituting it into the first equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}ax(1-hx)-bx(0) & =0 \\ ax(1-hx) & =0 \\ x & =0,\,\frac{1}{h}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the first two equilibria are $(0,0)$ and $\left(\dfrac{1}{h},0\right).$

- If $x=\dfrac{c}{d},$ substituting it into the first equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}a(\frac{c}{d})(1-h(\frac{c}{d}))-b(\frac{c}{d})y & =0 \\ a(1-\frac{c}{d}h)-by & =0 \\ a(1-\frac{c}{d}h) & =by \\ y & =\frac{a}{b}(1-\frac{c}{d}h).\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, another equilibrium is $\left(\dfrac{c}{d}, \dfrac{a}{b}\left(1-\dfrac{c}{d}h\right)\right).$

Therefore, the equilibria of the model are

$$
(0,0), \qquad
\left(\dfrac{1}{h},0\right), \qquad
\left(\dfrac{c}{d}, \dfrac{a}{b}\left(1-\dfrac{c}{d}h\right)\right).
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186168029 :tutorial/content "Consider the modified Lotka–Volterra predator-prey model with carrying capacity 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=ax(1-hx)-bxy \\ {y}^{′}=-cy+dxy\end{aligned}
$$

where $a,b,c,d,h$ are positive real constants, $x=x(t)$ is the prey population, and $y=y(t)$ is the predator population.

To classify the equilibrium at the origin, we need to find the corresponding Jacobian matrix.

Let's denote $f_1(x,y)=ax(1-hx)-bxy$ and $f_2(x,y)=-cy+dxy.$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(ax(1\,-\,hx)-bxy)=a(1\,-\,2hx)-by, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(ax(1\,-\,hx)-bxy)=-bx, \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-cy+dxy)=dy, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-cy+dxy)=-c+dx.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is
![](images/1d/1db459c6fd9f3bad4e5f044d8de8a4e185aeecadddcd73fac75dff09e6fa607d.svg)

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ![](images/03/035a074e405004b43a3f5e509b46affa6e0e53dbf53e26e01149b7ae545c6f64.svg) to get

![](images/cf/cf1eb1b02f6d0dd1b690ac3a69abd1ac6777f592c713060920ef1dcee3fb5600.svg)

The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are $\lambda_1 = a > 0$ and $\lambda_2 = -c < 0.$ Since eigenvalues are real with opposite signs, our equilibrium is an *unstable saddle*.

Thus, the equilibrium at the origin for this model behaves identically to that of the standard Lotka–Volterra model." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186168016 :tutorial/content "Recall that the system

$$

$$
S(x)=\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{L}x).
$$

Then, the series converges for all $x\in R.$

- If $f(x)$ is continuous at $x,$ then the series converges to the value of the function at this point:

$$
S(x)=f(x)
$$

- If $f(x)$ has a jump discontinuity at $x,$ then the series converges to the midpoint between the values of left- and right-sided limits of the function at this point:

$$
S(x)=\frac{{f}^{-}(x)+{f}^{+}(x)}{2}
$$

where ${f}^{-}(x)$ and ${f}^{+}(x)$ are the left- and right-sided limits of the function at this point, respectively.

Notice that the $6$-periodic extension $f(x)$ of our function $F(x)$ is not continuous at $x=-3.$ The one-sided limits at this point are the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{-}(-3) & ={lim}_{x\to -{3}^{-}}f(x)=4 \\ {f}^{+}(-3) & ={lim}_{x\to -{3}^{+}}f(x)=-2\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, the Fourier series of $f(x)$ converges to 

$$
\frac{{f}^{-}(-3)+{f}^{+}(-3)}{2}=\frac{4+(-2)}{2}=1.
$$"] ["question-ac1dfb2b-dc39-5a8f-bb78-6916e280fb3b" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-8e653195-c3d5-582e-822a-b0c443f4aade" :answer-field/id #uuid "8e653195-c3d5-582e-822a-b0c443f4aade"] ["answer-857250c9-a9b1-5080-b2c5-1728296672ed" :answer/id #uuid "857250c9-a9b1-5080-b2c5-1728296672ed"] ["answer-857250c9-a9b1-5080-b2c5-1728296672ed" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-857250c9-a9b1-5080-b2c5-1728296672ed" :answer/value "1"] ["answer-field-8e653195-c3d5-582e-822a-b0c443f4aade" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-8e653195-c3d5-582e-822a-b0c443f4aade" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-8e653195-c3d5-582e-822a-b0c443f4aade" :answer-field/correct "answer-857250c9-a9b1-5080-b2c5-1728296672ed"] ["answer-field-8e653195-c3d5-582e-822a-b0c443f4aade" :answer-field/choices "answer-857250c9-a9b1-5080-b2c5-1728296672ed"] ["question-ac1dfb2b-dc39-5a8f-bb78-6916e280fb3b" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-8e653195-c3d5-582e-822a-b0c443f4aade"] [17592186166960 :knowledge-point/questions "question-ac1dfb2b-dc39-5a8f-bb78-6916e280fb3b"] ["question-967d4b0f-c5b8-576b-b414-bb183f8a1110" :question/id #uuid "967d4b0f-c5b8-576b-b414-bb183f8a1110"] ["question-967d4b0f-c5b8-576b-b414-bb183f8a1110" :question/math-academy-id "q-343368"] ["question-967d4b0f-c5b8-576b-b414-bb183f8a1110" :question/problem "$$

"question-4f10acf7-191a-5a7b-ad4b-e4a80fb0c241"] [17592186107174 :tutorial/content "The **scalar projection** of a vector $\mathbf{a}$ onto another vector $\mathbf{b}$ is the distance that the vector $\mathbf{a}$ extends in the direction of $\mathbf{b}.$

For example, consider two vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ shown below. Suppose we know that $|\,\mathbf{a}\,|=2$ and that the angle between the vectors is $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{4}.$

![](images/a2/a28278cf12885ab7f845407ac2fa7f4ffa00dbe30849a3f8ff41f02e134ed3a0.png)

To illustrate the projection of $\mathbf{a}$ along $\mathbf{b},$ consider the point $P$ on the line that contains $\mathbf{b}$ with $AP \perp \mathbf{b},$ as shown below.

![](images/fd/fd37bdb2a97b4125fb360990d3c4a36b48bcb50433de033a154799db00e474dd.png)

The length $OP$ is called the **scalar projection** of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}$ (or the **component** of $\mathbf{a}$ along $\mathbf{b}$). It is denoted as $\text{comp}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a},$ and we can compute it using cosine in $\triangle OPA$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{b}\,a & =OP \\  & =|\,a\,|\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =2\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

This formula is the general definition of the scalar projection:

$$
\text{comp}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a}= |\,\mathbf{a}\,| \cos\theta
$$"] [17592186107177 :tutorial/content "The scalar projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}$ can be negative. This happens when the vector $\mathbf{a}$ extends in the direction opposite to that of $\mathbf{b}.$

However, sometimes we are not given the angle between two vectors. In such cases, we can solve for $\cos \theta$ in terms of the dot product:

$$
\begin{aligned}a\cdot b & =|\,a\,|\,|\,b\,|\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{a\cdot b}{|\,a\,|\,|\,b\,|}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into our original formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{b}\,a & =|\,a\,|\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =|\,a\,|\cdot \frac{a\cdot b}{|\,a\,|\,|\,b\,|} \\  & =\frac{a\cdot b}{|\,b\,|}.\end{aligned}
$$

meters."] ["question-4f002498-444e-5f1e-b174-d456ccc0407b" :question/worked-solution "The width of the plot is $x+3$ meters, and its area is $2{x}^{2}+6x$ square meters. Since the $\text{area}=\text{length}\times \text{width},$ we factor the expression for the area to find the length.

First, we find the $\text{GCF}$ of the two terms:

$$
\text{GCF}(2{x}^{2},6x)=2x
$$

Then, we rewrite each term in the original expression as a product with the $\text{GCF}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}+6x & = \\ (2x\cdot x)+(2x\cdot 3)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we write the $\text{GCF}$ outside the parentheses and keep the remaining terms inside:

$$
\begin{aligned}(2x\cdot x)+(2x\cdot 3) & = \\ 2x(x+3)\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we conclude that the length of the plot must be $2x$ meters.

First, we find the factor pairs of the constant term $(-10).$ The constant term is negative, so that means one of the factors is negative, and the other is positive:

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & \times (-10) \\ (-1) & \times 10 \\ 2 & \times (-5) \\ (-2) & \times 5\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find which factor pair adds up to the coefficient of the linear term $3:$

$$
\begin{aligned}1+(-10) & =-9 & \times  \\ -1+10 & =9 & \times  \\ 2+(-5) & =-3 & \times  \\ -2+5 & =3 & ✓\end{aligned}
$$

Using the factor pair identified above, write the linear term as $3x=5x-2x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+3x-10 & ={x}^{2}+5x-2x-10\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we factor the first two terms and the last two terms separately, and then factor the expression completely:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+5x-2x-10 & = \\ ({x}^{2}+5x)+(-2x-10) & = \\ x(x+5)-2(x+5) & = \\ (x-2)(x+5)\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we conclude that the width must be $x-2$ meters.

 thousand dollars."] ["question-378ec187-f25a-5aab-8757-77a5a8639517" :question/worked-solution "The land initially costs $200$ thousand, which increases at a rate of $10%$ per year.

$10%$ as a decimal is $0.1.$ Therefore, an increase of $10%$ corresponds to multiplication by a factor of

$$
1+0.1=1.1.
$$

Therefore, we have:

* After $1$ year, the value will be $200\cdot (1.1)$ thousand dollars.

* After $2$ years, the value will be $200\cdot (1.1)^{2}$ thousand dollars.

* After $3$ years, the value will be $200\cdot (1.1)^{3}$ thousand dollars.

* After $4$ years, the value will be $200\cdot (1.1)^{4}$ thousand dollars.

Evaluating the expression for the value after $4$ years, we get the following:

$$
200\cdot (1.1)^{4}=292.82≈293,
$$

rounded to the nearest integer.

Therefore, after $4$ years, the land will be worth approximately $293$ thousand dollars."] ["question-378ec187-f25a-5aab-8757-77a5a8639517" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-72f9737f-d640-5da4-81bf-c4cffe514f28" :answer-field/id #uuid "72f9737f-d640-5da4-81bf-c4cffe514f28"] ["answer-3d4de7d8-5d3b-5a06-9122-9e43959fa9aa" :answer/id #uuid "3d4de7d8-5d3b-5a06-9122-9e43959fa9aa"] ["answer-3d4de7d8-5d3b-5a06-9122-9e43959fa9aa" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-3d4de7d8-5d3b-5a06-9122-9e43959fa9aa" :answer/value "293"] ["answer-field-72f9737f-d640-5da4-81bf-c4cffe514f28" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-72f9737f-d640-5da4-81bf-c4cffe514f28" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-72f9737f-d640-5da4-81bf-c4cffe514f28" :answer-field/correct "answer-3d4de7d8-5d3b-5a06-9122-9e43959fa9aa"] ["answer-field-72f9737f-d640-5da4-81bf-c4cffe514f28" :answer-field/choices "answer-3d4de7d8-5d3b-5a06-9122-9e43959fa9aa"] ["question-378ec187-f25a-5aab-8757-77a5a8639517" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-72f9737f-d640-5da4-81bf-c4cffe514f28"] [17592186110626 :knowledge-point/questions "question-378ec187-f25a-5aab-8757-77a5a8639517"] ["question-f2953556-ba6d-59b1-a416-ed49b0dde4d7" :question/id #uuid "f2953556-ba6d-59b1-a416-ed49b0dde4d7"] ["question-f2953556-ba6d-59b1-a416-ed49b0dde4d7" :question/math-academy-id "q-133320"] ["question-f2953556-ba6d-59b1-a416-ed49b0dde4d7" :question/problem "The value $V(t)$ of Fred's plot of land, in thousands of dollars, can be modeled by the function $V(t)=200\cdot (1.1)^{t},$ where $t$ is the time in years since he bought the land. To do this, we sometimes need to factor the numerator and denominator before canceling.

For example, suppose that we wish to simplify $\dfrac {4x - 12} {10x + 4}.$ To do this, we factor the numerator and denominator and cancel any factors that they have in common.

$$
\eqalign{
		\dfrac {4x - 12} {10x + 4}
		&=\dfrac {4(x - 3)} {2(5x + 2)}\[5pt]
&=\dfrac {2 \cdot 2 \cdot (x - 3)} {2(5x + 2)}\[5pt]		
		&=\dfrac {\cancel{2} \cdot 2(x - 3)} {\cancel{2}(5x + 2)}\[5pt]	
		&=\dfrac {2(x - 3)} {5x + 2}
	}
$$"] [17592186068956 :activity/expected-seconds 540.0] ["question-2304365e-e658-571a-a752-03df743e6d8e" :question/id #uuid "2304365e-e658-571a-a752-03df743e6d8e"] ["question-2304365e-e658-571a-a752-03df743e6d8e" :question/math-academy-id "q-118578"] ["question-2304365e-e658-571a-a752-03df743e6d8e" :question/problem "Given that $y=y(t),$ what is the carrying capacity of the following logistic growth model?

$$

:question/problem "Consider the following differential equation for the function $y=y(t):$

$$

$$

What is ${lim}_{t\to \infty }y(t)?$"] ["question-da1f1140-0b6f-5e8e-98c1-c5bc7c260a47" :question/worked-solution "A logistic growth equation has the form

$$
{y}^{′}=ky(a-y),
$$

where $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality, and $a>y$ is the carrying capacity.

A diagram showing a typical logistic growth curve is shown below.

![](images/57/57f4b604c546daed4f1cb3895191fae0ccac33b5c17aac705f203f0a837c7e69.png)

First, let's rewrite the right-hand side of the given equation so that it matches the form above:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =9y(1-\frac{y}{1\,200}) \\  & =9y(\frac{1\,200-y}{1\,200}) \\  & =\frac{9y}{1\,200}(1\,200-y) \\  & =\frac{3y}{400}(1\,200-y)\end{aligned}
$$

From here, we see that $a=1\,200.$ Hence, the carrying capacity is $1\,200.$

For a given logistic growth model, $y\to a$ as $t\to \infty .$ Therefore,

$$
{lim}_{t\to \infty }y(t)=1\,200.
$$"] ["question-da1f1140-0b6f-5e8e-98c1-c5bc7c260a47" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-c9c885db-a51b-565f-802d-b5e3e3429fb9" :answer-field/id #uuid $$
y' = 5y(10-y), \qquad y(0) = y_0.
$$

The logistic growth curve for this problem is sketched below.

![](images/0a/0a225fd04f81bd65e1bad3ff14097563d112a16e3847aac26cc86591533ea5d0.png)

The curve contains an inflection point, that is, a point where $y(t)$ is growing at its fastest possible rate. What information can we deduce about this point? 

To find the inflection point, we solve $y''(t) = 0.$ First, we differentiate the differential equation using implicit differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{″} & =(5y)^{′}\cdot (10-y)+(5y)\cdot (10-y)^{′} \\  & =5\cdot (10-y)\cdot {y}^{′}+(5y)\cdot (-1)\cdot {y}^{′} \\  & ={y}^{′}\cdot (5\cdot (10-y)+(5y)\cdot (-1)) \\  & ={y}^{′}\cdot (50-5y-5y) \\  & ={y}^{′}\cdot (50-10y)\end{aligned}
$$

We now need to solve $y''(t) = 0,$ i.e.,

$$
y'\cdot\left(50-10y\right) = 0.
$$

We know that $y'$ is increasing for all $t,$ so $y'\neq 0.$ Therefore, we must have

$$
50-10y = 0\quad \Rightarrow\quad y = 5.
$$

Let's mark this on our diagram.

![](images/75/75d0363483e1bda70decb171466fe9e506eb0da80d0e78ed893bb61551ae9d44.png)

The fact that the inflection point occurs when $y$ is precisely half the carrying capacity is *not* a coincidence. In fact, this is always the case. The general situation is shown below.

![](images/77/7754f42adbb938c1d07ab2636a4c24f1cd0bc8536c974af2497e997589efa115.png)"] [17592186176102 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0] [17592186106111 :question/problem "Suppose that $|\,a\,|=8$, $|\,b\,|=2$ and that the angle between the vectors is $\theta ={120}^{∘}.$ Find the vector projection of $a$ onto $b$ in terms of the vector $b.$"] [17592186106111 :question/worked-solution "First, we find the scalar projection as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{b}\,a & =|\,a\,|\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =8\operatorname{cos}⁡({120}^{∘}) \\  & =8\cdot (-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the unit vector that is parallel to $b:$

$$
u=\frac{b}{|\,b\,|}=\frac{b}{2}=\frac{1}{2}b
$$

Finally, we compute the vector projection as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,a & ={\text{comp}}_{b}\,a\cdot u \\  & =(-4)\cdot \frac{1}{2}b \\  & =-2b\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186106111 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] [17592186102542 :answer-field/correct 17592186102547] ["question-b6749b1c-5bbb-5e2e-a55f-6596daa98287" :question/id #uuid "b6749b1c-5bbb-5e2e-a55f-6596daa98287"] ["question-b6749b1c-5bbb-5e2e-a55f-6596daa98287" :question/math-academy-id "q-126505"] ["question-b6749b1c-5bbb-5e2e-a55f-6596daa98287" :question/problem "Suppose that $|\,p\,|=3$, $|\,q\,|=6\sqrt{2}$ and that the angle between the vectors is $\theta =\frac{3\pi }{4}.$ Find the vector projection of $q$ onto $p$ in terms of the vector $p.$"] ["question-b6749b1c-5bbb-5e2e-a55f-6596daa98287" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the scalar projection as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{p}\,q & =|\,q\,|\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =6\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{4}) \\  & =6\sqrt{2}\cdot (-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) \\  & =-6\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the unit vector that is parallel to $p:$

$$
u=\frac{p}{|\,p\,|}=\frac{p}{3}=\frac{1}{3}p
$$

Finally, we compute the vector projection as follows:

$$

:question/worked-solution "Since $a$ is a nonzero vector, its projection onto another nonzero vector $b$ equals the zero vector only when the vectors are perpendicular. 

So, we must have

$$
a⊥b\,⟹\,a\cdot b=0.
$$

Computing the dot product, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}a\cdot b & ={a}_{x}\cdot {b}_{x}+{a}_{y}\cdot {b}_{y}+{a}_{z}\cdot {b}_{z} \\  & =1\cdot 1+2\cdot x+(-1)\cdot 2 \\  & =2x-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting the dot product equal to $0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}a\cdot b & =0 \\ 2x-1 & =0 \\ 2x & =1 \\ x & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-1d98c763-a05e-5de6-913c-903735959780" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-0dfe0b7a-7e87-551d-9c63-3d3fbe0f0ee6" :answer-field/id #uuid ${9}^{-5}\times {9}^{3}=${{field-1}}."] ["question-0c468631-3494-5a5c-8263-59a9e6ef38aa" :question/worked-solution "To multiply powers of the same base, we add the exponents:

$$
{9}^{-5}\times {9}^{3}={9}^{-5+3}={9}^{-2}
$$

To evaluate ${9}^{-2},$ we find the reciprocal of the base $(9)$ and then raise that reciprocal to the same power but with the opposite sign:

$$
{9}^{-2}={(\frac{1}{9})}^{2}=\frac{1}{9}\times \frac{1}{9}=\frac{1}{81}
$$"] ["question-0c468631-3494-5a5c-8263-59a9e6ef38aa" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-e83883fd-0df1-5652-851f-22e92beb519e" :answer-field/id #uuid "e83883fd-0df1-5652-851f-22e92beb519e"] ["answer-40a24c23-247d-5712-9a28-a78576688a6a" :answer/id #uuid "40a24c23-247d-5712-9a28-a78576688a6a"] ["answer-40a24c23-247d-5712-9a28-a78576688a6a" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-40a24c23-247d-5712-9a28-a78576688a6a" :answer/value "\frac{1}{81}"] ["answer-field-e83883fd-0df1-5652-851f-22e92beb519e" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-e83883fd-0df1-5652-851f-22e92beb519e" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-e83883fd-0df1-5652-851f-22e92beb519e" :answer-field/correct "answer-40a24c23-247d-5712-9a28-a78576688a6a"] ["answer-field-e83883fd-0df1-5652-851f-22e92beb519e" :answer-field/choices "answer-40a24c23-247d-5712-9a28-a78576688a6a"] ["question-0c468631-3494-5a5c-8263-59a9e6ef38aa" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-e83883fd-0df1-5652-851f-22e92beb519e"] [17592186059873 :knowledge-point/questions "question-0c468631-3494-5a5c-8263-59a9e6ef38aa"] ["question-9f94c748-cc3f-548a-899d-563289a823a1" :question/id #uuid "9f94c748-cc3f-548a-899d-563289a823a1"] ["question-9f94c748-cc3f-548a-899d-563289a823a1" :question/math-academy-id "q-185302"] ["question-9f94c748-cc3f-548a-899d-563289a823a1" :question/problem "Evaluate the following:

${9}^{7}\times {9}^{-7}=$
{{field-1}}"] ["question-9f94c748-cc3f-548a-899d-563289a823a1" :question/worked-solution "To multiply powers of the same base, we add the exponents:

$$
{9}^{7}\times {9}^{-7}={9}^{7-7}={9}^{0}
$$

Any number raised to the power of zero is equal to $1.$ So, 

$$
{9}^{0}=1.
$$"] ["question-9f94c748-cc3f-548a-899d-563289a823a1" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-50df2db3-7cd5-5db4-9261-95bd3ad3d338" :answer-field/id #uuid "50df2db3-7cd5-5db4-9261-95bd3ad3d338"] ["answer-3b1d0bba-a1da-5243-9c9b-11bf413194b9" :answer/id #uuid "3b1d0bba-a1da-5243-9c9b-11bf413194b9"] ["answer-3b1d0bba-a1da-5243-9c9b-11bf413194b9" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-3b1d0bba-a1da-5243-9c9b-11bf413194b9" :answer/value "1"] ["answer-field-50df2db3-7cd5-5db4-9261-95bd3ad3d338" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-50df2db3-7cd5-5db4-9261-95bd3ad3d338" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-50df2db3-7cd5-5db4-9261-95bd3ad3d338" :answer-field/correct "answer-3b1d0bba-a1da-5243-9c9b-11bf413194b9"] ["answer-field-50df2db3-7cd5-5db4-9261-95bd3ad3d338" :answer-field/choices "answer-3b1d0bba-a1da-5243-9c9b-11bf413194b9"] ["question-9f94c748-cc3f-548a-899d-563289a823a1" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-50df2db3-7cd5-5db4-9261-95bd3ad3d338"] [17592186059873 :knowledge-point/questions "question-9f94c748-cc3f-548a-899d-563289a823a1"] [17592186060989 :tutorial/content "To multiply powers of the same base, we simply *add* the exponents. This is called the **product rule for exponents**.
For example, in the expression 

$$
{\color{blue}3}^4 \times {\color{blue}3}^2,
$$

both powers have the same base $({\color{blue}3}).$ Therefore, we can simplify this expression by adding the exponents:

$$
{\color{blue}3}^4 \times {\color{blue}3}^2 = {\color{blue}3}^{4+2} = {\color{blue}3}^6
$$

**Note:** The product rule for exponents is really just a quicker alternative to using repeated multiplication, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{3}^{4}\times {3}^{2} & = \\ {{3\times 3\times 3\times 3}_{⏟}}_{4\text{ copies}}\times {{3\times 3}_{⏟}}_{2\text{ copies}} & = \\ {{3\times 3\times 3\times 3\times 3\times 3}_{⏟}}_{6\text{ copies}} & = \\ {3}^{6}\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186060990 :tutorial/content "We can use the product rule for exponents with negative exponents too. For instance, to simplify $3^3\times 3^{-5},$ we add the exponents:

$$
3^{3} \times 3^{-5} = 3^{3-5} = 3^{-2}
$$

Now, to evaluate $3^{-2},$ we find the reciprocal of the base $(3)$ and then raise that reciprocal to the same power but with the opposite sign:

$$
3^{-2}  = \left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^2 =\dfrac{1}{3} \times \dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{1}{9}
$$"] [17592186059942 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0] [17592186054396 :question/worked-solution "To evaluate this expression, we use PEMDAS. First, we compute the exponents:

$$
\begin{aligned}{{(-3)^{3}}_{⏟}}_{-27}÷6=(-27)÷6\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we divide:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-27)÷6 & = \\ \frac{(-27)}{6} & = \\ -\frac{27}{6} & = \\ -\frac{27÷3}{6÷3} & = \\ -\frac{9}{2}\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186054397 :question/problem "Evaluate $(1-4)^2 \times \dfrac{1}{12}.$"] [17592186054397 :question/worked-solution "To evaluate this expression, we use PEMDAS. First, we perform the operation inside the parentheses:

$$
\begin{aligned}({{1-4}_{⏟}}_{-3})^{2}\times \frac{1}{12} & =(-3)^{2}\times \frac{1}{12}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the exponents:

$$
\begin{aligned}{{(-3)^{2}}_{⏟}}_{9}\times \frac{1}{12} & =9\times \frac{1}{12}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we multiply:

$$
\begin{aligned}9\times \frac{1}{12} & = \\ \frac{9}{1}\times \frac{1}{12} & = \\ \frac{9\times 1}{1\times 12} & = \\ \frac{9}{12} & = \\ \frac{9÷3}{12÷3} & = \\ \frac{3}{4}\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186054398 :question/problem "What is the value of $\left( 5 \div (-2)^2 \right) \times \left( -\dfrac{4}{5} \right).$"] [17592186054398 :question/worked-solution "To evaluate this expression, we use PEMDAS. First, consider the expression inside the parenthesis:

$$
\begin{aligned}5÷(-2)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Applying PEMDAS to this expression, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}5÷(-2)^{2} & = \\ 5÷4 & = \\ \frac{5}{4} & \end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we multiply:

$$
\begin{aligned}(\overset{\frac{5}{4}}{\overset{⏞}{5÷(-2)^{2}}})\times (-\frac{4}{5}) & = \\ \frac{5}{4}\times (-\frac{4}{5}) & = \\ -\frac{5}{4}\times \frac{4}{5} & = \\ -\frac{5\times 4}{4\times 5} & = \\ -\frac{\cancel{5}\times \cancel{4}}{\cancel{4}\times \cancel{5}} & = \\ -1\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186055269 :question/problem "${(-3)}^{3}+{4}^{3}=$"] [17592186055269 :question/worked-solution "To evaluate the given expression, we use PEMDAS. 

First, we compute the exponents:

$$
\begin{aligned}{(-3)}^{3}+{4}^{3}=(-27)+64\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we add:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-27)+64 & = \\ -27+64 & = \\ 37\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186055269 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] [17592186052851 :answer-field/correct 17592186052852] ["question-60199b98-6c64-506f-9047-6445f428ee81" :question/id #uuid "60199b98-6c64-506f-9047-6445f428ee81"] ["question-60199b98-6c64-506f-9047-6445f428ee81" :question/math-academy-id "q-184045"] ["question-60199b98-6c64-506f-9047-6445f428ee81" :question/problem "${6}^{3}÷{(-3)}^{2}+10=${{field-1}}"] ["question-60199b98-6c64-506f-9047-6445f428ee81" :question/worked-solution "To evaluate the given expression, we use PEMDAS. 

First, we compute the exponent:

$$
\begin{aligned}{6}^{3}÷{(-3)}^{2}+10 & =216÷9+10\end{aligned}

Next, we divide:

$$
\begin{aligned}216÷9+10 & =24+10\end{aligned}

Finally, we add:

$$
\begin{aligned}24+10 & =34\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-60199b98-6c64-506f-9047-6445f428ee81" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-066805a8-839c-56e1-9e27-03e5c7c1c20b" :answer-field/id #uuid "066805a8-839c-56e1-9e27-03e5c7c1c20b"] ["answer-d4140eae-8d2c-5e0e-99c8-5016610f0c02" :answer/id #uuid "d4140eae-8d2c-5e0e-99c8-5016610f0c02"] ["answer-d4140eae-8d2c-5e0e-99c8-5016610f0c02" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-d4140eae-8d2c-5e0e-99c8-5016610f0c02" :answer/value "34"] ["answer-field-066805a8-839c-56e1-9e27-03e5c7c1c20b" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-066805a8-839c-56e1-9e27-03e5c7c1c20b" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-066805a8-839c-56e1-9e27-03e5c7c1c20b" :answer-field/correct "answer-d4140eae-8d2c-5e0e-99c8-5016610f0c02"] ["answer-field-066805a8-839c-56e1-9e27-03e5c7c1c20b" :answer-field/choices "answer-d4140eae-8d2c-5e0e-99c8-5016610f0c02"] ["question-60199b98-6c64-506f-9047-6445f428ee81" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-066805a8-839c-56e1-9e27-03e5c7c1c20b"] [17592186054606 :knowledge-point/questions "question-60199b98-6c64-506f-9047-6445f428ee81"] ["question-d7d9db10-3db0-5298-a1d1-4ea150f26c84" :question/id #uuid "d7d9db10-3db0-5298-a1d1-4ea150f26c84"] ["question-d7d9db10-3db0-5298-a1d1-4ea150f26c84" :question/math-academy-id "q-184053"] ["question-d7d9db10-3db0-5298-a1d1-4ea150f26c84" :question/problem "${(2-(-1))}^{4}=${{field-1}}"] ["question-d7d9db10-3db0-5298-a1d1-4ea150f26c84" :question/worked-solution "To evaluate this expression, we use PEMDAS.

["question-92e6407b-23f0-522c-8861-cf43d1d90280" :question/worked-solution "To evaluate this expression, we use PEMDAS.

First, consider the expression inside the parentheses:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-3)^{4}÷9\end{aligned}
$$

Applying PEMDAS to this expression, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-3)^{4}÷9 & = \\ 81÷9 & = \\ \frac{81}{9} & = \\ 9\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-18)÷((-3)^{4}÷9) & = \\ (-18)÷9 & = \\ \frac{(-18)}{9} & = \\ -\frac{18}{9} & = \\ -2\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-92e6407b-23f0-522c-8861-cf43d1d90280" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-06fd876a-80c1-5d01-8d82-49f786db185b" :answer-field/id #uuid "06fd876a-80c1-5d01-8d82-49f786db185b"] ["answer-8bbbd880-d7e2-5a44-b42a-0dfce6cf9fa9" :answer/id #uuid "8bbbd880-d7e2-5a44-b42a-0dfce6cf9fa9"] ["answer-8bbbd880-d7e2-5a44-b42a-0dfce6cf9fa9" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-8bbbd880-d7e2-5a44-b42a-0dfce6cf9fa9" :answer/value "-2"] ["answer-field-06fd876a-80c1-5d01-8d82-49f786db185b" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-06fd876a-80c1-5d01-8d82-49f786db185b" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-06fd876a-80c1-5d01-8d82-49f786db185b" :answer-field/correct "answer-8bbbd880-d7e2-5a44-b42a-0dfce6cf9fa9"] ["answer-field-06fd876a-80c1-5d01-8d82-49f786db185b" :answer-field/choices "answer-8bbbd880-d7e2-5a44-b42a-0dfce6cf9fa9"] ["question-92e6407b-23f0-522c-8861-cf43d1d90280" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-06fd876a-80c1-5d01-8d82-49f786db185b"] [17592186054608 :knowledge-point/questions "question-92e6407b-23f0-522c-8861-cf43d1d90280"] ["question-6b52aa6c-ff41-5226-8eac-b56efc594a90" :question/id #uuid "6b52aa6c-ff41-5226-8eac-b56efc594a90"] ["question-6b52aa6c-ff41-5226-8eac-b56efc594a90" :question/math-academy-id "q-100159"] ["question-6b52aa6c-ff41-5226-8eac-b56efc594a90" :question/problem "Evaluate $(3\times (-5)^{2})÷\frac{5}{2}.$"] ["question-6b52aa6c-ff41-5226-8eac-b56efc594a90" :question/worked-solution "To evaluate this expression, we use PEMDAS.

"question-6b52aa6c-ff41-5226-8eac-b56efc594a90"] [17592186056019 :tutorial/content "As we already know, to evaluate numerical expressions with a mix of different operations, we must follow the order of operations (PEMDAS).

The same rules apply to numerical expressions with negative numbers. For example, let's compute the value of

$$
(-2) \times (-3)^2.
$$

To evaluate this expression, we use PEMDAS.  First, we compute the exponents:

$$
(-2)\,\times\overbrace{(-3)^2}^{\large\color{blue} 9}  = (-2) \times {\color{blue} 9}
$$

 

Then, we multiply:

$$
(-2) \times 9 = -18
$$

Therefore,

$$
(-2) \times (-3)^2 = -18.
$$"] [17592186054876 :activity/expected-seconds 480.0] [17592186133592 :question/problem "Let ![](images/25/2501c175aa25fd5d70af201c3bd0788da58b674c5782984e06a089a4447299a1.svg) and ![](images/f4/f455effab674ae3ee3a0c2b0773c011735f3d3885a1c392b0233b7c5d164ee9b.svg) Find the orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\text{Span}\{\mathbf{b}\}.$"] [17592186133593 :question/problem "Let ![](images/47/479dd80d441e3da4c3f2c20a18dd124f061f47cc2ab421a1499003a70caf3465.svg) and ![](images/1f/1f190dbb10618181ed258e192d8e005947a1d38aaaf5d6e63e162ad4f399e302.svg) If $\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{y} + \mathbf{z},$ where $\mathbf{y} \in \text{Span}\{\mathbf{a}\}$ and $\mathbf{z} \perp \text{Span}\{\mathbf{a}\},$ then find $\mathbf{z}.$"] [17592186133594 :question/problem "Given the vector $\mathbf{x}$ and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of $\mathbf{x}$ onto the solution space of the system.

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:    

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 4 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are $2$ pivot columns ($1$st and $2$nd). Thus, $x_3$ is a free variable. Now, from the second equation, we get $x_2=4x_3.$ 
Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain  

$$
x_1+4x_3+4x_3= 0
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
x_1=-8x_3.
$$

So, the general solution is
![](images/4b/4b13b3d4dbb889a07cece9dde6f9caf69d09b4eed2dc23e77407b9b5697775a6.svg)
Consequently, ![](images/ff/ff7ca7de3065a85bdf61586cf2a021acca8b62ac7eb2f8ec5d73f0291074ebd8.svg) is a basis of the solution space of the system.

Finally, we find the projection of $\mathbf{x}$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot b}{b\cdot b}b \\  & =\frac{(-10)\cdot (-8)+20\cdot 4+2\cdot 1}{{(-8)}^{2}+{4}^{2}+{1}^{2}}b \\  & =\frac{80+80+2}{64+16+1}b \\  & =\frac{162}{81}b \\  & =2b \\  & =2[\begin{aligned}-8 \\ 4 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-16 \\ 8 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-7284284d-f752-5dcb-a337-d7dc9bc05a72" :question/id #uuid "7284284d-f752-5dcb-a337-d7dc9bc05a72"] ["question-7284284d-f752-5dcb-a337-d7dc9bc05a72" :question/math-academy-id "q-81403"] ["question-7284284d-f752-5dcb-a337-d7dc9bc05a72" :question/problem "Let $a=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ and $b=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Find the orthogonal projection of $a$ onto $\text{Span}\{b\}.$"] ["question-7284284d-f752-5dcb-a337-d7dc9bc05a72" :question/worked-solution "The orthogonal projection of $a$ onto $\text{Span}\{b\}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 0 \\ 2 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

$$
[\begin{aligned}2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]={x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.

$$

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & -3 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & -3 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are $2$ pivot columns ($1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. Now, from the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}=\frac{3}{5}{x}_{3}.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
{x}_{1}-2(\frac{3}{5}{x}_{3})=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=\frac{6}{5}{x}_{3}.
$$

So, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{6}{5}{x}_{3} \\ \frac{3}{5}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{5}{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 3 \\ 5\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Consequently, $B=\{[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 3 \\ 5\end{aligned}]\}$ is a basis of the solution space of the system.

Finally, we find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot b}{b\cdot b}b \\  & =\frac{(-10)\cdot 6+(-15)\cdot 3+28\cdot 5}{{6}^{2}+{3}^{2}+{5}^{2}}b \\  & =\frac{-60-45+140}{36+9+25}b \\  & =\frac{35}{70}b \\  & =\frac{1}{2}b \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 3 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ \frac{3}{2} \\ \frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186394133 :question/problem "Given the vector $x$ and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system.
