vector $b$ equals the zero vector only when the vectors are perpendicular. 

So, we must have

$$
a⊥b\,⟹\,a\cdot b=0.
$$

Computing the dot product, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}a\cdot b & ={a}_{x}\cdot {b}_{x}+{a}_{y}\cdot {b}_{y}+{a}_{z}\cdot {b}_{z} \\  & =-4\cdot 4+4\cdot (-1)+1\cdot x \\  & =x-20.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting the dot product equal to $0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}a\cdot b & =0 \\ x-20 & =0 \\ x & =20.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186106479 :question/id #uuid "ab29d467-5294-537a-b48f-a1d1aefe0cab" :question/math-academy-id "q-71668"} {:db/id 17592186290292 :question/id #uuid :topic/math-academy-id 1295} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186106562 :step/content {:db/id 17592186107166 :tutorial/content "The **vector projection** of a vector $\mathbf{a}$ onto another vector $\mathbf{b}$ is the portion that the vector $\mathbf{a}$ extends along $\mathbf{b}.$

For example, consider two vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ shown below. Suppose we know that $|\mathbf{a}|=2,$ $|\mathbf{b}|=3,$ and the angle between the vectors is $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{4}.$

![](images/a2/a28278cf12885ab7f845407ac2fa7f4ffa00dbe30849a3f8ff41f02e134ed3a0.png)

The starting point of the vector projection is $O,$ and the ending point will be the point $P$ that lies on the line containing $\mathbf{b}$ with $AP \perp \mathbf{b},$ as shown below.

![](images/f0/f0b267fb009e79eb16f86be42edc2c835808b28aa3eaf1c7e857300224ee01ec.png)

The vector $\overrightarrow{OP}$ is called the **vector projection** of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}.$ It is denoted as $\text{proj}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a},$ and it is computed as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,a & =OP\cdot u \\  & ={\text{comp}}_{b}\,a\cdot u\end{aligned}
$$

where $\text{comp}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a} = |\,\mathbf{a}\,| \cos\theta$ is the scalar projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}$ and $\mathbf{u}$ is a unit vector in the direction of $\mathbf{b}.$

First, we compute the scalar projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{b}\,a & =|\,a\,|\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the unit vector that is parallel to $\mathbf{b}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\mathbf{u} = \dfrac{\mathbf{b}}{|\,\mathbf{b}\,|} = \dfrac{\mathbf{b}}{3} = \dfrac{1}{3} \mathbf{b}
$$

Therefore, the vector projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,a & ={\text{comp}}_{b}\,a\cdot u \\  & =\sqrt{2}\cdot \frac{1}{3}b \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}b.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "5962a19e-bb12-54d8-b53a-24578711fa53" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9051 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "26031206-512a-5b41-90d5-299987889655" :step/math-academy-id 121755 :step/next {:db/id 17592186106650}} {:db/id 17592186106563 :step/content {:db/id 17592186105701 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186105478 :question/id #uuid "3278333b-a29e-54c5-bc94-b5525bc6f751" :question/math-academy-id "e-14617"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "7c9317eb-d1ce-5f42-b69b-a37e643b865b" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049360} {:db/id 17592186049653}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186106111} {:db/id 17592186106480} {:db/id 17592186287856} {:db/id 17592186287939} {:db/id 17592186292817} {:db/id 17592186292818} {:db/id 17592186297479} {:db/id 17592186297480} {:db/id 17592186339000} {:db/id 17592186339001} {:db/id 17592186339002} {:db/id 17592186441580} {:db/id 17592186441582} {:db/id 17592186441585} {:db/id 17592186441586}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating a Vector Projection Using Angle and Magnitude"} :step/id #uuid "e6fd410f-37e5-5a4e-a29d-c160c7d2a397" :step/math-academy-id 121756 :step/next {:db/id 17592186106564}} {:db/id 17592186106564 :step/content {:db/id 17592186107167 :tutorial/content "We have been using the following formula for the vector projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\text{proj}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a} =\text{comp}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{u}
$$

However, we can write an alternative formula using the formula for the scalar projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{b}\,a & =\frac{a\cdot b}{|\,b\,|}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the original formula for the vector projection, and also substituting $\mathbf{u} = \dfrac{\mathbf{b}}{| \, \mathbf{b} \, |},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,a & =\frac{a\cdot b}{|\,b\,|}\cdot \frac{b}{|\,b\,|} \\  & =\frac{a\cdot b}{|\,b\,{|}^{2}}b \\  & =\frac{a\cdot b}{b\cdot b}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, another general formula for the vector projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,a & =\frac{a\cdot b}{b\cdot b}b.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "e4098700-6d5c-5618-90a8-8dea2d4dbed0" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9052 :tutorial/title "A General Formula"} :step/id #uuid "a78e2420-8af1-50c7-9a19-b4ceac9bcde4" :step/math-academy-id 121763} {:db/id 17592186106567 :step/content {:db/id 17592186107168 :tutorial/content "Notice that if two vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ are perpendicular, then by projecting $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}$ (or $\mathbf{b}$ onto $\mathbf{a}$), we obtain the zero vector.

For example, the projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto a perpendicular vector $\mathbf{b}$ looks as follows:

![](images/91/9163eda36b752f1e36195b8b5a1d40bf545ec21a3988f5480d6ddcbb926c00ea.png)

Furthermore, we have the following fact:

*If $\mathbf{a}$ is a nonzero vector, its projection onto another nonzero vector $\mathbf{b}$ equals the zero vector if and only if the vectors are perpendicular.*" :tutorial/id #uuid "97117437-4034-5cb8-84a6-675d75d4f874" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9059 :tutorial/title "Projecting Perpendicular Vectors"} :step/id #uuid "ec38d18e-577a-5ebc-8349-60991ef75b80" :step/math-academy-id 121766 :step/next {:db/id 17592186106566}} {:db/id 17592186106650 :step/content {:db/id 17592186107181 :tutorial/content "When finding the projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b},$ we sometimes find that the resulting projection vector points in the opposite direction to $\mathbf{b}.$ This happens when the vector $\mathbf{a}$ extends in the direction opposite to that of $\mathbf{b}.$

![](images/0e/0e973e6f6484a9aad863ebfe89fc1ea6356d6a50844931306c6aa2b63be18a8a.png)

Consider two vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b},$ where it is known that 

$$
|\,\mathbf{a}\,|=2,\qquad |\,\mathbf{b}\,|=3,\qquad \theta = 135^\circ.
$$

Let's calculate $\textrm{proj}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a}.$ 

First, notice that the angle between $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ is obtuse. This means we expect the projection vector to point in the opposite direction to that of $\mathbf b.$

Next, we compute the scalar projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{b}\,a & =|\,a\,|\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡({135}^{∘}) \\  & =2\cdot (-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) \\  & =-\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the scalar projection is negative. 

Then, we find the unit vector that is parallel to $\mathbf{b}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\mathbf{u} = \dfrac{\mathbf{b}}{|\,\mathbf{b}\,|} = \dfrac{\mathbf{b}}{3} = \dfrac{1}{3} \mathbf{b}
$$

Therefore, the vector projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,a & ={\text{comp}}_{b}\,a\cdot u \\  & =-\sqrt{2}\cdot \frac{1}{3}b \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}b.\end{aligned}
$$

This vector points in the direction opposite to $\mathbf{b},$ as expected." :tutorial/id #uuid "2df5fde5-316c-5962-8f0d-56362287c447" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9677 :tutorial/title "The Direction of the Projection Vector"} :step/id #uuid "fdc39c18-bf51-5a32-a828-404d1e341f7a" :step/math-academy-id 187844 :step/next {:db/id 17592186106563}}] :activity/title "Calculating a Vector Projection" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186105967} {:db/id 17592186106562 :step/content {:db/id 17592186107166 :tutorial/content "The **vector projection** of a vector $\mathbf{a}$ onto another vector $\mathbf{b}$ is the portion that the vector $\mathbf{a}$ extends along $\mathbf{b}.$

where $\text{comp}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a} = |\,\mathbf{a}\,| \cos\theta$ is the scalar projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}$ and $\mathbf{u}$ is a unit vector in the direction of $\mathbf{b}.$

First, we compute the scalar projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{b}\,a & =|\,a\,|\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the unit vector that is parallel to $\mathbf{b}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\mathbf{u} = \dfrac{\mathbf{b}}{|\,\mathbf{b}\,|} = \dfrac{\mathbf{b}}{3} = \dfrac{1}{3} \mathbf{b}
$$

Therefore, the vector projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,a & ={\text{comp}}_{b}\,a\cdot u \\  & =\sqrt{2}\cdot \frac{1}{3}b \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}b.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "5962a19e-bb12-54d8-b53a-24578711fa53" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9051 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "26031206-512a-5b41-90d5-299987889655" :step/math-academy-id 121755 :step/next {:db/id 17592186106650}} {:db/id 17592186107166 :tutorial/content "The **vector projection** of a vector $\mathbf{a}$ onto another vector $\mathbf{b}$ is the portion that the vector $\mathbf{a}$ extends along $\mathbf{b}.$

For example, consider two vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ shown below. Suppose we know that $|\mathbf{a}|=2,$ $|\mathbf{b}|=3,$ and the angle between the vectors is $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{4}.$

![](images/a2/a28278cf12885ab7f845407ac2fa7f4ffa00dbe30849a3f8ff41f02e134ed3a0.png)

The starting point of the vector projection is $O,$ and the ending point will be the point $P$ that lies on the line containing $\mathbf{b}$ with $AP \perp \mathbf{b},$ as shown below.

![](images/f0/f0b267fb009e79eb16f86be42edc2c835808b28aa3eaf1c7e857300224ee01ec.png)

The vector $\overrightarrow{OP}$ is called the **vector projection** of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}.$ It is denoted as $\text{proj}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a},$ and it is computed as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,a & =OP\cdot u \\  & ={\text{comp}}_{b}\,a\cdot u\end{aligned}
$$

where $\text{comp}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a} = |\,\mathbf{a}\,| \cos\theta$ is the scalar projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}$ and $\mathbf{u}$ is a unit vector in the direction of $\mathbf{b}.$

First, we compute the scalar projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{b}\,a & =|\,a\,|\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the unit vector that is parallel to $\mathbf{b}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\mathbf{u} = \dfrac{\mathbf{b}}{|\,\mathbf{b}\,|} = \dfrac{\mathbf{b}}{3} = \dfrac{1}{3} \mathbf{b}
$$

Therefore, the vector projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,a & ={\text{comp}}_{b}\,a\cdot u \\  & =\sqrt{2}\cdot \frac{1}{3}b \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}b.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "5962a19e-bb12-54d8-b53a-24578711fa53" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9051 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186106650 :step/content {:db/id 17592186107181 :tutorial/content "When finding the projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b},$ we sometimes find that the resulting projection vector points in the opposite direction to $\mathbf{b}.$ This happens when the vector $\mathbf{a}$ extends in the direction opposite to that of $\mathbf{b}.$

![](images/0e/0e973e6f6484a9aad863ebfe89fc1ea6356d6a50844931306c6aa2b63be18a8a.png)

Consider two vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b},$ where it is known that 

$$
|\,\mathbf{a}\,|=2,\qquad |\,\mathbf{b}\,|=3,\qquad \theta = 135^\circ.
$$

Let's calculate $\textrm{proj}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a}.$ 

First, notice that the angle between $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ is obtuse. This means we expect the projection vector to point in the opposite direction to that of $\mathbf b.$

Next, we compute the scalar projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{b}\,a & =|\,a\,|\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡({135}^{∘}) \\  & =2\cdot (-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) \\  & =-\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the scalar projection is negative. 

Then, we find the unit vector that is parallel to $\mathbf{b}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\mathbf{u} = \dfrac{\mathbf{b}}{|\,\mathbf{b}\,|} = \dfrac{\mathbf{b}}{3} = \dfrac{1}{3} \mathbf{b}
$$

Therefore, the vector projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,a & ={\text{comp}}_{b}\,a\cdot u \\  & =-\sqrt{2}\cdot \frac{1}{3}b \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}b.\end{aligned}
$$

This vector points in the direction opposite to $\mathbf{b},$ as expected." :tutorial/id #uuid "2df5fde5-316c-5962-8f0d-56362287c447" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9677 :tutorial/title "The Direction of the Projection Vector"} :step/id #uuid "fdc39c18-bf51-5a32-a828-404d1e341f7a" :step/math-academy-id 187844 :step/next {:db/id 17592186106563}} {:db/id 17592186106563 :step/content {:db/id 17592186105701 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186105478 :question/id #uuid "3278333b-a29e-54c5-bc94-b5525bc6f751" :question/math-academy-id "e-14617"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "7c9317eb-d1ce-5f42-b69b-a37e643b865b" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049360} {:db/id 17592186049653}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186106111} {:db/id 17592186106480} {:db/id 17592186287856} {:db/id 17592186287939} {:db/id 17592186292817} {:db/id 17592186292818} {:db/id 17592186297479} {:db/id 17592186297480} {:db/id 17592186339000} {:db/id 17592186339001} {:db/id 17592186339002} {:db/id 17592186441580} {:db/id 17592186441582} {:db/id 17592186441585} {:db/id 17592186441586}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating a Vector Projection Using Angle and Magnitude"} :step/id #uuid "e6fd410f-37e5-5a4e-a29d-c160c7d2a397" :step/math-academy-id 121756 :step/next {:db/id 17592186106564}} {:db/id 17592186106564 :step/content {:db/id 17592186107167 :tutorial/content "We have been using the following formula for the vector projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\text{proj}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a} =\text{comp}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{u}
$$

However, we can write an alternative formula using the formula for the scalar projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{b}\,a & =\frac{a\cdot b}{|\,b\,|}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the original formula for the vector projection, and also substituting $\mathbf{u} = \dfrac{\mathbf{b}}{| \, \mathbf{b} \, |},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,a & =\frac{a\cdot b}{|\,b\,|}\cdot \frac{b}{|\,b\,|} \\  & =\frac{a\cdot b}{|\,b\,{|}^{2}}b \\  & =\frac{a\cdot b}{b\cdot b}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, another general formula for the vector projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,a & =\frac{a\cdot b}{b\cdot b}b.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "e4098700-6d5c-5618-90a8-8dea2d4dbed0" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9052 :tutorial/title "A General Formula"} :step/id #uuid "a78e2420-8af1-50c7-9a19-b4ceac9bcde4" :step/math-academy-id 121759 :step/next {:db/id 17592186106565}} {:db/id 17592186107167 :tutorial/content "We have been using the following formula for the vector projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}\mathbin{:}$

Furthermore, we have the following fact:

Consider two vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b},$ where it is known that

$$

Notice that the scalar projection is negative. 

Then, we find the unit vector that is parallel to $\mathbf{b}\mathbin{:}$

\mathbf{u} = \dfrac{\mathbf{b}}{|\,\mathbf{b}\,|} = \dfrac{\mathbf{b}}{3} = \dfrac{1}{3} \mathbf{b}
$$

Therefore, the vector projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,a & ={\text{comp}}_{b}\,a\cdot u \\  & =-\sqrt{2}\cdot \frac{1}{3}b \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}b.\end{aligned}

This vector points in the direction opposite to $\mathbf{b},$ as expected." :tutorial/id #uuid "2df5fde5-316c-5962-8f0d-56362287c447" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9677 :tutorial/title "The Direction of the Projection Vector"} {:db/id 17592186059871 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186059422 :question/id #uuid "3625f2a9-3103-551e-b350-b0c83d9b241f" :question/math-academy-id "e-13039"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "997d255f-89af-5563-b10f-eecaae62d8c0" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049714}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186060380 :question/id #uuid "c1a5b299-faff-5d4c-81aa-f10fb4f8e0cd" :question/math-academy-id "q-68264"} {:db/id 17592186060381 :question/id #uuid "ea5e6910-d57e-5906-aecc-df42fa08ad0a" :question/math-academy-id "q-68266"}] :knowledge-point/title "Applying the Power Rule for Exponents With Integer Bases"} {:db/id 17592186059422 :question/id #uuid "3625f2a9-3103-551e-b350-b0c83d9b241f" :question/math-academy-id "e-13039" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186059871 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "997d255f-89af-5563-b10f-eecaae62d8c0" :knowledge-point/title "Applying the Power Rule for Exponents With Integer Bases"}] :question/problem "Express $5(5^2) \times 5^4$ as a base raised to a single exponent." :question/worked-solution "First, we write

$$
5(5^2) = 5^1 \times 5^2
$$

So our expression can be written as
$5^1 \times 5^2 \times 5^4$

To multiply powers of the same base, we simply add the exponents:

$$
5^1 \times 5^2 \times 5^4 = 5^{1+2+4} = 5^7
$$"} {:db/id 17592186060380 :question/id #uuid "c1a5b299-faff-5d4c-81aa-f10fb4f8e0cd" :question/math-academy-id "q-68264"} {:db/id 17592186060381 :question/id #uuid "ea5e6910-d57e-5906-aecc-df42fa08ad0a" :question/math-academy-id "q-68266"} {:db/id 17592186059872 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186059423 :question/id #uuid "edac9b20-71bf-544e-8e28-833c376097d5" :question/math-academy-id "e-13040"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "0aa91f9b-e324-557c-9a6b-fb3389bbeaf8" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186060379 :question/id #uuid "678be690-dbdd-53c9-ba17-1fa622e9f7f7" :question/math-academy-id "q-68079"} {:db/id 17592186060383 :question/id #uuid "544b38f7-745b-57d8-bc3d-22266cc44488" :question/math-academy-id "q-68299"}] :knowledge-point/title "Applying the Product Rule for Exponents With Fractional or Decimal Bases"} {:db/id 17592186059423 :question/id #uuid "edac9b20-71bf-544e-8e28-833c376097d5" :question/math-academy-id "e-13040" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186059872 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "0aa91f9b-e324-557c-9a6b-fb3389bbeaf8" :knowledge-point/title "Applying the Product Rule for Exponents With Fractional or Decimal Bases"}] :question/problem "Express $\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^2\times \left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^2$ as a base raised to a single exponent." :question/worked-solution "To multiply powers of the same base, we add the exponents:

$$
\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^2\times \left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^2 = \left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^{2+2} = \left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^4
$$"} {:db/id 17592186060379 :question/id #uuid "678be690-dbdd-53c9-ba17-1fa622e9f7f7" :question/math-academy-id "q-68079"} {:db/id 17592186060383 :question/id #uuid "544b38f7-745b-57d8-bc3d-22266cc44488" :question/math-academy-id "q-68299"} {:db/id 17592186059873 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186059424 :question/id #uuid "81027692-8570-59a6-a6f9-b31211baa681" :question/math-academy-id "e-13041"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "908d5434-7533-5d33-bc0d-99f4cc9dd44b" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050495}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186059954 :question/id #uuid "50b3ee94-84c8-5b9d-9c68-f53e4eb7f64b" :question/math-academy-id "q-100314"} {:db/id 17592186059955 :question/id #uuid "23138674-0223-5e27-8df4-e0fdbd55a86c" :question/math-academy-id "q-100318"} {:db/id 17592186060384 :question/id #uuid "88743230-6d06-57f0-81d0-31dfae837330" :question/math-academy-id "q-68319"}] :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating Products with Negative Exponents Using the Product Rule"} {:db/id 17592186059424 :question/id #uuid "81027692-8570-59a6-a6f9-b31211baa681" :question/math-academy-id "e-13041" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186059873 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "908d5434-7533-5d33-bc0d-99f4cc9dd44b" :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating Products with Negative Exponents Using the Product Rule"}] :question/problem "Evaluate $2^2\times 2^{-5}$." :question/worked-solution "To multiply powers of the same base, we add the exponents:

$$
2^2\times 2^{-5} =2^{2+(-5)} = 2^{-3}
$$

To evaluate $2^{-3}$, we find the reciprocal of the base $(2)$ and then raise that reciprocal to the same power but with the opposite sign:

$$
2^{-3} = \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^3 =\dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{1}{8}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186059954 :question/id #uuid "50b3ee94-84c8-5b9d-9c68-f53e4eb7f64b" :question/math-academy-id "q-100314"} {:db/id 17592186059955 :question/id #uuid This is called the **product rule for exponents**.
For example, in the expression

$$
{\color{blue}3}^4 \times {\color{blue}3}^2
$$

both powers have the same base $({\color{blue}3})$. Therefore, we can simplify this expression by adding the exponents:

$$
{\color{blue}3}^4 \times {\color{blue}3}^2 = {\color{blue}3}^{4+2} = {\color{blue}3}^6
$$

**Note:** The product rule for exponents is really just a quicker alternative to using repeated multiplication, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
3^{4} \cdot 3^{2} &=  \\
3 \cdot 3 \cdot 3 \cdot 3_(⏟)_(4copies) \cdot 3 \cdot 3_(⏟)_(2copies) &=  \\
3 \cdot 3 \cdot 3 \cdot 3 \cdot 3 \cdot 3_(⏟)_(6copies) &=  \\
&= 3^{6}
\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "3baed7a9-d08b-5c41-8d2c-77d4f4daf35d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8156 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "3f48be73-d211-5343-8cf8-db9420dc3457" :step/math-academy-id 72192 :step/next {:db/id 17592186060852}} {:db/id 17592186060852 :step/content {:db/id 17592186059871 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186059422 :question/id #uuid "3625f2a9-3103-551e-b350-b0c83d9b241f" :question/math-academy-id "e-13039"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "997d255f-89af-5563-b10f-eecaae62d8c0" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049714}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186060380} {:db/id 17592186060381}] :knowledge-point/title "Applying the Power Rule for Exponents With Integer Bases"} :step/id #uuid "16cd0938-867d-5ee4-8e29-6f087478cb3f" :step/math-academy-id 72193 :step/next {:db/id 17592186060853}} {:db/id 17592186060853 :step/content {:db/id 17592186059872 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186059423 :question/id #uuid "edac9b20-71bf-544e-8e28-833c376097d5" :question/math-academy-id "e-13040"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "0aa91f9b-e324-557c-9a6b-fb3389bbeaf8" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186060379} {:db/id 17592186060383}] :knowledge-point/title "Applying the Product Rule for Exponents With Fractional or Decimal Bases"} :step/id #uuid "5b9cd7c8-3ecb-51f1-93ab-7c849fe2f4c7" :step/math-academy-id 72196 :step/next {:db/id 17592186060854}} {:db/id 17592186060854 :step/content {:db/id 17592186060990 :tutorial/content "We can use the product rule for exponents with negative exponents too. $$
5 \div (-2)^{2}
$$

Applying PEMDAS to this expression, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}
5 \div (-2)^{2} &=  \\
5 \div 4 &=  \\
&= \frac{5}{4}
\end{aligned}
$$

$$

linear equations below, find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system.

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}-10 \\ -15 \\ 28\end{aligned}],\,{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}=0 \\ 2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}-3{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we need to find a basis of the solution space of the system. 

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & -3 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & -3 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are $2$ pivot columns ($1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. Now, from the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}=\frac{3}{5}{x}_{3}.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
{x}_{1}-2(\frac{3}{5}{x}_{3})=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=\frac{6}{5}{x}_{3}.
$$

So, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{6}{5}{x}_{3} \\ \frac{3}{5}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{5}{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 3 \\ 5\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Consequently, $B={[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 3 \\ 5\end{aligned}]}$ is a basis of the solution space of the system.

Finally, we find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot b}{b\cdot b}b \\  & =\frac{(-10)\cdot 6+(-15)\cdot 3+28\cdot 5}{{6}^{2}+{3}^{2}+{5}^{2}}b \\  & =\frac{-60-45+140}{36+9+25}b \\  & =\frac{35}{70}b \\  & =\frac{1}{2}b \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 3 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ \frac{3}{2} \\ \frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186134288 :question/id #uuid "c185f4ac-1057-5248-8964-7fb26d1dea03" :question/math-academy-id "q-40425"} {:db/id 17592186272025 :question/id #uuid {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Given the vector $x$ and the system of  linear equations below, find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system.

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -2\end{aligned}],\,{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}=0 \\ -2{x}_{1}+6{x}_{2}=0\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we need to find a basis of the solution space of the system. 

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 0 \\ -2 & 6 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is $1$ pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}=3{x}_{2}.$ So, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}3{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]={x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Consequently, $B={[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}$ is a basis of the solution space of the system.

Finally, we find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$

**orthogonal projection** of a vector $\mathbf{x}$ onto a span $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}\}$ is the vector in $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}\}$ that is "closest" to $\mathbf{x}.$ Let's work an example to clarify what we mean by "closest."

Consider the following two vectors:

$$
[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

 

Geometrically, $\mathbf{x}$ can be written as the sum of a vector $k{\mathbf{a}}$ that lies in $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}\}$ and 
another vector $\mathbf{z}$ that belongs to the orthogonal complement of $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}\}$, as illustrated in the picture below.

![](images/a4/a4754bf048aa6c05cd7ef574af306150c30d435f90afec36f492ed4b8013e899.png)

The vector $k\mathbf a$ is called the **orthogonal projection** of $\mathbf{x}$ onto $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}\}.$

Symbolically, we can write the vector $\mathbf{x}$ as the sum

$$
\mathbf{x} = k \mathbf{a} + \mathbf{z},
$$

for some $k \in \mathbb{R}$ and ${\mathbf{z}} \perp \mathbf{a}.$ 

To compute the orthogonal projection $k \mathbf{a},$ we can first find the dot product of both sides of the equation above with $\mathbf{a}$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}x\cdot a & =(ka+z)\cdot a \\ x\cdot a & =k(a\cdot a)+z\cdot a.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\mathbf{a} \perp \mathbf{z},$ we have $\mathbf{z} \cdot \mathbf{a} = 0.$ As a result,

$$
\begin{aligned}x\cdot a & =k(a\cdot a) \\ k & =\frac{x\cdot a}{a\cdot a} \\ k & =\frac{5\cdot 3+(-1)\cdot (-6)+0\cdot 0+1\cdot 6}{{3}^{2}+(-6)^{2}+{6}^{2}} \\ k & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the orthogonal projection is

$$
\begin{aligned}ka=\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -6 \\ 0 \\ 6\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** There is a shortcut! Instead of going through this process each time, we can compute the orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{x}$ onto $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}\}$ using the following formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{a}\,x & =\frac{a\cdot x}{a\cdot a}\,a\end{aligned}

:activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186134001} {:db/id 17592186134666 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135046 :tutorial/content "The **orthogonal projection** of a vector $\mathbf{x}$ onto a span $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}\}$ is the vector in $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}\}$ that is "closest" to $\mathbf{x}.$ Let's work an example to clarify what we mean by "closest."

Consider the following two vectors:

$$
[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

 

Geometrically, $\mathbf{x}$ can be written as the sum of a vector $k{\mathbf{a}}$ that lies in $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}\}$ and 
another vector $\mathbf{z}$ that belongs to the orthogonal complement of $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}\}$, as illustrated in the picture below.

![](images/a4/a4754bf048aa6c05cd7ef574af306150c30d435f90afec36f492ed4b8013e899.png)

The vector $k\mathbf a$ is called the **orthogonal projection** of $\mathbf{x}$ onto $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}\}.$

Symbolically, we can write the vector $\mathbf{x}$ as the sum

$$
\mathbf{x} = k \mathbf{a} + \mathbf{z},
$$

for some $k \in \mathbb{R}$ and ${\mathbf{z}} \perp \mathbf{a}.$ 

To compute the orthogonal projection $k \mathbf{a},$ we can first find the dot product of both sides of the equation above with $\mathbf{a}$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}x\cdot a & =(ka+z)\cdot a \\ x\cdot a & =k(a\cdot a)+z\cdot a.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\mathbf{a} \perp \mathbf{z},$ we have $\mathbf{z} \cdot \mathbf{a} = 0.$ As a result,

$$
\begin{aligned}x\cdot a & =k(a\cdot a) \\ k & =\frac{x\cdot a}{a\cdot a} \\ k & =\frac{5\cdot 3+(-1)\cdot (-6)+0\cdot 0+1\cdot 6}{{3}^{2}+(-6)^{2}+{6}^{2}} \\ k & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the orthogonal projection is

$$
\begin{aligned}ka=\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -6 \\ 0 \\ 6\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** There is a shortcut! Instead of going through this process each time, we can compute the orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{x}$ onto $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}\}$ using the following formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{a}\,x & =\frac{a\cdot x}{a\cdot a}\,a\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "8c57e0ac-99f7-5b01-ace0-7afa2449f0af" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3622 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "102b1c5a-b877-5357-9263-23e920a24266" :step/math-academy-id 20237 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134667}} {:db/id 17592186135046 :tutorial/content "The **orthogonal projection** of a vector $\mathbf{x}$ onto a span $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}\}$ is the vector in $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}\}$ that is "closest" to $\mathbf{x}.$ Let's work an example to clarify what we mean by "closest."

1\end{aligned}].$ Find the distance between $u$ and $\text{Span}{w}.$" :question/worked-solution "The distance between the vector $u$ and the vector space $\text{Span}{w}$ is given by $‖u-\overset{^}{u}‖$, where $\overset{^}{u}$ in the orthogonal projection of $u$ onto $\text{Span}{w}.$ 

First, we find the orthogonal projection of $u$ onto $\text{Span}{w}.$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{w}\,u & =\frac{w\cdot u}{w\cdot w}w \\  & =\frac{2\cdot 4+1\cdot 2+(-2)\cdot (-2)+1\cdot 6}{{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{1}^{2}}w \\  & =\frac{8+2+4+6}{4+1+4+1}w \\  & =\frac{20}{10}w \\  & =2w \\  & =2[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 2 \\ -4 \\ 2\end{aligned}]=\overset{^}{u}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}‖u-\overset{^}{u}‖ & =\sqrt{({u}_{1}-{\overset{^}{u}}_{1})^{2}+({u}_{2}-{\overset{^}{u}}_{2})^{2}+({u}_{3}-{\overset{^}{u}}_{3})^{2}+({u}_{4}-{\overset{^}{u}}_{4})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(4-4)^{2}+(2-2)^{2}+(-2-(-4))^{2}+(6-2)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{0+0+4+16} \\  & =\sqrt{20} \\  & =2\sqrt{5}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "62a4d3df-d96d-5ff1-bcdc-6b9572844deb" :step/next {:db/id 17592186417874}} {:db/id 17592186417874 :step/content {:db/id 17592186417871 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1eea3622-1f9b-5d11-8dea-d8c47cf376cc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "z=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186417843} {:answer/id #uuid "2667df2c-9f3d-591c-b400-004bf838a4aa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "z=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186417844} {:answer/id #uuid "7876d49c-79f4-5357-89f7-c467fcc3fef7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "z=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186417856} {:answer/id #uuid "9045d64a-6a59-57ea-bac4-733ec53b1337" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "z=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186417858} {:answer/id #uuid "c8161b4f-175c-56ad-8c8c-3bb5a54a6cf2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "z=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186417860}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186417860} :answer-field/id #uuid "5bd6575e-57c0-5c94-ab1b-632324adbb58" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186417866}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "3365c089-bf35-5299-ad47-d460e03b5d34" :question/math-academy-id "q-40381" :question/problem "Let $x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 7 \\ -6 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ and $a=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3 \\ -3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ If $x=y+z,$ where $y\in \text{Span}{a}$ and $z⊥\text{Span}{a},$ then $z=$" :question/worked-solution "![](images/d8/d887852fe51f08cb7296437e69b6a9632721cfd155558e6abf9a99b4f59f7ad6.png)

First, we find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto $\text{Span}{a}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{a}\,x & =\frac{a\cdot x}{a\cdot a}a \\  & =\frac{2\cdot 3+3\cdot 7+(-3)(-6)+1\cdot 1}{{2}^{2}+{3}^{2}+(-3)^{2}+{1}^{2}}a \\  & =\frac{6+21+18+1}{4+9+9+1}a \\  & =\frac{46}{23}a \\  & =2a \\  & =2[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3 \\ -3 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 6 \\ -6 \\ 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={\text{proj}}_{a}\,x=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 6 \\ -6 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\ z & =x-{\text{proj}}_{a}\,x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 7 \\ -6 \\ 1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 6 \\ -6 \\ 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

the exponents:

$$
a^n\cdot a^m=a^{n+m}
$$

For example,

$$
a^2\cdot a^3 = a^{2+3} = a^5
$$

To see why the product rule is true, let's take the above example and work it out again, the long way.

For the two factors $a^2$ and $a^3$ we have

$$
a^2=a\cdot a
$$

and

$$
a^3= a\cdot a\cdot a
$$

If we now substitute these two expressions into $a^2\cdot a^3$, we get the same result:

$$
\begin{aligned} a^2\cdot a^3 \\ &= (a\cdot a) \cdot (a\cdot a\cdot a) \\ &= a\cdot a\cdot a\cdot a\cdot a \\ &= a^5 \end{aligned}
$$

The product rule is just a shortcut for the process above." :tutorial/id #uuid "e5759844-cfcd-53d9-9411-c5a117bf0fc6" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1476 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid Consider the matrix $[\mathbf{T}]_{\mathcal{B}}$ of a linear transformation $\mathbf{T}$ with respect to the basis $\mathcal{B}$ and the change-of-coordinates matrix $P_{\small \mathcal{B} \to \mathcal{C}}$ shown above. Find the matrix of $\mathbf{T}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C}.$" :question/worked-solution "The connection between the matrices of our linear transformation $\mathbf{T}$ relative to the bases $\mathcal{B}$ and $\mathcal{C}$ is given by the following diagram:

![](images/1b/1b81504d6fdcabee0e1f586fef3dd2af5a57a8411ba4d22429e00e09b171a4d1.png)

 

Here, moving along an arrow means pre-multiplying by the corresponding matrix. Algebraically, we can write this as

$$
[\mathbf{T}]_{\mathcal{C}} = P_{\small{\mathcal{B}}\to{\mathcal{C}}} \cdot [\mathbf{T}]_{\mathcal{B}} \cdot P_{\small{\mathcal{B}}\to{\mathcal{C}}}^{-1}\,,
$$

where $P_{\small{\mathcal{B}}\to{\mathcal{C}}}$ is the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{C}.$

Our goal is to compute $[\mathbf{T}]_{\mathcal{C}}.$ First, we compute the inverse of $P_{\small{\mathcal{B}}\to{\mathcal{C}}} \mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to C}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{1\cdot 1-0\cdot (-1)}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can compute the matrix of $\mathbf{T}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C} \mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}[T]_{C} & ={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ 5 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & -7 \\ 5 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & -10 \\ 5 & 9\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186049548} {:db/id 17592186050407} {:db/id 17592186129630 :question/id #uuid "ba13dd29-8b1d-5a17-aa9e-1e011399048f" :question/math-academy-id "q-38096"} {:db/id 17592186129639 The change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{C}$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of vectors from $\mathcal{B}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C}.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of $\mathbf{b}_1$ and $\mathbf{b}_2$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C}.$ To do this, we consider the matrix

We reduce $M$ using Gaussian elimination until we get the identity matrix on the left. By doing this, we obtain the required change-of-coordinates matrix on the right.

$$

Here, moving along an arrow means pre-multiplying by the corresponding matrix. Algebraically, we can write this as

$$
[T]_{C}={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1},
$$

where ${P}_{B\to C}$ is the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C.$

First, let's denote the vectors of $B$ and $C$ as ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ and ${{c}_{1},{c}_{2}}$, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of vectors from $B$ relative to the basis $C.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ relative to the basis $C.$ To do this, we consider the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} & {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

We reduce $M$ using Gaussian elimination until we get the identity matrix on the left. By doing this, we obtain the required change-of-coordinates matrix on the right.

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -1 & -1 \\ -1 & 3 & 4 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+2{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 5 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}5 & 3 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to C}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to C}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}5 & 3 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\cdot 5-3\cdot 3}[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -3 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -3 & 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can compute the matrix of $T$ relative to the basis $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[T]_{C} & ={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 3 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & -3 \\ 4 & 6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -3 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}7 & 3 \\ 5 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -3 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & -6 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

$$
[T]_{C}={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1},
$$

where ${P}_{B\to C}$ is the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C.$

First, let's denote the vectors of $B$ and $C$ as ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ and ${{c}_{1},{c}_{2}}$, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of vectors from $B$ relative to the basis $C.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ relative to the basis $C.$ To do this, we consider the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} & {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

We reduce $M$ using Gaussian elimination until we get the identity matrix on the left. By doing this, we obtain the required change-of-coordinates matrix on the right.

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 8 & -5 \\ -2 & -3 & -7 & 4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 8 & -5 \\ 0 & 3 & 9 & -6\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 8 & -5 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 & -2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-3){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 & -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

[{:db/id 17592186129967 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130348 :tutorial/content "Recall that the matrices $[\mathbf{T}]_{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}$ and $[\mathbf{T}]_{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}$ of a linear transformation $\mathbf{T} : V \to V$ relative to two bases $\color{blue}\mathcal{B}$ and $\color{red}\mathcal{C}$ of a vector space $V$ are different.

If we are given the matrix $[\mathbf{T}]_{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}},$ how do we find the matrix $[\mathbf{T}]_{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}?$
To find $[\mathbf{T}]_{\color{red}\mathcal{C}},$ we use the change-of-coordinates matrix $P_{\small {\color{blue}\mathcal{B}} \to {\color{red}\mathcal{C}}}$ from $\color{blue}\mathcal{B}$ to ${\color{red}\mathcal{C}}.$

The diagram below is a commutative diagram that shows how a change of basis works at each step.

![](images/df/dff02d9f46eb7ded23f418765a50dd1971145cd0e585a82beeef1a45812df8a7.png)

Here, moving along an arrow means pre-multiplying by the corresponding matrix. So algebraically, we can write this as

$$
[\mathbf{T}]_{\color{red}\mathcal{C}} = P_{\small{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}\to{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}} \cdot [\mathbf{T}]_{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}} \cdot P_{\small{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}\to{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}}^{-1}.
$$

For instance, if $[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]$ and $[\begin{aligned}-1 & -3 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]$, we use this formula to obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}[T]_{C} & ={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -3 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}-1 & -3 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -3 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 7 \\ -2 & -3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the formula for $[\mathbf{T}]_{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}},$ we obtain the alternative formulation

$$
[\mathbf{T}]_{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}} = P_{\small{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}\to{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}}^{-1} \cdot [\mathbf{T}]_{\color{red}\mathcal{C}} \cdot P_{\small{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}\to{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}}.
$$

**Note:** Alternatively, if we know the change-of-coordinates matrix $P_{\small {\color{red}\mathcal{C}} \to {\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}}$ from $\color{red}\mathcal{C}$ to $\color{blue}\mathcal{B},$ we can construct a similar diagram:

![](images/d6/d6cd195ccd42804ea91debabd23563bb0f6903fdd1b5d708b712c75417fff2a9.png)

From this, we can derive the equation

$$
[\mathbf{T}]_{\color{red}\mathcal{C}} = P_{\small{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}\to{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}}^{-1} \cdot [\mathbf{T}]_{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}} \cdot P_{\small{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}\to{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}}.
$$

Solving this equation for $[\mathbf{T}]_{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}},$ we obtain the alternative formulation

$$
[\mathbf{T}]_{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}} =
	P_{\small{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}\to{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}} \cdot [\mathbf{T}]_{\color{red}\mathcal{C}} \cdot P_{\small{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}\to{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}}^{-1}.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "daf756b8-28df-5435-a304-0c32de77cc02" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3585 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "997bad3a-19a8-5b8c-ba06-b960fea4fabc" :step/math-academy-id 20144 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130108}} {:db/id 17592186129968 :step/content {:db/id 17592186129130 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186128941 :question/id #uuid "76ff3ea8-e07c-5dba-a9af-a4f68b03fadb" :question/math-academy-id "e-5516"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "61bd0b4f-165c-5f31-b4ec-e0eff7e758e1" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049548} {:db/id 17592186050407}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186129630} {:db/id 17592186129639} {:db/id 17592186326682} {:db/id 17592186360752} {:db/id 17592186360753} {:db/id 17592186375096} {:db/id 17592186388702} {:db/id 17592186395222} {:db/id 17592186395229} {:db/id 17592186395236} {:db/id 17592186419683}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Matrix of a Linear Transformation Relative to a Basis Using a Change-of-Coordinates Matrix"} :step/id #uuid "a9f19301-a016-578d-9241-cc7262d6f30f" :step/math-academy-id 20145 :step/next {:db/id 17592186129970}} {:db/id 17592186129969 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130349 :tutorial/content "Consider the bases $\color{blue}\mathcal{B}=\{ \mathbf{b}_1, \, \ldots, \, \mathbf{b}_n \}$ and $\color{red}\mathcal{C}=\{ \mathbf{c}_1, \, \ldots, \, \mathbf{c}_n \}$ of a vector space $V,$ and the matrix $[\mathbf{T}]_{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}$ of a linear transformation $\mathbf{T}$ with respect to the basis $\color{blue}\mathcal{B}.$
Then the matrix of $\mathbf{T}$ relative to the basis ${\color{red}\mathcal{C}}$ is given by

$$
[\mathbf{T}]_{\color{red}\mathcal{C}} =P_{\small {\color{blue}\mathcal{B}} \to {\color{red}\mathcal{C}}} \cdot [\mathbf{T}]_{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}} \cdot P_{\small {\color{blue}\mathcal{B}} \to {\color{red}\mathcal{C}}}^{-1},
$$

where $P_{\small {\color{blue}\mathcal{B}} \to {\color{red}\mathcal{C}}}$ is the change of basis matrix from ${\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}$ to ${\color{red}\mathcal{C}}.$

When written in expanded form, this formula becomes:

$$
[\begin{aligned}| &  & | \\ \,[T(\,{c}_{1}\,)]_{C} & \,\,\,\,⋯\,\,\,\, & [T(\,{c}_{n}\,)]_{C}\, \\ | &  & |\end{aligned}]
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "f7eacd50-63e4-53d3-9c15-d3a1b6a42ad1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3586 :tutorial/title "The Expanded Form of the Change of Basis"} :step/id #uuid Here, moving along an arrow means pre-multiplying by the corresponding matrix. Algebraically, we can write this as

$$
[T]_{S}={P}_{B\to S}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to S}^{-1},
$$

and the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

First, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to S}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to S}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3\cdot 1-2\cdot 2}[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 2 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can compute the matrix of $T$ relative to the standard basis $S:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[T]_{S} & ={P}_{B\to S}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to S}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-3 & 2 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-3 & 2 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & -3 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "0b2e1e0a-a93e-5b2b-ba4a-b6011da00e9b" :step/next {:db/id 17592186419689}} {:db/id 17592186419688 :step/content {:db/id 17592186129640 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "03a7c2b7-b4a3-5168-84dc-aab27f106193" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186448614} {:answer/id #uuid "2902f1ff-cac7-5d97-a5a9-24543413f25f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186448615}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186448615} :answer-field/id #uuid "918a8f88-e411-59fb-b196-0dadf7f4fcbc" :answer-field/key "I" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186449347} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "533a5b8f-639e-5a45-8484-cb33ae7d5e46" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186448616} {:answer/id #uuid "e69f24f0-07c6-5983-ac28-bd000fd09e27" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186448617}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186448616} :answer-field/id #uuid "54d6a6ae-1fa2-556d-9175-9c73166225ee" :answer-field/key "II" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186449348} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "c2c7db1c-97d8-53db-84ae-5422607ceccf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186448618} {:answer/id #uuid "3c254231-3e39-568b-8359-80c766da4887" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186448619}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186448619} :answer-field/id #uuid "db2048e9-209c-59b8-a528-935ef72da977" :answer-field/key "III" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186449349}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "4a7452af-fe2e-5944-8a03-a396c12645a4" :question/math-academy-id "q-38360" :question/problem "Let $[T]_{B}$ and $[T]_{C}$ be the matrices of a linear transformation $T$ relative to the bases $B$ and $C,$ respectively. Here, moving along an arrow means pre-multiplying by the corresponding matrix. Algebraically, we can write this as

$$
[T]_{C}={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1},
$$

where ${P}_{B\to C}$ is the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C.$

First, let's denote the vectors of $B$ and $C$ as ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ and ${{c}_{1},{c}_{2}}$, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of vectors from $B$ relative to the basis $C.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ relative to the basis $C.$ To do this, we consider the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} & {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

We reduce $M$ using Gaussian elimination until we get the identity matrix on the left. By doing this, we obtain the required change-of-coordinates matrix on the right.

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0 & -1 \\ -2 & -1 & 3 & -4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 3 & 3 & -6\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & -2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-2){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to C}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to C}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{(-2)\cdot (-2)-1\cdot 3}[\begin{aligned}-2 & -3 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -3 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can compute the matrix of $T$ relative to the basis $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[T]_{C} & ={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 3 \\ 2 & 5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-2 & -3 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 9 \\ 0 & -7\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-2 & -3 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & -12 \\ 7 & 14\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "49084fac-fe76-5f2f-8b13-058b89e81921" :step/next {:db/id 17592186419691}} {:db/id 17592186419690 :step/content {:db/id 17592186419686 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "573ba886-20ef-53c9-9024-a795a327b2ea" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186454244} {:answer/id #uuid "75fa156d-1a39-536a-ab92-cd46c3d568a6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186454245}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186454245} :answer-field/id #uuid "6c352d4a-a883-55eb-8913-4568682a7132" :answer-field/key "I" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186454872} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "a493b3a0-15e1-540d-9b9a-49e179799c67" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186454246} {:answer/id #uuid "6b0b13f5-b674-5518-b581-93c06913cf58" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186454247}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186454246} :answer-field/id #uuid "139440a5-d4e1-5ab8-ba4c-c3d86f2c0c74" :answer-field/key "II" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186454873} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "41af9a8e-a9d1-5b00-b3e8-b95a4c022fcf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186454248} {:answer/id #uuid "3a437d50-f3c9-5ac5-8e9a-de9b7e0b61f0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186454249}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186454249} :answer-field/id #uuid "08c42cdc-f60a-5dff-99c5-7c1367615b5d" :answer-field/key "III" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186454874}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "e737a421-d643-51f0-9d67-b9556fcc15c6" :question/math-academy-id "q-97060" :question/problem "Let $[T]_{B}$ and $[T]_{C}$ be the matrices of a linear transformation $T$ relative to the bases $B$ and $C,$ respectively. $$
[T]_{C}={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1},
$$

where ${P}_{B\to C}$ is the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C.$

First, let's denote the vectors of $B$ and $C$ as ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ and ${{c}_{1},{c}_{2}}$, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of vectors from $B$ relative to the basis $C.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ relative to the basis $C.$ To do this, we consider the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} & {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

We reduce $M$ using Gaussian elimination until we get the identity matrix on the left. By doing this, we obtain the required change-of-coordinates matrix on the right.

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0 & -1 \\ -2 & -1 & 3 & -4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 3 & 3 & -6\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & -2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-2){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$

![](images/1b/1b81504d6fdcabee0e1f586fef3dd2af5a57a8411ba4d22429e00e09b171a4d1.png)

 

Here, moving along an arrow means pre-multiplying by the corresponding matrix. Algebraically, we can write this as

$$
[T]_{C}={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1}\,,
$$

where ${P}_{B\to C}$ is the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C.$

Our goal is to compute $[T]_{C}.$ First, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to C}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to C}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{1\cdot 1-(-2)\cdot (-1)}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can compute the matrix of $T$ relative to the basis $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[T]_{C} & ={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ 4 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -4 \\ 0 & 7\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}10 & 6 \\ -14 & -7\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "bf368b08-5b21-5ea2-9201-b8d34ec52b51"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "573ba886-20ef-53c9-9024-a795a327b2ea" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" $a{x}^{3},$ where $a\in R.$ Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** The zero-polynomial belongs to $U.$

- **II.** For any $p(x),q(x)\in U,$ we have $p(x)+q(x)=q(x)+p(x).$

- **III.** For any $p(x),q(x),r(x)\in U,$ we have $[p(x)-q(x)]-r(x)=p(x)-[q(x)-r(x)].$" :question/worked-solution "Let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the zero-polynomial can be represented as 

$$
0=0\cdot {x}^{3}.
$$

 
Hence, $0\in U.$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, for any polynomials $p(x),q(x)\in U,$ we obtain that 

$$
p(x)+q(x)=q(x)+p(x)
$$

since polynomial addition is commutative.

- Statement III is false. For example, consider polynomials $p(x)={x}^{3},$ $q(x)=2{x}^{3},$ and $r(x)=3{x}^{3}$ from $U.$ Then: 

$$
\begin{aligned}[p(x)-q(x)]-r(x) & =[{x}^{3}-2{x}^{3}]-3{x}^{3} \\  & =-{x}^{3}-3{x}^{3} \\  & =-4{x}^{3} \\ p(x)-[q(x)-r(x)] & ={x}^{3}-[2{x}^{3}-3{x}^{3}] \\  & ={x}^{3}-[-{x}^{3}] \\  & =2{x}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $[p(x)-q(x)]-r(x)\ne p(x)-[q(x)-r(x)].$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only.""} {:db/id 17592186243917 :question/id #uuid "0880be83-dbd5-5dc8-a3cc-bdb045c80795" :question/math-academy-id "q-106684"} {:db/id 17592186243920 :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Let $C$ be the set of all polynomials $p(x)$ such that $p(0)<0.$  Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** The zero-polynomial belongs to $C.$
- **II.** For any $p(x),q(x)\in C,$ we have $p(x)+q(x)=q(x)+p(x).$
- **III.** The addition of polynomials in $C$ is associative." :question/worked-solution "Let's verify the statements one by one.

- Statement I is false. The set $C$ contains only polynomials that evaluate to a negative number at $0.$ However, the zero-polynomial is *not* such a polynomial, as it equals $0≮0$ at $0.$ So, $0\notin C.$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, for any polynomials $p(x),q(x)\in C,$ we obtain that

$$
p(x)+q(x)=q(x)+p(x)
$$

since polynomial addition is commutative.

- Statement III is true. Indeed, for any polynomials $p(x),q(x),r(x)\in C,$ we obtain that

$$
[p(x)+q(x)]+r(x)=p(x)+[q(x)+r(x)]
$$

since polynomial addition is associative.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only.""} {:db/id 17592186281463 :question/id #uuid "f9060a6c-635e-5bea-91ee-1f014ee29783" :question/math-academy-id "q-162391"} {:db/id 17592186281464 - Statement II is true. Indeed, as for any $2\times 2$ matrix $A,$ with real entries, we have

$$
A+O=A.
$$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, For any matrices $A,B\in F$ we obtain that 

$$

$$

since matrix addition is commutative.

- **I.** For any $f(x)\in G,$ we have $1\cdot f(x)=f(x).$
- **II.** For any $f(x)\in G$ and $\alpha ,\beta \in R$, we have $(\alpha -\beta )f(x)=\alpha f(x)-\beta f(x).$
- **III.** The scalar multiplication of functions in $G$ is associative." :question/worked-solution "Let's examine each of our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, for any $f(x)\in G$ and for any fixed $x\in R,$ the result of $f(x)$ is just a real number. Thus,

$$
(1\cdot f)(x)=1\cdot f(x)=f(x).
$$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, for any $f(x)\in G$ and for any fixed $x\in R,$ the result of $f(x)$ is just a real number. Thus, for any $\alpha ,\beta \in R,$ we obtain that

$$
(\alpha -\beta )f(x)=\alpha f(x)-\beta f(x).
$$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, for any $f(x)\in G$ and for any fixed $x\in R,$ the result of $f(x)$ is just a real number. Thus, for any $\alpha ,\beta \in R,$ we obtain that

$$
\alpha (\beta f(x))=(\alpha \beta )f(x).
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III.""} {:db/id 17592186281525 :question/id #uuid "ff69a5c1-505a-5719-b6b9-7ec69e0931ef" :question/math-academy-id "q-162664" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "7e2779fb-9930-5fcd-bcd1-7e1f1104d4a0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186450066} {:answer/id #uuid "91b3e3fc-389a-585f-96b5-7db78750f42a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186450067}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186450067} :answer-field/id #uuid "5f7c9859-71fa-5115-a310-1182f4bf63bc" :answer-field/key "I" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186450987} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "662847ba-aeb6-5cbd-8649-2265e32224d0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186450068} {:answer/id #uuid "bf79e41d-5399-5862-8d64-f981b0f2cf1c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186450069}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186450069} :answer-field/id #uuid "b083e9d7-fb4e-5c84-9a1a-a1c99a0f9d6c" :answer-field/key "II" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186450988} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "69cd0a9e-9920-5b05-8ece-dcad3cae55ae" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186450070} {:answer/id #uuid "dc7468af-0186-5e65-ab49-7c01cd3fc068" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186450071}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186450071} :answer-field/id #uuid "b050593e-e59b-5bdf-835e-4f773eafb358" :answer-field/key "III" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186450989}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Let $Q$ be the set of all functions of the form $f(x)=a{x}^{2},$ where $a\in R.$ Which of the following statements are true?

$$

:question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Let $R$ be the set of all $2\times 2$ matrices of the form $[\begin{aligned}a & b \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],$ where $a,b\in R.$ Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** For any $A\in R,$ we have $1\cdot A=A.$

- **II.** For any $A\in R,$ we have $-1(-1\cdot A)=-A.$

- **III.** For any $A\in R$ and $\alpha ,\beta \in R$, we have $(\alpha +\beta )A=\alpha A+\beta A.$" :question/worked-solution "Let's examine each of our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, for any $2\times 2$ real matrix $A=({a}_{ij})\in R$ with real entries, we have

$$
1\cdot {a}_{ij}={a}_{ij}
$$

and, hence,

$$
1\cdot A=A.
$$

- Statement II is false. For example, consider the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]$ from $R.$  Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}-1(-1\cdot A) & =-1(-1\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]) \\  & =-1([\begin{aligned}(-1)\cdot 1 & (-1)\cdot 2 \\ (-1)\cdot 0 & (-1)\cdot 1\end{aligned}]) \\  & =-1\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}(-1)\cdot (-1) & (-1)\cdot (-2) \\ (-1)\cdot 0 & (-1)\cdot (-1)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =A\ne -A.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statements III is true. Indeed, for any $2\times 2$ matrix $A=({a}_{ij})\in R,$ the entries are just real numbers. Thus, for any $\alpha ,\beta \in R,$ we obtain that

$$
(\alpha +\beta ){a}_{ij}=\alpha {a}_{ij}+\beta {a}_{ij},
$$

and hence,

$$
(\alpha +\beta )A=\alpha A+\beta A.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only.""} {:db/id 17592186360476 :question/id #uuid "0778fc80-bc7a-5da8-b455-9670cb2d5afb" :question/math-academy-id "q-94711" :knowledge-point/_questions - **I.** For any $p(x),q(x)\in L,$ we have $2(p(x)+q(x))=2p(x)-2q(x).$
- **II.** For any $p(x)\in L$ and $\alpha ,\beta \in R,$ we have $(\alpha +\beta )p(x)=\alpha p(x)+\beta p(x).$
- **III.** For any $p(x)\in L,$ we have $1\cdot p(x)=p(x).$" :question/worked-solution "Let's examine each of our statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. For example, consider the polynomials $p(x)=x+1$ and $q(x)=x-1$ from $L.$ Then:

$$
\begin{aligned}2(p(x)+q(x)) & =2(x+1+x-1) \\  & =2(2x) \\  & =4x \\ 2p(x)-2q(x) & =2(x+1)-2(x-1) \\  & =2x+2-2x+2 \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, for any $p(x)\in L$ and for any fixed $x\in R,$ the result of $p(x)$ is just a real number. Thus, for any $\alpha ,\beta \in R,$ we obtain that

$$
(\alpha +\beta )p(x)=\alpha p(x)+\beta p(x).
$$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, for any $p(x)\in L$ and for any fixed $x\in R,$ the result of $p(x)$ is just a real number. Thus,

$$
1\cdot p(x)=p(x).
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only.""} {:db/id 17592186360478 :question/id #uuid "03514ad7-d8b6-5b82-8d41-07ae43d6027c" :question/math-academy-id "q-94723"} {:db/id 17592186360481 :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186454515}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Let $R$ be the set of all $2\times 2$ matrices of the form $[\begin{aligned}{a}^{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],$ where $a\in Z.$ Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** For any $A\in R,$ we have $(-1)\cdot A\in R.$

- **II.** For any $A\in R,$ we have $2\cdot A\in R.$

- **III.** For any $A\in R$ and $\alpha \in R$, we have $(\alpha +1)A=\alpha A+A.$" :question/worked-solution "Let's examine each of our statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. For example,the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\in R,$ since $4={2}^{2}$ and $2\in Z.$ However

$$
(-1)\cdot A=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]\notin R,
$$

because a negative number ($-4$) can't be a square.

- Statement II is false. For example, consider the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]$ from $R.$ Then, we have 

$$
2\cdot A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]\notin R
$$

because the $22$-entry of $2\cdot A$ is not equal to $1.$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, for any $2\times 2$ matrix $A=({a}_{ij})\in R,$ the entries are just real numbers. Thus, for any $\alpha \in R,$ we obtain that

$$
(\alpha +1){a}_{ij}=\alpha {a}_{ij}+{a}_{ij},
$$

and hence,

$$
(\alpha +1)A=\alpha A+A.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only.""} {:db/id 17592186124628 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186124432 :question/id #uuid "ff4fdeaf-bdb3-54d7-b5e9-2f3ad88b55a1" :topic/math-academy-id 1906} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186125341 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125759 :tutorial/content "Let's now compare some properties of addition in $\mathbb{R}^2$ and $\text{M}_2(\mathbb{R}).$ 
It turns out that the addition of two matrices in $\mathrm{M}_2(\mathbb{R})$ is *very* similar to the addition of two vectors in $\mathbb{R}^n.$ See the table below.

<table align="center" cellpadding="10" rules="all" width="700">
<tbody><tr>
<td align="center" width="30"><b></b></td>
<td align="center" bgcolor="#D6EAF8" width="200"><b>$\mathbb{R}^2$</b></td>
<td align="center" bgcolor="#D6EAF8" width="200"><b>$\text{M}_2(\mathbb{R})$</b></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td align="center" colspan="3"><strong>Addition is Commutative:</strong></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td align="center" bgcolor="#D6EAF8">A1</td>
<td align="center">For any vectors $\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^2,$ we have $\color{blue}\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{v}+\mathbf{u}$</td>
<td align="center">For any matrices $A, B \in \text{M}_2(\mathbb{R}),$ we have $\color{blue}A+B = B+A$</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td align="center" colspan="3"><strong>Addition is Associative:</strong></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td align="center" bgcolor="#D6EAF8">A2</td>
<td align="center">For any vectors $\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{w} \in \mathbb{R}^2,$ we have $\color{blue}(\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v})+\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{u}+(\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{w})$</td>
<td align="center">For any matrices $A, B, C \in \text{M}_2(\mathbb{R}),$ we have $\color{blue}(A+B) + C = A + (B+C)$</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td align="center" colspan="3"><strong>Existence of a Unique Zero Element:</strong></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td align="center" bgcolor="#D6EAF8">A3</td>
<td align="center">For the zero-vector $\mathbf{0}$ and any $\mathbf{u} \in \mathbb{R}^2,$ we have $\color{blue} \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{0} = \mathbf{u}$</td>
<td align="center">For the zero-matrix $O$ and any $A \in \text{M}_2(\mathbb{R}),$ we have $\color{blue} A + O = A$</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td align="center" colspan="3"><strong>Existence of a Unique Opposite Element:</strong></td>
</tr>
<tr><td align="center" bgcolor="#D6EAF8">A4</td>
<td align="center">For any vector $\mathbf{u} \in \mathbb{R}^2$ we can find the corresponding negative vector $-\mathbf{u} \in \mathbb{R}$ such that $\color{blue} \mathbf{u} + (-\mathbf{u}) = \mathbf{0}$</td>
<td align="center">For any matrix $A \in \text{M}_2(\mathbb{R})$ we can find the corresponding negative matrix $-A \in \text{M}_2(\mathbb{R})$ such that $\color{blue} A + (-A) = O$</td>
</tr>
</tbody></table>

And it's not just matrices that have additive properties similar to those of $\mathbb R^n.$ Many mathematical structures do. Let's see some more examples." :tutorial/id #uuid "e21e1a72-75b8-5ae3-9b7d-96f08d2ffa86" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3184 :tutorial/title "Addition of Vectors"} :step/id #uuid some properties of scalar multiplication in $\mathbb{R}^2$ and $\text{M}_2(\mathbb{R}).$ It turns out that the multiplication of a matrix in $\mathrm{M}_2(\mathbb{R})$ by a scalar is *very* similar to the multiplication of a vector in $\mathbb{R}^n$ by a real number. See the table below.

<table align="center" cellpadding="10" rules="all" width="700">
<tbody><tr>
<td align="center" width="30"><b></b></td>
<td align="center" bgcolor="#D6EAF8" width="200"><b>$\mathbb{R}^2$</b></td>
<td align="center" bgcolor="#D6EAF8" width="200"><b>$\text{M}_2(\mathbb{R})$</b></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td align="center" colspan="3"><strong>Invariance Under Multiplication by $1$:</strong></td>
</tr>
<tr><td align="center" bgcolor="#D6EAF8">A5</td>
<td align="center">For any vector $\mathbf{u} \in \mathbb{R}^2$, we have $\color{blue} 1 \cdot \mathbf{u} = \mathbf{u}$</td>
<td align="center">For any matrix $A \in \text{M}_2(\mathbb{R})$, we have $\color{blue} 1 \cdot A = A$</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td align="center" colspan="3"><strong>Scalar Multiplication is Associative:</strong></td>
</tr>
<tr><td align="center" bgcolor="#D6EAF8">A6</td>
<td align="center">For any numbers $\alpha, \beta$ and any vector $\mathbf{u} \in \mathbb{R}^2$, we have $\color{blue} \alpha (\beta \mathbf{u}) = (\alpha\beta) \mathbf{u}$</td>
<td align="center">For any numbers $\alpha, \beta$ and any matrix $A \in \text{M}_2(\mathbb{R})$, we have $\color{blue} \alpha (\beta A) = (\alpha\beta) A$</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td align="center" colspan="3"><strong>Distributive Laws:</strong></td>
</tr>
<tr><td align="center" bgcolor="#D6EAF8">A7</td>
<td align="center">For any numbers $\alpha, \beta$ and any vector $\mathbf{u} \in \mathbb{R}^2$, we have $\color{blue} (\alpha + \beta)\mathbf{u} = \alpha \mathbf{u} + \beta \mathbf{u}$</td>
<td align="center">For any numbers $\alpha, \beta$ and any matrix $A \in \text{M}_2(\mathbb{R})$, we have $\color{blue} (\alpha + \beta)A = \alpha A + \beta A$</td>
</tr>
<tr><td align="center" bgcolor="#D6EAF8">A8</td>
<td align="center">For any number $\alpha$ and any vectors $\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^2$, we have $\color{blue} \alpha (\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}) = \alpha \mathbf{u} + \alpha \mathbf{v}$</td>
<td align="center">For any number $\alpha$ and any matrices $A, B \in \text{M}_2(\mathbb{R})$, we have $\color{blue} \alpha (A + B) = \alpha A + \alpha B$</td>
</tr>
</tbody></table>" :tutorial/id #uuid "05cdf1b2-a823-5410-8df1-42fa4da19240" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4934 :tutorial/title "Scalar Multiplication and the Distributive Laws"} :step/id #uuid "605b2c91-28e4-589e-9ea6-93545635ab1c" :step/math-academy-id 30789 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125521}} {:db/id 17592186125523 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125833 :tutorial/content "The structure $\mathbb{R}^n$ is called a **vector space**. However, many other structures possess properties similar to $\mathbb{R}^n.$ These other structures can be called vector spaces too. 

In this lesson, we'll learn about some important properties used to construct vector spaces. We begin by discussing what it means for a set to be **closed** under addition and scalar multiplication.

As an example, consider the set $\mathrm{M}_2(\mathbb{R})$ of all $2 \times 2$ matrices with real entries:

![](images/a5/a53ec7e9416ae5eee4a1408df358302567a5aa98a393d6ddcb19e861645d2317.svg)

For this set of matrices, we can define two operations:

- the addition of two matrices, and

- the multiplication of a matrix by a real number (called a scalar).

Now, notice the following:

- $\mathrm{M}_2(\mathbb{R})$ is **closed under addition**. This means that the sum of *any* two matrices from $\mathrm{M}_2(\mathbb{R})$ is also a matrix in $\mathrm{M}_2(\mathbb{R}).$

- $\mathrm{M}_2(\mathbb{R})$ is **closed under scalar multiplication**. This means that the product of *any* scalar and *any* matrix from $\mathrm{M}_2(\mathbb{R})$ is also a matrix in $\mathrm{M}_2(\mathbb{R}).$

Identifying that a set is closed under addition and scalar multiplication is an essential first step in determining whether a set can form a vector space." :tutorial/id #uuid "18653f19-b4cf-5f0f-ab39-b1ae33ecdc6b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4935 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "befa8020-1248-59aa-b092-5fd7f5b45c2e" :step/math-academy-id 30790 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125600}} {:db/id 17592186125590 :step/content {:db/id 17592186124628 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186124432 :question/id #uuid "ff4fdeaf-bdb3-54d7-b5e9-2f3ad88b55a1" :question/math-academy-id "e-9960"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "cb02b67c-90d9-5baf-b00e-590e9271d89e" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049304} {:db/id 17592186049755} {:db/id 17592186050782} {:db/id 17592186050979}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186125240} {:db/id 17592186125241} {:db/id 17592186278339} {:db/id 17592186278340} {:db/id 17592186278341} {:db/id 17592186278342} {:db/id 17592186281458} {:db/id 17592186323707} {:db/id 17592186329743} {:db/id 17592186440653} {:db/id 17592186440654} {:db/id 17592186440655} {:db/id 17592186445223}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Sets Closed Under Addition and Scalar Multiplication"} :step/id #uuid "78f1d4af-7528-5705-8b7b-224b627efd47" :step/math-academy-id 37506 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125341}} {:db/id 17592186125600 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125860 :tutorial/content "It's important to realize that not all sets are closed under addition and scalar multiplication. Sets not closed under addition and scalar multiplication *cannot* be vector spaces. 

For instance, let $S$ be the set of all polynomials with real coefficients whose degree is greater than or equal to $5.$  

We note that $S$ is not closed under addition. To see why this is the case, let's define the polynomials $p(x),q(x)\in S$ as 

$$
p(x) = x^5, \qquad q(x) = 1-x^5.
$$

Adding the two polynomials using regular polynomial addition, we get

$$
p(x) + q(x) = x^5 + (1-x^5) = 1\notin S
$$

The sum $p(x) + q(x)$ is not in $S$ because it is a polynomial of degree zero, which is less than $5.$

Therefore, we conclude that our set $S$ is *not* closed under addition." :tutorial/id #uuid "b014039e-61b6-58d7-8f35-a72e6153c126" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6230 :tutorial/title "Sets That Are Not Closed"} :step/id #uuid "1402186a-b64d-5406-9767-99815ff7ecc1" :step/math-academy-id 37838 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125590}} {:db/id 17592186125601 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125861 :tutorial/content "In this lesson, we discussed several properties exhibited by vectors in $\mathbb R^n$ and other sets.
Let's consolidate these properties into a single list.

| **Label** | **Name** | **Description** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A1 | **Addition is Commutative** | For any vectors $\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^2,$ we have $\color{blue}\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{v}+\mathbf{u}$ |
| A2 | **Addition is Associative** | For any vectors $\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{w} \in \mathbb{R}^2,$ we have $\color{blue}(\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v})+\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{u}+(\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{w})$ |
| A3 | **Existence of a Unique Zero Element** | For the zero-vector $\mathbf{0}$ and any $\mathbf{u} \in \mathbb{R}^2,$ we have $\color{blue} \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{0} = \mathbf{u}$ |
| A4 | **Existence of a Unique Opposite Element** | For any vector $\mathbf{u} \in \mathbb{R}^2$ we can find the corresponding negative vector $-\mathbf{u} \in \mathbb{R}$ such that $\color{blue} \mathbf{u} + (-\mathbf{u}) = \mathbf{0}$ |
| A5 | **Invariance Under Multiplication by $1$** | For any vector $\mathbf{u} \in \mathbb{R}^2$, we have $\color{blue} 1 \cdot \mathbf{u} = \mathbf{u}$ |
| A6 | **Scalar Multiplication is Associative** | For any numbers $\alpha, \beta$ and any vector $\mathbf{u} \in \mathbb{R}^2$, we have $\color{blue} \alpha (\beta \mathbf{u}) = (\alpha\beta) \mathbf{u}$ |
| A7 | **Distributive Laws:** | For any numbers $\alpha, \beta$ and any vector $\mathbf{u} \in \mathbb{R}^2$, we have $\color{blue} (\alpha + \beta)\mathbf{u} = \alpha \mathbf{u} + \beta \mathbf{u}$ |
| A8 | **Distributive Laws:** | For any number $\alpha$ and any vectors $\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^2$, we have $\color{blue} \alpha (\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}) = \alpha \mathbf{u} + \alpha \mathbf{v}$ |

We'll meet these properties again in a future lesson, where we'll formally define what we mean by a vector space." :tutorial/id #uuid "72e9ea87-7b8e-5d00-821a-31813b203a2b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6231 :tutorial/title "A Summary of the Addition and Scalar Multiplication Properties of Euclidian Space"} :step/id #uuid "be30c408-bfbc-549b-b14c-3f8724059c1b" :step/math-academy-id 37839}] :activity/title "Introduction to Abstract Vector Spaces" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186124706} {:db/id 17592186125523 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125833 :tutorial/content "The structure $\mathbb{R}^n$ is called a **vector space**.
